papers.title: TRAIL: A Human–AI Teaming Research Platform
papers.authors: Mohammad Amin Samadi, Aziz Rangwala, Nia Nixon
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: TRAIL (Team Research and AI Integration Lab) is a research platform for studying human–AI teamwork and collaborative learning in postsecondary contexts. The system enables multi-condition experiments where human participants work together on a collaborative task with or without an AI teammate. AI teammate behaviors are configured through a personality interface grounded in the Big Five framework. TRAIL provides real-time team chat, automated team formation, integrated survey workflows, experiment chaining for longitudinal designs, and multi-level analytics. Its dual-memory architecture maintains coherent AI behavior across extended interactions, while rich datasets capture communication, trust, and team dynamics. This demo showcases how TRAIL functions as both a classroom and research tool, enabling controlled studies of collaboration, persona alignment, and group processes.

papers.title: TeamLearn: A Multimodal, AI-enhanced Dashboard for Reflection During Collaborative Problem-Solving
papers.authors: Rogers Kaliisa, Crina Damşa, Jan Arild Dolonen, Malcolm Langford, Runar Hilleren Lie, Terje Kristian Lian Thoresen, Richard Nesnass, Krishna Siddharth Rajasekaran
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: This demo presents TeamLearn, a multimodal collaboration analytics dashboard designed to facilitate reflection and provide feedback on developing group artifacts during long- term collaborative problem-solving projects. By integrating meetings, documents, and collaboration experience analytics, the dashboard offers visualisations that help groups monitor participation, task progress, and collaboration dynamics. Developed through a design-based research process, the TeamLearn dashboard provides structured opportunities for reflective dialogue. The demo will showcase the dashboard’s core features and illustrate how it can be integrated into collaborative project activities.

papers.title: Transformative Disruptions: Using Call-In Strategies To Enact Solidarity In Community Partnerships
papers.authors: Chasity Mayo, LuEttaMae Lawrence, Stephen Kwiatek, Indu Garg
papers.design_stakeholders: Special Education Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: As the Learning Sciences have continued discussing subtle nuances related to community partnerships, there has been emphasis on how to enact solidarity, healing, and care. In this piece, we reflect on our enactments of solidarity and care by sharing about moments of calling-in, which we refer to as moments of curiously challenging. We use examples from our co-design sessions to showcase how call -ins function as transformative disruptions of harmful knowledges and how these moments are situated within other relationship building practices. We call on other scholars within the Learning Sciences community to consider the complexities surrounding systemized mindsets and how to attend to harmful productions and reproductions of knowledge within community-based partnerships.

papers.title: Learning With and About AI: Building Capacity for Equitable Participation in an AI-Shaped Future
papers.authors: Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: My research investigates how learners and educators understand, design with, and collaborate with AI systems, and how these sociotechnical interactions shape equity and participation. Using design-based research, participatory design, and qualitative and computational methods, I study AI education and disciplinary integration of AI in K–12 contexts. My work aims to design equitable learning environments, develop theoretical models of learner engagement with AI, and build cross-disciplinary approaches to teaching with and about AI. Theoretical and methodological foundations that inform my work My research sits at the intersection of the learning sciences, data science and artificial intelligence (AI) education. I am particularly interested in how educators and learners understand, design with, and collaborate with AI systems, and how these sociotechnical interactions shape equity and participation in society. In my work, I frame learning as a socially and materially mediated practice, drawing on sociocultural perspectives that conceptualize knowing as participation in activity systems rather than simply the acquisition of decontextualized concepts (Vygotsky, 1987; Wertsch, 1991). Within this view, AI tools and data infrastructures function as cultural tools (Cole, 1996; Saxe, 1991) that shape what becomes visible, what is considered authoritative, and whose perspectives are deemed valid as knowledge. I also draw on constructionist (Holbert et al., 2020; Kafai & Resnick, 1996; Papert & Harel, 1991) and design-oriented traditions that treat building computational artifacts as a powerful avenue for learning. When students build or critique AI applications and data stories, they are engaging in epistemic work that reveals their assumptions about what counts as evidence, how models relate to the world, and whose experiences are encoded in data (Vakil et al., 2022). I am particularly attentive to how young learners develop both conceptual and sociotechnical understandings of the affordances and limits of AI technologies, and how educators can support these competencies in ways that foster agency, critique, and creativity.

papers.title: Sowing Futures: Developing Curriculum Materials for Urban Agriculture within a Community- Based Partnership
papers.authors: Jessica Bautista, Candi Fentress, Mark Fentress, Leslie R. Herrenkohl
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: In this practice -oriented paper, we underscore ICLS’s 2026 theme of “Partnering with Purpose” by describing the process and outcomes of a collaborative project between community members and a large public university. By attending to values of reciprocity, relationships, community expertise, and the power of place, we developed a set of curriculum materials that draw on the expertise of two Black urban farmers in their work to transform educational and agricultural experiences for youth. We outline our collaborative process, project outcomes, and next steps for supporting this and other innovative community partnerships.

papers.title: Supporting Classroom Orchestration and Collaborative Programming with Jupyter Analytics
papers.authors: Zhenyu Cai, Richard Lee Davis, Roland Tormey, Pierre Dillenbourg
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: Jupyter notebooks have been widely adopted in STEM courses that have programming or data science integrated. Jupyter Analytics, a learning analytics system, has been built to provide teachers with visibility into student activity. In combination with its existing functions as an awareness and reflection tool, this demo illustrates how the new code- sharing feature can address the real needs of both instructors and learners within Jupyter notebooks. Specifically, we discuss its potential value in two use cases: (1) supporting teachers in orchestrating live-coding lectures, and (2) helping students merge and synchronize work in collaborative programming. This covers two common pedagogical contexts in higher education: teacher-led lectures and student-centered active learning environments with group projects or collaborative sessions.

papers.title: “It’s aligned with my personal beliefs, i can do this”: How Science Educators Navigate Tensions Between Official and Counter Scripts of Science and Learning
papers.authors: Shaghig Chaparian, Olivia Ortiz, Maia Yoshida, Kam Waugh, Jasmine Ma, Ronni Hayden, Latasha Wright
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study examines how informal science educators transform their lived experiences of migration, activism, and encounters with marginalization into pedagogical commitments focused on social justice. Drawing on Holland and Lave’s history-in-person and Gutiérrez’s third-space concepts, we explore how educators’ histories serve as mediational resources that shape teaching philosophies and reconfigure who belongs in science. Using semi- structured interviews with community scientists from Daphnia , an after -school science organization serving marginalized youth, the analysis traces how educators navigated and re - authored official and unofficial scripts about legitimate science and participation. Findings reveal that educators mobilize personal histories to create hybrid pedagogical spaces emphasizing freedom, flexibility, and epistemic justice. These third-space negotiations obscure boundaries between scientific and community knowledge, transforming science into a relational, participatory practice rooted in care and belonging. By conceptualizing informal educators as historical actors, this study highlights their critical role in social transformation.

papers.title: Construal Level Theory of Psychological Distance: Preservice Teacher Learning in Artificial Intelligence-supported Simulations
papers.authors: Chih-Pu Dai, Fengfeng Ke, Nuodi Zhang, Alex Barrett, Sherry Southerland, Saptarshi Bhowmik, Xin Yuan
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: This study explores how preservice teachers engage with artificial intelligence (AI)- powered virtual students in VR classrooms, focusing on psychological distance and construal - level theory. Using a mixed- methods approach, we analyzed interaction data from 29 participants. Findings show higher levels of abstract thinking and temporal imme diacy during teaching decisions. These results highlight how cognitive distance influences pedagogical reasoning. Insights inform the design of AI agents in immersive environments, supporting adaptive teacher learning through reflective, experience-oriented simulations.

papers.title: Renewing Socio-Cultural Theory in a Networked, Decentralized Supercapitalist Society
papers.authors: Kurt Squire, Constance Steinkuehler, Richard Martinez, Rose Bigheart O’Leary, Michael Cole
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Socio-cultural theory, with its emphasis on identity, culture, critique, and power, offers both an explanatory toolkit given the rise in extremism, authoritarianism, and tribalism, but also faces significant challenges, given the increasingly fractured and dynamically-changing nature of life in online worlds. Traditional metaphors of enculturating students into communities of scientific practice face external threats from a public suspicious toward social institutions. This session asks what socio -cultural theory might have to offer for understanding the current moment, and how this current state of the world may be pushing back on our understanding of socio-cultural theory. This session offers three papers and a robust discussion session by four leading researcher / theorist / practitioners from socio -cultural traditions. Each paper offers a look at how learning is occurring in a networked, digital age, with community partners that include Homeboy Industries, the Network of Academic Esports Federations, and with Indigenous Education Partners. This session is particularly focused on how macro trends across culture, specifically occurring through supercapitalist economic and online cultural structures contribute to cultural logics operating upon us. Socio-cultural theory for a supercapitalist society Vygotsky’s formulation that higher order cognitive functions are learned through social processes, occurring first on an outer plane through social interaction preceding internal ization is a cornerstone of socio-cultural learning theory (Vygotsky, 1978). Learning from this perspective is a process of mediation , whereby people internalize the language, tools, and concepts of a culture (Daniels, Cole, & Wertsch, 2007). Appropriation occurs as people make such tools their own, expanding their application to new situations (Wertsch, 1997). Play, the creation of imagined, liminal contexts in which learners can engage within a zone of proximal development, is crucial for understanding rule systems, appropriating representational systems, and employing imagination toward expanding one’s experiences beyond that which has been directly experienced (Vygotsky, 1967). Schools may be important locations of academic learning, but experiences outside of school largely form the experiential foundation for future understanding, provide social identification and belonging, shape the identities and dispositions we bring toward school, and govern how we mobilize such identities outside of school (Cole, 1999; Gutiérrez & Rogoff, 2003; Wertsch, 1997). Cultural historical learning theorists look beyond individual or familial interactions and focus on how learning occurs in complex settings, including workplaces , classrooms, and after school settings (Cole, 1999 ). Cultural Historical Activity Theorists (CHAT) are particularly interested in studying learning as it occurs in complex activity, stretched across people, their tools, and social institutions (including their formal and informal rules and divisions of labor, (Engeström, 2014; Hutchins, 1995). Such analyses reveal the complex social achievement embodied by such professional performances, and outcomes (learning) is shaped by social context. Values, identity, and culture co -constitute emergent understandings; competent action in the world involves identifying resources, employing tools, navigating social structures and institutions, appropriating formal and informal rules, and coordinating with complex networks of divisions of labor (Gee, 1990; Lave & Wenger, 1991). A defining feature of socio -cultural work is learning through participation as a social achievement, recruiting identities from learners as “certain kinds of people” with dispositions, values, and ways of being in the world (Lave & Wenger, 1991). Nowhere is such identity formation clearer than through language , where such work meaning-making work is coordinated, negotiated, and manifested into action (Gee, 1990; Wertsch, 1997). Learning scientists within the socio-cultural tradition have turned toward informal learning spaces, where complex learning configurations can be designed, according to specific values, which might become habits of mind for those engaged in such programs . The 5 th Dimension project (Cole, 2006) uses a game -based metaphor 2504 to engage kids in game-based learning activities, under the mentorship of college students, who themselves gained learning experiences toward their development as teachers, driven by values of diversity. The Migrant Student Leadership Institute created a collective Third Space in which every day and institutional literacy practices are mobilized for critical social thought, using literacy practices to link historical practices, current situations, and possible futures (Gutiérrez, 2008). FUSE Studio creates paths for engaging youth in STEAM practices in after - school settings by challenges based designed in response to youth interests (Stevens et al., 2016). These are but a few design -based research programs that build on socio- cultural learning theory but propose learning environments based on specific underlying social commitments or values that are orthogonal, if not contradictory to those of school, which are often based on sorting. Underlying such socio- cultural approaches to learning is a commitment to defining and articulating underlying values, although recently, values driving such efforts (diversity, equality of opportunity, social justice) are under assault. Re-examining socio-cultural theory in a super capitalist society This session asks what socio-cultural theory might have to offer for understanding the current state of the world, particularly in the United States, and how this current state of the world may be pushing back on our understanding of socio-cultural theory. On the one hand, socio-cultural theorists offer a toolkit with explanatory power: Identity, belonging, and group membership appear to be driving national discourse more than any sort of traditional rational discourse, with the entire enterprise of science being questioned, history rewritten, and institutions such as universities or medicine under assault (Mann & Hotez, 2025). Socio-cultural theory, with its emphasis on identity, culture, power, and social enterprise as the result of historical actors (rather than depoliticized, ahistorical reasoning processes) offer potential tools for understanding this predicament . On the other hand, socio-cultural approaches have often treated contexts as relatively fixed and knowable entities. Communities of practice center definable practices, whether it be tailoring or massively multiplayer gaming) with relatively definable, observable boundaries . Affinity Spaces (Gee, 2018) are one model for describing the ephemeral, less formal spaces that attract people of like- minded interests. However, some of the more pernicious online spaces (QAnon, Red Pill Internet) are less dedicated locations, and more resentment - driven ideologies mobilized over public channel s and are less well described by a ffinity spaces (Lavin, 2020; Marche, 2016). To a degree, fractured selves and participation in distinct, orthogonal, or self-contradictory spaces are part of post -modern existence. How do we conceptualize the nature of such spaces and participation within them? How do we conceptualize participati on within them? What might learning sciences learn from contemporary efforts to moderate and govern activities in sites such as gaming communities? How might research on and in such communities inform our understanding of socio-cultural theories? If understanding the broader social context outside of school is crucial for understanding learning, knowing and participation, what is the impact of the broader socio- cultural systems in which youth are being enculturated? What values and dispositions are being recruited by these systems from youth? In the United States, the top 1% controls roughly half the nation’s wealth, while the bottom half of the country controls roughly 2.5%, meaning that the middle class has in many ways disappeared (Federal Reserve, 2025). Replacing this middle class is a top 10% of America, which controls 2/3 of the country’s wealth. With wealth concentrated within the hands of the view, it is little wonder that confidence in such institutions is at historic lows (Gallup, 2025). Skepticism runs the gamut of institutions; over 70% of American say higher education is headed in the wrong direction (Parker, 2025). Only 1/3 of Americans trust the United States Health care system (Hopkins, 2023). Robert Reich describes this broad pattern as supercapitalism, which is a system marked by extreme wealth and poverty, corporations that exert substantial power over the marketplace, media outlets controlled by individuals or corporate conglomerates, and systems wherein those entities exert undo influence on government to shape regulations (Reich, 2007). Writ large, this process of increased economic concentration, leading to gross power imbalances, creating a lack of social trust, leading to alienation, and then a “take what you can get” mentality has been referred to as “Gangster capitalism.” Gangster capitalism might be best illustrated by the recent pardoning of former Representative George Santos, who lied about his credentials, pled guilty to identity theft and wire fraud, and was expelled from Congress had his sentence commuted by the Pre sident because he was loyalist. In “America is a Scam” Cory Doctorow (2025) articulates this theory of government and business, concluding, “If you are convinced that being honest will get you taken advantage of, there’s nothing for it but to turn scammer yourself.” In the words of President Donald Trump, “That makes me smart. How does living in such a system remediate our goals, drives, and dispositions? What kinds of dispositions does this recruit, and what are the implications for systems such as schools and the designs of learning environments? Socio -cultural theory has long concerned itself with questions of equity, resistance, interest, identity, and resourcefulness among marginalized people, and often posits formal education as a route toward social and economic advancement. How might tools from socio- cultural research be applied to students from 2505 different socio -cultural backgrounds? What models of resistance are there? Should socio -cultural theorists engaged in design-based research embrace counter value systems more explicitly? Papers This panel format proposes five short papers, paired with four discussants. The objective of the panel is to engage a discussion among socio- cultural theorists to discuss opportunities for leveraging socio -cultural theory to understand the current cultural predicament and opportunities to rethink socio- cultural theory in light of recent developments. Whereas the typical ISLS symposi um is a set of papers with a s ingle discussant, this symposium proposes 5-7minutes for each paper, followed by 5- 7 minutes of prepared remarks by each discussant . Each of these discussants is an accomplished researcher and three of the four discussants are members of the National Academies of Education. The panel will leave 20 minutes for discussion and question and answer. Each of these 4 papers investigates issues related to contemporary issue in socio-cultural learning theory, providing a context for a deeper discussion of contemporary issues facing the field. Homeboy technology: Learning digital arts practices among formerly incarcerated and gang-affiliated youth with trauma-informed pedagogy Richard Martinez, Kurt Squire Emerging technologies such as Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) are posited as potentially transforming learning and work, yet if history is a guide, they might exacerbate digital divides in access to employment, education, healthcare, and social services (Lee, Hui, & Dillahunt, 2025; Vogels, 2021). This ongoing, 3 year creative technology program introduced emerging technologies to an arts education program for formerly incarcerated and gang-impacted youth, using trauma-informed pedagogy techniques. Context Based out of Boyle Heights, Los Angeles, Homeboy Technology is a part of The Homeboy Art Academy (HBAA), a trauma-informed art center which itself is embedded in Homeboy Industries, which founded by Father Greg Boyle is the world’s largest and most successful gang rehabilitation program. HBAA serves justice - impacted, gang-affiliated youth who are considered “in crisis” and beyond “at risk” between the ages of 18 -24. HBAA was created by award -winning artist Fabian Debora, a former member of Homeboy Industries and accomplished artist within the Chicano muralist tradition. Under Debora’s direction, the HBAA itself is part of a larger struggle to reclaim creative agency, assert cultural sovereignty, and build alternative pathways into technological and artistic futures—on their terms. Debora’s art studio is located on site, in the building. The study examines freeform exploring emerging technologies, followed by structured design experiences might help youth leverage such skills for their own social, economic, or political advancement, which might be described as appropriation (see also Van Duersen & Helsper, 2015). Program designers sought to improve community digital capacity, which describes “the extent to which the culture, infrastructure, and digital competence of family and community enable and support digital practices.” (Dillahunt et al., 2022) This communal notion of digital capacities seeks to capture the “village- like” sharing economy that exists within underserved communities and that we have observed in Boyle Heights and East Los Angeles, where this work occurs (Karusala et al., 2021).

papers.title: From Doing to Doing Together: A Design Framework for Hands-On and Open Science Engagement In K-5
papers.authors: Kolawole Kushimo, Olayinka Joshua Oyewole, Peter Damilare Idowu, Oluwatosin Deborah Akande
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This conceptual paper explores how hands -on and open science frameworks can be synthesized as design principles for fostering authentic student engagement in science learning. Building on sociocultural and constructivist theories, the paper examines engagement not as compliance or activity, but as participatory meaning -making situated in shared inquiry and collaboration. By integrating literature on embodied learning, democratic participation, and scientific literacy, the paper proposes that combining hands -on and open science approaches supports engagement as both experiential and communal. This paper aligns with the ISLS mission to advance design- based theories of learning through participatory and equitable practices. Four propositions and design principl es are presented to guide pedagogical and research innovations that promote more inclusive, participatory, and equitable science education.

papers.title: Supporting K-12 Science Teachers in Equitable Science Teaching through Co-design
papers.authors: Yang Zhang
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: My research explores how to support K-12 science teachers’ professional development toward equitable and justice-centered teaching. Positioning teachers and students as those who decide what matters to them in their local contexts, I leverage design-based research to co-design, test, and co-refine pedagogical tools with practitioners. Through this process, I study teacher learning by drawing upon a professional identity development lens. In my most recent work, I study how to support middle school science teachers in customizing high-quality instructional materials and investigate how curriculum customization catalyzes teacher teaching. Looking forward, I hope to explore how community-based curriculum design and customization help science teachers create equitable learning experiences for their students.

papers.title: Understanding Play and Inclusion through Interaction Analysis
papers.authors: Mikaela Zetley, Christine Lee
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: In this poster, we present interaction analysis from video data of a playful learning episode in an inclusive elementary classroom. We found that, as a methodology, interaction analysis revealed the ways that adults’ instructional moves expansively position children’s ideas as valid contributions. We aim to spark conversation in the Learning Science community around intersections of dignity, inclusion, and playful learning.

papers.title: Systems, Values, and Conceptions Shaping Computing Education in Refugee Support Organizations
papers.authors: F. Megumi Kivuva, Eman Sherif, Belén Edgar, Amy J. Ko
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Refugee support organizations (RSOs) provide computing education for refugee youth. However, prior work has not yet examined how organizational systems and values shape learning about computing. These dynamics are important because RSOs' structures and practices directly influence access to equitable computing opportunities. We conducted a case study of one Youth STEAM Program, analyzing observations, interviews, and lesson plans to examine computing education through the lens of the Ecological Systems The ory and critical pedagogy. We found that multi -level constraints, such as funding, transportation, and translation, staff content knowledge, and reliance on external partnerships, restricted access to and depth of computing education. Culturally responsive and justice-centered practices built belonging and engagement, but tension at the micro, meso, and exosystem levels curtailed participation. Addressing these limits requires justice -centered coordination that aligns organizational values, resources, and pedagogy.

papers.title: Humanizing Institutional Landscapes of Ability Differences and Learning
papers.authors: Cathery Yeh, Erin McCloskey, Alfredo J. Artiles, Mimi Ito
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Humanizing Institutional Landscapes of Ability Differences and Learning Cathery Yeh, Erin McCloskey, Alfredo J. Artiles, Mimi Ito How can schools, universities, and community spaces construct, reinforce, or challenge how ability differences and disabilities are understood and organized in relation to race, language, and culture? This session brings together researchers working in schools, higher education, and out-of-school settings to study, reconceptualize, and redesign institutional, programmatic, and pedagogical practices. Through an engaging, dialogic format, the panelists will share stories and artifacts from four participatory design projects and explore common themes and challenges. The goal is to grapple with institutional landscapes that unevenly distribute learning opportunities, and to consider what equitable, culturally sustaining approaches to ability differences and disabilities in learning might look like. papers.title: Trend Trackers: Building Data Literacy Through Problem-Based Learning
papers.authors: Anna Amato Shao, Jessica Ochoa Hendrix, Mandë Holford, Noelle Posadas Shang, Christopher Pollati
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Middle School Students; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: In this demo, we discuss the co-design of an interactive, problem-based science supplement called Trend Trackers. Trend Trackers aims to engage middle school students with socioscientific issues that impact cities and communities all over the world. Students take up the role of a data scientist to address public health problems within the fictional city of Springfield. In this demo, we will explore a challenge in which students are asked to design a vaccination plan to reduce the rates of flu in Springfield. Students engage in interactive and immersive activities to collect wastewater samples, measure rates of flu in the community, and generate evidence through a series of wrangling, visualization, and analysis activities. Students then share their findings and collaborate with their team to co-construct a vaccination plan for Springfield.

papers.title: The Language Between Us: Using CHAT to Explore a STEM Coach-Researcher Collaborations
papers.authors: Jessica McClain, Jerika Miller, Linette Victor, Judi Fusco, Joshua Danish, Cindy E. Hmelo- Silver
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study examined how collaborative language empowers STEM coaches' agency through researcher -practitioner partnerships. Using Cultural -Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) to analyze the collaboration between one STEM coach and researcher, data from professional learning sessions, videos, and artifacts were analyzed through thematic analysis. Findings revealed that empowering language functioned as a mediating tool in transforming traditional hierarchies and encouraging collaborative partnerships.

papers.title: More Than Meets the Eye: Transforming Black Boys’ STEM Identities through Liberatory Co-Design and Computational Making
papers.authors: Kareem Edouard
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper examines how liberatory co- design within computational making fosters agency and technical skill development among Black boys. Drawing on a pilot program in the Black Male Animation Lab, we show how connecting students’ cultural interests like Transformers and anime to stop- motion animation created co -designed learning. Findings highlight three themes: storytelling functioned as identity work through community narratives; collaboration and co-design shaped the lab as students negotiated problem-solving, positioning themselves as leaders; and students bridged cultural and technical literacies by connecting fabrication to culturally relevant themes. These findings demonstrate how liberatory co- design transformed the lab into a space where Black boys resisted deficit framings, affirmed identities, and pursued STEM on their own terms, offering a methodological contribution to equity- centered learning.

papers.title: Designing for Affective Equity in Partnerships
papers.authors: Blanca Gamez-Djokic
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) have become central to the learning sciences as infrastructures for addressing educational challenges. While much scholarship emphasizes their design principles and effectiveness, less attention has been paid to the affective life of partnerships. This paper advances a conceptual argument that RPPs function as pedagogical sites of affectivity. They not only rely on dispositions such as trust, humility, or perseverance but also cultivate, normalize, and organize which affective orientations become legitimate forms of participation. I call this the ontological goodness of RPPs – the assumption that collaboration is inherently moral and transformative which imbues partnerships with affective demands that shape who can participate fully and on what terms. Reframing purpose as an affective terrain highlights a hidden curriculum of partnership and raises new learning and design questions: what would it mean to design RPPs for affective equity where multiple orientations are legible and recognized as legitimate forms of participation?

papers.title: Playing A/Part: Considering Directors in Ensemble Learning
papers.authors: Lana Ćosić, Suraj Uttamchandani
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Learning in ensembles is “learning…that cannot be done alone” (Ma & Hall, 2018, p. 508). While researchers have examined the infrastructure necessary to sustain ensemble learning, they have yet to fully consider the role of the teacher(s) and the “part” they play in relation to th e ensemble. In this paper, we explore the range of ways directors participate in ensembles and examine how their practices position them in relation to the wider group. We ground our discussion in video ethnographic cases of a college choir and an undergraduate theatre ensemble. We present four critical cases: two in which ensemble directors call attention to their unique role in the ensemble and two in which directors’ participation positions them as “just another” member of the ensemble ––although within limits. These findings highlight the fluid nature of directorial participation and raise important questions about theorizing directors’ membership in an ensemble’s community of practice.

papers.title: Reconceptualizing Activity Theory for Human-AI Teaming in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning
papers.authors: Jaeyoon Choi, Nia Nixon
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) are reshaping the role of technology in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL). Once viewed as mediating tools, AI systems can now act as active teammates that co -construct meaning, share responsibility, and influence team cognition. This paper addresses the lack of theoretical grounding in existing human-AI teaming research by reconceptualizing Engeström’s Activity Theory. Specifically, we extend the six components of the activity system (subject, tool, rules, community, division of labor, and object) to account for AI’s dual role as both tool and quasi-subject within collaborative learning activities. Through this theoretical mapping, we highlight emerging questions for fut ure research, including but not limited to issues of learner agency, trust, equity, and epistemic alignment. We conclude with a call for the CSCL community to revisit and expand its theoretical frameworks to better capture the evolving dynamics of human-AI teaming.

papers.title: From Enrichment to Essential: The Value of the Arts in Education and Learning
papers.authors: Harper Staples, Anna Keune, Sinyoung Kim, Kristiina Kumpulainen, Naomi Thompson, Mary DiCioccio
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This symposium positions the arts as central to learning. Arts -based education has been shown to cultivate creativity, empathy, and cultural awareness, while supporting academic achievement and well -being. Despite this , the arts remain marginalized in curricula, with funding cuts and narrow evaluation frameworks obscuring their value. Responding to calls to advance knowledge on learning in and through the arts, this symposium seeks to demonstrate approaches to valuing the arts through six contributions that show methodological and theoretical innovations, alongside purposeful partnerships, that capture the value of arts-based education. The symposium will include roundtable presentations within a participatory fishbowl and co-creation of a tangible emotional cartography of insights, advancing future directions for evidencing the value of arts-based education through research, policy, and practice. Symposium overview The arts are central to how we understand learning and knowing and are therefore crucial to the learning sciences (Halverson & Sawyer, 2022). The arts have long been recognized as powerful contexts for cultivating empathy, creativity, and cultural awareness (Eisner, 200 2; Venkatesh et al., 2023) . The arts have also supported academic achievement and positively impacted mental health and wellness (Peppler et al., 2014; Fancourt & Finn, 2019). Unlike other domains, arts -based education engages learners in per sonally meaningful experiences that link identity, community, and imagination (Halverson et al., 2023; Peppler et al., 2023). Importantly, these experiences are also democratic: arts -based education can nurture the pluralism and inclusivity that underpin participatory societies. This value has been affirmed globally; UNESCO, for example, through its 2022 MONDIACULT declaration, emphasizes that culture and the arts are integral to human development, well -being, and creativity, forming the foundation for respect and openness to otherness , which are all skills essential for 21st- century life (UNESCO, 2024). Despite its crucial role, arts -based education often remains marginal in curricula, positioned as “auxiliary” rather than central (Halverson, Saplan & Martin, 2024, p. 300). One challenge lies in evaluating the impact of arts-based education. As Jindal-Snape et al. (2018, p.60) note, attempts to measure “a range of aesthetic and emotive experiences which themselves defy categorization” risk reducing the richness of artistic engagement and obscuring its intrinsic value, namely, its distinctive capacity to “i lluminate our inner lives and enrich our emotional world” (Mowlah et al., 2014, p.4). Compounding this issue, even amid increasing global attention, there remains uncertainty about how the arts are and should be connected to education and assessment (Fleming, Bresler & O’Toole, 2015, p. 1). To address these gaps, more robust and responsive ways of articulating arts -based education, its role, and its purposes are essential. Building on this prior work crystallizes an important opportunity: To articulate the value of arts- based education through approaches that can capture both the distinctive ‘ ways of knowing ’ (Wright, 2012) and the “examples of success that are possible” in arts -based educat ion (Halverson et al., 2024, p. 310), while also 2375 foregrounding the broader social outcomes it enables . Making sense of artistic and cultural experiences requires situated, learner-centered, and embodied perspectives in which “senses, cognition, and emotions are developed together” (Chemi & Du, 2022, pp. 6- 7). This socio -cultural and situative approach to learning through the arts strongly resonates with the learning sciences (Halverson & Peppler, 2018). As such, t he learning sciences are uniquely positioned to advance richer understandings of both how the arts -based approaches shape what can be learned through the arts and how this learning can be made visible and valued. This symposium responds to calls to further investigate how we can show the value of arts -based education in powerful ways. It brings together researchers and practitioners to share and examine diverse ways of valuing arts-based education, whether through methodological and theoretical innovations or through purposeful partnerships with community stakeholders across contexts. It is our hope that these perspectives cumulatively illustrate how insights from the learning sciences, and particularly attention to learning across contexts, evolving

papers.title: Of Stars and Constellations: Culture and Identity within Collaborative Interactive Computational Art
papers.authors: Kayla DesPortes, Francisco Castro, Elizabeth Leonard, Cass Scheirer, Nichelle Ryan, Sabria Islam
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: O f Stars and Constellations: Culture and Identity within Collaborative Interactive Computational Art Artistic computing education offers opportunities to explore disciplinary intersections that can support culturally sustaining experiences with technology. We present five computational art pieces created by 15 NYC high school students as part of CWP 2.0—an art & tech residency co-designed and facilitated by NYU researchers and Community Word Project Teaching Artists. Students combined visual and literary arts with electronics and coding as they reflected on oneself as a “star” in a constellation within their communities and society. Each piece includes sensors and output components the students programmed and embedded into sculptural and wearable artifacts. The artifacts are representative of various societies the learning community envisioned at the intersections of their cultures and identities. The pieces include: Threads of Our Community—a woven tapestry, An Ode to Identity— an interactive crown, An Ode to Peace—an interactive hat/pot, An ode to Unity—an interactive cape, and An Ode to Music-ing—an interactive music box & headphones. papers.title: Designing Digital Enhancements for Social Emotional Skill in a Collaborative Learning Environment
papers.authors: Enruo Guo, Emily Kerzabi, Jessica Andrews-Todd, Jiangang Hao, Patrick Kyllonen, Stephen Elliott
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This study presents the design and implementation of a fifth- grade Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) curriculum within a hybrid digital collaborative environment. Using a user -centered design approach, we engaged teachers and a school administrator as co - designers over a four -month period to iteratively refine the features and tools from a collaborative learning and assessment system (EPCAL). Key design decisions, such as tailoring class analytics to SEL and integrating feedback and rewards systems, were informed by teacher input. A semester-long pilot study involving two teachers and 22 students demonstrated the feasibility of delivering SEL through a hybrid model using EPCAL. Findings highlight strong teacher engagement and meaningful student participation. This research contributes a scalable framework for hybrid SEL delivery, demonstrating how a participatory design approach can be effectively applied to curriculum and technology enhancements - an approach that can be generalized to other hybrid learning contexts.

papers.title: Graphs Are Arguments: Modeling Choices, Belonging, and Critical Statistical Literacy in Climate Data Visualizations
papers.authors: Eva Thanheiser
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents
papers.abstract: This paper explores how graphs operate as arguments through modeling choices including time window, scale, framing, aggregation, and audience. Drawing on contrasting climate visualizations built from the same data, it shows how representational choices sha pe interpretation and support different claims. It also argues that students were able to critique these choices because the classroom was organized as a Beloved Community, where belonging functioned as participation infrastructure for critical statistical literacy. Overview Public data visualizations are often treated as neutral displays of information, yet they are constructed through choices that shape what becomes visible, what counts as evidence, and what interpretations appear plausible. This paper argues that modeling choices such as time window, scale, framing, aggregation, and audience are central to how graphs make arguments (D’Ignazio & Klein, 2020; Weiland, 2017). It further argues that students were able to critique those choices because the classroom had been organized as a Beloved Community in which belonging functioned as participation infrastructure (Love, 2019). Using contrasting climate visualizations built from the same data but displayed across different time windows as a central example, this paper examines how representational decisions shape interpretation and how students moved from reading graphs to critiquing them. The analysis draws on classroom activity in which students engaged public data visualizations as objects of interpretation, comparison, and redesign. In particular, students examined contrasting climate graphs built from the same underlying data but displayed with different time windows, and they discussed how design choices shaped the claims each graph appeared to support. The analysis focuses on students’ discourse as they interpreted, questioned, and revised visualizations, with attention to the representational choices they named and the forms of critique they developed (Sfard, 2008). A central modeling contrast in this analysis is time window. When the same climate data are shown across a long historical span, the pattern can appear gradual and may invite familiar responses such as “Earth has changed before.” When the time window narrows to the recent past, the same underlying data can instead foreground the rate of increase and support a different interpretation, such as “Climate change is accelerating.” The point is not that one graph is true and the other false. Rather, representational choices shape salience. They influence what viewers notice, what kinds of arguments seem reasonable, and what conclusions become easier to draw. In this sense, graphs do not simply report reality. They organize attention and render some stories more visible than others (D’Ignazio & Klein, 2020). Time window is especially powerful because it often appears innocuous. Yet it works alongside other modeling choices such as scale, framing, aggregation, and attention to audience. Scale influences whether change looks dramatic or muted. Framing shapes how a graph is introduced, labeled, and interpreted in relation to a broader issue. Aggregation can either highlight patterns across groups or flatten important differences within them. Audience matters because graphs are built for someone, and design decisions anticipate particular readers, questions, and consequences. Taken together, these choices show that data visualization is not merely technical presentation. It is rhetorical and political work carried out through mathematical representation (Gutiérrez, 2013; Weiland, 2017). Within this framing, students’ discourse shifted from reading graphs as visual objects to critiquing graphs as designed arguments. Early responses focused on visible features of the display. Students noticed what a graph looked like, identified lines and labels, and described overall patterns. Over time, however, their talk became more analytic and more critical. They began to ask how the graph had been constructed, why certain choices had been made, and what those choices accomplished rhetorically. This movement from reading graphs to critiquing graphs matters because public visualizations often circulate as if they were transparent windows onto the world (D’Ignazio & Klein, 2020). In fact, they are composed artifacts shaped by inclusion, omission, emphasis, and intended audience. These shifts can also be understood as changes in classroom discourse, where students increasingly participated in forms of accountable and sociomathematical argumentation (O’Connor & Michaels, 1996; Yackel & Cobb, 1996). Early in discussion, students described graphs primarily in terms of visible features such as lines, labels, and overall shape. Later, they began to ask what the selected time span emphasized, why that span had been 2566 chosen, and how different viewers might interpret the same data differently. This shift marked a movement from noticing what a graph showed to interrogating how the graph had been built to make a claim. Two interrelated clusters of practice are especially important in this analysis. The first is argument-with- evidence. Students justified scale choices, explained uncertainty, and documented data provenance. In the climate example, this meant treating time window as part of the mathematical argument rather than as a cosmetic formatting decision. Students increasingly recognized that a graph’s domain, labels, and contextual features shape interpretation. They also came to see that uncertainty bands, source notes, and framing devices do mathematical work because they guide what counts as evidence and what can reasonably be inferred (Philip et al., 2016; Weiland, 2017). In this way, representation became a form of warrant rather than decoration. The second cluster of practice involved audience and ethics reasoning. Students questioned categories, disaggregated groups, and critiqued representation choices in relation to who would read the graph and what consequences might follow from the way it was built. These moves extended beyond technical correctness alone. A graph can be statistically defensible and still be ethically misleading if its categories flatten important differences, if its framing obscures the stakes of the issue, or if its design invites viewers toward a simplistic conclusion. Students therefore learned to ask not only whether a display was mathematically acceptable, but also what story it told, what story it hid, and whose experiences were made visible or invisible. This shift positioned critique as both an intellectual and a civic practice (Philip et al., 2016; Weiland, 2024). These critical practices did not emerge in a vacuum. Belonging functioned as participation infrastructure, organized through connection, norms, and shared purpose. In this framing, belonging is not a soft supplement to rigorous mathematical work. It is part of the classroom architecture that enables students to speak publicly, challenge one another’s interpretations, and revise claims without disproportionate interpersonal risk. When students experience connection to one another, participate in negotiated norms, and share a collective purpose, critique can become a communal responsibility rather than a threat to status or safety. Belonging, in other words, supports the conditions under which critical reasoning becomes possible (Goodenow, 1993; Nasir et al., 2014; Walton & Cohen, 2011). This view is consistent with learning sciences work that treats participation, relationship -building, and social change as co-constitutive dimensions of learning (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). This claim is especially important in work with public data visualizations. To question framing, audience, omission, or aggregation is to question decisions that are often treated as settled, objective, or authoritative. Students are more likely to engage in that questioning when the classroom makes room for uncertainty, disagreement, and accountability to others. In this sense, belonging does not sit beside critical statistical literacy as a separate concern. It helps constitute the social conditions through which such literacy can develop. If educators want students to engage critically with graphs in civic life, instructional design must address not only technical tasks but also the relational and normative conditions that make critique possible (Goodenow, 1993; Walton & Cohen, 2011). This work contributes to research on critical statistical literacy by showing that critique of data visualization is not only a matter of technical competence, but also of the social and relational conditions that make participation possible (Weiland, 2017) . It also contributes to learning sciences discussions of classroom discourse by arguing that belonging operates as infrastructure for critique. When students experience connection, shared norms, and collective purpose, they are better positioned to question authoritative-looking representations, make interpretive claims in public, and revise those claims in response to others (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; O’Connor & Michaels, 1996; Yackel & Cobb, 1996). A key design principle emerging from this work is to show multiple representations of the same data. Representational contrast makes hidden assumptions visible because students can compare what changes in a graph and what changes in interpretation. In the climate example, holding the data constant while changing the time window exposed how design choices shape the story a graph appears to tell. More broadly, such comparison can support critical statistical literacy by inviting students to ask: What story does this graph tell? What story is hidden? Which modeling choices shaped this interpretation? These questions matter beyond a single classroom or a single climate example. They position students to participate more critically in a world saturated with charts, dashboards, and politically consequential data displays (Gutiérrez, 2013; Weiland, 2017, 2024). Taken together, this paper advances a compact but significant claim. Graphs shape arguments. Students can learn to identify and critique that shaping. Belonging is one of the conditions that makes such critique possible in classroom life. When learners com pare representations, attend to audience and ethics, and work within a classroom organized for belonging, they can move from consuming visualizations to interrogating them. That movement is central to critical statistical literacy and to preparing future educators and students to read, question, and remake the quantitative stories that organize public life (Gutstein, 2006; Weiland, 2017). 2567 References Bang, M., & Vossoughi, S. papers.title: Co-design as Transformative Pedagogical Spaces: what zooming out teaches us about learning to co-design together
papers.authors: Michael Chang, Areej Mawasi, Angel Osorio Pizarro, Thomas M. Philip, Amani Rohana, Jool Farra
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This symposium brings together Learning Scientists and practitioners engaged in co- design practices embedded in diverse traditions (participatory design, human- centered design, youth participatory action research, design- based implementation research, and research practice partnerships) across diverse geographies. In different ways, these collections of papers challenge two artificially imposed constraints on how many co- design spaces are (a) designed, as short, condensed, irregular, or infrequent activities, and (b) studied, as analysis primarily focused on the interactions happening within the formal co -design activities themselves. By zooming out temporally and analytically, we make visible co- design processes that are deeply context-dependent, relational, political, and ethical practices, ones that researchers and participants construct a nd hone together over longer units of time. Through our collective discussions, we show how co- design spaces are unique spaces of being, doing, and becoming, for researchers and participants alike. Objective of the session In recent years, collaborative design has emerged in the learning sciences as a key method supporting the development of learning artifacts (Yoon et al., 2016; Gomez et al., 2018). Like other design-oriented disciplines, co-design in the learning sciences seeks to surface participants’ lived experiences and needs to directly inform the design of some learning artifact. Unlike other design-oriented disciplines, co-design in the learning sciences has focused on the relational, social, and dynamic learning processes that occur within co-design spaces (Mawasi et al., 2023; Penuel, 2019; Philip et al., 2022). This burgeoning line of research from the learning sciences complicates how we design, analyze, and assess co -design spaces, particularly when time constraints often necessitate that these co -design sessions occur over short or infrequent periods. Extrapolating concrete design decisions from co- design spaces can be exceptionally difficult given the fluidity, tensions, and outright contradictions that emerge ( Chang & Philip, 2025). Here, rather than narrowly conceptualizing the telos of co- design spaces as surfacing fixed designs, we build on Rogoff’s conceptualization of “learning as a process of transformation of participation” (1994) and argue that co- design spaces must be understood as sites where participants and researchers dynamically learn to co -design together. In this way, we understand co- design as a deeply context-dependent, relational, political, and ethical practice that researchers and participants construct and hone together; design decisions thus emerge as an ever-evolving byproduct of these practices (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Vossoughi et al., 2021). Past work in the learning sciences offers several starting points for exploring co-design spaces as sites of mutual learning about co-design itself. McKercher (2020) argues that building conditions for co-design workshops 2274 require intentional power sharing, relationship and trust building, and creating safe spaces for participants. The relational nature of co -design spaces presents a key challenge, as co -design engagements (in practice) typically occur over a short, condensed time period (10s of hours). Such tensions, even when unintended, raise important questions for the Learning Sciences community regarding what co-design entails and how to educate participants and researchers in co-design. Prior work has begun to conceptualize co-design as co-researching with participants and youth (e.g., Clark et al., 2022), while educating learners about the research process. While past work gestures towards the deep relational work that happens in co- design processes, our understanding of how those relational processes unfold is often constrained by two artificially imposed constraints on how many co- design spaces are (a) desi gned, as short, condensed, irregular, or infrequent activities, and (b) studied, as analysis primarily focused on the interactions happening within the formal co -design activities themselves. This symposium brings together five projects that seek to zoom out from these constraints in different ways and conceptualize co -design as a pedagogical space that generates educational possibilities (Freire, 1976) for transformation and shifts in interactions, dynamics, relations, roles, and knowledge, while positioning both researchers and participants as learners of co-design. The projects offered here are hardly the only projects in the learning sciences that thoughtfully challenge those constraints; we seek to make a humble contribution by bringing together a highly diverse group of co-design projects that engage with those constraints and possibilities in creative ways. By exploring these constraints and possibilities, we collectively explore different approaches we have taken in exploring this argument, by focusing on five examples of what we consider a form of co-design research work. Across these projects, we take care to highlight the conditions for co- design, describing the process of mutual becoming and what is transformed in the process, emerging issues in the co-design process (e.g., relational trust, context, power, shifts, ideologies, axiologies), and the tensions or possibilities between desired outcomes and what was eventually achieved. This focus enables us to make the following contributions: (1) We bridge between various co-design projects in the field to recognize the multiplicity of approaches to co-design, and to refine our conceptualization of co-design. (2) We outline key challenges for conceptualizing co -design spaces in the learning sciences for both technology-mediated environments and work with educators, practitioners, and learners using participatory methods. (3) We examine the kind of learning co-design environments afford to participants and, researchers in their collaborative learning process. (4) We examine the ways co -design can be a potential space for creative and constructive exploration and deconstruction and construction of ideas, among participants and researchers with no necessarily defined outcomes needing to emerge - enabling possibilities for critical thinking, liberatory education, and fluid outcomes that create new possibilities for groups and that could be similar to group work in psychology treatments. Overall, the symposium provides guidance on addressing co- design not only as a methodological approach, but also as a learning environment design that enables diverse possibilities for learning for both participants and researchers. Each of the five projects here identifies different ways to zoom out from the typical frames used to study co-design spaces, thereby illustrating different ways that researchers and/or participants learn from each other in ways that enrich the co -design process: (1) Chang et al. zoom out from one -off co-design intensives to show how researchers and youth participants negotiate the aims of co- designing AI-for-education tools over a three -year period. (2) Mawasi et al. zoom out from the formal co- design activities and show how a team of researchers/designers, themselves operating from the margins, learn from each other in order to create co- design spaces around ethical AI that respond to the political contexts of Arab/Palestinian youth. (3) Romero & Lee zoom out from simplified descriptions of participant needs to demonstrate how decision junctures during long-term co -design processes, both big and small, shape how researchers and participants participate in co- designing math and computer science curriculum. (4) Takeuchi et al. zoom out from recent history to demonstrate how researchers and participants learn to attune themselves to the agency and teachings of the Land through mutual learning and imagining, spanning approximately 12,000 years of land stewardship by indigenous communities. (5) Ehrenfeld et al. zoom out from the seemingly convenient touchpoints between researcher and academic during co-design and demonstrate how mismatched rhythms of co-design create pedagogical and ethical tensions when researchers partner with math educators. Collectively, these projects illustrate heterogeneity in co -design research enactment across geographies, topics, and methodological choices of design- based research, and demonstrate how co -design can serve as a productive framework across disciplines, including AI in Education, Mathematics Education, and STEM Education. Together, these contributions assert the need for teams t o co-design for co- design—to continually 2275 examine and refine the very processes and relationships that make co-design possible. As a final point, to illustrate our conceptualization of co-design across these five papers, we share Figure 1, an example of tatreez, Palestinian embroidery art. The art of tatreez , as described by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO, 2021), particularly among women, is an intergenerational and sociocultural practice whose symbols and motifs (e.g., birds, trees, flowers, and places ) carry knowledge, stories, memories, and epistemologies. It has been, and continues to be, widely practiced within Palestinian communities. By “zooming out,” the front and reverse offer two vantage points on a single, entangled practice in which the product carries the process: some makers keep the reverse deliberately neat; others show thread paths and revisions. As Palestinian women engage in tatreez , they enact several choices while being intentional about what they are creating; they often do so in community and in circles, talking with one another. Like co -design, tatreez interweaves structure and improvisation, and ties knowledge to land, relations, and stories. Made collectively—in circles and conversation—the practice is both what is created -and-process itself, a space for care and knowledge-building. Figure 1 Tatreez Tatreez (noun and verb) as co -design: form-and-process as one entangled practice. The patterned front and the reverse—whether kept deliberately neat or showing thread paths —are complementary views of the same iterative making. As in co -design, meaning emerges through interwoven structure and improvisation, situated relations, ties to land, and storytelling. Handmade by Areej Mawasi. Overview of the symposium A key theme of this year’s International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS) conference centers on creating learning experiences that “partner with purpose” with the communities we design with and for. However, such intentions for purposeful partnership require a nuanced understanding of the educational ecologies that shape research–practice partnerships and collaborative design efforts. These intentions also call for an acknowledgment of the resources, capacities, and constraints at play for both communities and researchers across the various cycles of design and partnership—such as temporality, sociocultural and political contexts, histories, relational dynamics, and the lived experiences of participants (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Ehrenfeld & Stengel, 2025; Mawasi et al., 2023). While we expect this symposium to be held entirely in person at the conference venue, we will intentionally build in the option for remote participation by presenters to accommodate emergent circumstances that affect presenters’ ability to travel. papers.title: Cultivating Relational Trust in Community-Engaged Educational Research Partnerships for Environmental Justice
papers.authors: Chris Jadallah, Emily V. Reigh, Symone Gyles, Devon Azzam, Lauren Daus, Sam Burmester, Minjung Shin, Amanda Gonzaga, Danielle Harlow, Julie A. Bianchini, Hosun Kang
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Community-engaged educational research partnerships have the potential to catalyze new approaches to environmental justice teaching and learning by bringing together multiple actors with different lenses, positionalities, epistemologies, and expertise to unsettle normative approaches to educational practice. Such work, however, requires situating relational trust as central to partnership development. In this paper, we examine how relational trust was built across four different educational partnerships working toward environmental justice. We identify five themes that support developing and sustaining relational trust: (a) collectively working toward socio-ecological change, (b) naming and disrupting hierarchies, (c) purposeful processes, (d) centering relationality, and (e) redistributing resources. Theoretically, this paper advances our understanding of relational trust as central to partnership work; methodologically, it deepens our understanding of using partnership artifacts to understand partnership dynamics; and practically, it provides insights and tools for researchers who aspire to cultivate and sustain relational trust in partnership activities. Major issue(s) addressed In the face of ever -increasing environmental challenges, there is a growing need to innovate novel forms of teaching and learning that support youth and communities in understanding, interrogating, and taking action to address environmental injustice and to work toward socio- ecological well -being. Taking this as a point of departure, this paper examines community -engaged educational research partnerships as having the potential to catalyze novel frameworks, models, and approaches for environmental justice education. These types of partnerships involve collaborations that extend beyond researchers and school districts; they intentionally include researchers, youth, families, teachers, administrators, frontline communities, land workers, and other actors who are collectively working toward educational and environmental improvement. Such partnerships are uniquely positioned to support this work because they bring together people with different perspectives to jointly identify problems of practice, co-design potential solutions, and monitor their effectiveness across iterations (Bang et al., 2010; Coburn & Penuel, 2016; Ishimaru et al., 2016). Within these partnership processes, diverse sets of actors bring together different sets of expertise in order to envision, implement, and evaluate novel curricular, pedagogical, and material interventions in support of environmental justice education - from new infrastructures like green schoolyards and outdoor classrooms, to new curriculum that engages environmental justice as an anchoring phenomenon of inquiry. In examining community -engaged educational research partnerships, we focus on the construct of relational trust. Relational trust is defined here as the willingness to participate in relationships that potentially involve risk, vulnerability, and tension on the basis of interactions premised on benevolence, competence, reliability, and respect (Kolleck, 2023). Specifically, we ask, how is relational trust built in community -engaged educational research partnerships working toward environmental justice? Theoretical and methodological approach(es) pursued Theoretically, we draw on literature on research-practice partnerships (Coburn & Penuel, 2016) and participatory design research (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) to frame our study of relational trust. From these perspectives, we understand partnerships and design processes as spaces of learning in and of themselves, where researchers, teachers, and, in the present cases, additional community-based partners collaborate across boundaries to negotiate 388 goals, engage in shared practices, and innovate pedagogical and curricular practices (Goldman et al., 2022; Morales-Doyle et al., 2025). Engaging in boundary crossing necessitates nurturing sustained relational trust. Cultivating relational trust happens over time and is a continuous process, entailing a deliberate, intentional focus on power and privilege given partners’ diverse histories, social positions, and range of prior experiences (Henrick et al., 2023; Vakil et al., 2016). When partners with diverse organizational and personal identities, structures, and routines come together, there is opportunity and risk, both of which may be amplified in work to address environmental justice given different histories of marginalization, contested meanings and values associated with the environment, and intersecting challenges that cut across political, cultural, and ecological lines (Morales - Doyle et al., 2025). This makes relational trust all the more important as an area of inquiry.

papers.title: Semi-Formal Learning Groups as Design Interventions in Doctoral Education
papers.authors: Somi Lee, Rachel Gu, Ava Maken Ali
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: A semi-formal learning group of four doctoral students and one faculty member in art education met biweekly over two years (2023- 2025) to share artworks, written reflections, and personal narratives. The group formed organically and later adopted design-based research to identify the design choices that shaped emotional safety and creative risk- taking. Data included written reflections, meeting transcripts, photographs of artworks, and reflexive journals. Qualitative analysis produced three initial design conjectures: lightweight routines that stabilize participation without pressure, emotion -centered feedback that foregrounds empath y over correction, and shared documentation that links private reflection to public pedagogy.

papers.title: What Children’s Books Do and Do Not Teach About AI: An Analysis Using the AI4K12 Framework
papers.authors: Feiwen Xiao, Shiyan Jiang
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Although many storybooks introducing artificial intelligence (AI) to young children are now available, their quality and educational value have not been systematically or empirically examined. This study addresses this gap by analyzing how AI- themed storybooks conceptualize and communicate foundational AI ideas, practices, and values to young learners. Guided by the AI4K12 framework, this study shows that while most books make AI approachable through friendly robots and playful visuals, they rarely explain how AI actually works. Concepts such as representation, reasoning, and learning were largely introduced as vocabulary rather than as processes, and ethical or responsible AI use was largely absent. These portrayals risk reinforcing AI as magical or infallible. The study offers implications for designing AI literacy materials for young children that balance engagement with conceptual transparency and critical awareness.
