papers.title: Living the Impossible: Designing Life Happens, an AI-Supported Budget and Justice Simulation
papers.authors: Devan Walton, Haesol Bae, Jaesung Park, Yingru Zhao, Raymond Weiss, Susan Tashjian
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This paper reports on the design of Life Happens, a classroom simulation in which students manage household budgets across twelve months while encountering criminal justice– related financial obligations. Grounded in situated learning theory, the simulatio n develops quantitative reasoning and perspective -taking through authentic financial dilemmas. Initial prototypes relied on large language models, producing inconsistencies and outputs that reinforced harmful stereotypes. Informed by a trauma -aware framework, the team restructured the system into a three -layer architecture: a deterministic core, a curated event layer, and a bounded AI layer limited to brief affective text messages. This paper focuses on design principles that emerged from documented failures during deployments at a Hispanic -Serving community college and a Minority-Serving state university. Context, theoretical framing, and focus Faculty at a Hispanic -Serving community college and a Minority- Serving state university in the northeastern United States identified a need for experiential tools conveying how criminal justice involvement compounds household financial hardship (García et al., 2019). The interdisciplinary partnership brought together computer science pedagogy and criminal justice education to serve predominantly first-generation college students (Penuel et al., 2013). Institutional constraints, including limited class time, variable devices, and diverse student demographics, shaped every design decision. We conceptualize learning through situated learning theory (Lave & Wenger, 1991), which holds that knowledge develops through participation in authentic practices. Life Happens situates students within household financial management under justice- system co nstraints, requiring arithmetic computation, budgeting, and quantitative trade-off reasoning as disciplinary competencies that emerge through meaningful decision- making (Gee, 2007). Simultaneously, students develop perspective -taking as they experience cascading consequences of systemic inequities (Belman & Flanagan, 2010). This paper focuses on the simulation’s design and AI integration, tracing how concrete prototype failures led to the principled architecture presented here. Simulation design and learning affordances Life Happens positions students as household decision- makers managing limited resources across twelve simulated months. Each cycle requires allocating funds across housing, food, transportation, healthcare, and phone services. Justice -related obligations such as probation fees, court -ordered payments, and commissary contributions impose additional mandatory costs (Harper et al., 2020). Five well -being indicators update transparently based on decisions, with visible arithmetic enabling students to anticipate consequences (Chernikova et al., 2020). Quarterly reflection prompts emphasize metacognition and discussion (Squire, 2011). The system employs a three -layer architecture. The deterministic core maintains authored family compositions, income parameters, and cost data from regional economic sources, ensuring reproducibility and enabling instructor customization. The event layer introduces curated disruptions ranging from routine expenses to justice -related challenges, each with specified costs and well -being consequences. The affective AI layer generates brief text messages that translate numerical outcomes into personal narratives, adding emotional context while the core mechanics remain fully deterministic. AI integration: From unconstrained generation to bounded use Initial prototypes relied on large language models to generate family scenarios, event narratives, and financial parameters (Yan et al., 2024), producing three categories of documented failure. Generated family compositions contained logical inconsistencies that confused students and undermined budgeting strategies. AI- produced cost structures varied unpredictably across similar scenarios, making it difficult for students to develop reliable 2865 quantitative intuitions. Generated content also perpetuated harmful stereotypes about poverty and justice involvement, particularly affecting overrepresented communities (Lee et al., 2024). These failures demanded a framework for addressing stereotypes and trauma. Drawing on trauma - informed pedagogy (Carello & Butler, 2015), we committed to ensuring that scenarios allow full participation independent of personal history, that content represents systemic patterns while honoring individual complexity, and that instructors retain the ability to modify or disable any element they judge inappropriate. This framework guided the restructuring of AI’s role. Because educator control over sensitive elements is a pedagogical and ethical requirement, all factual elements became authored content maintained in versioned databases (Gibson, 2023). AI was retained solely for generating 280- character text messages formatted as communications from family members, employers, and service providers (see Figure 1). Prompts incorporate strict constraints on tone, relationship dynamics, and prohibited content, and each message passes validation filters before display. Pre - authored fallback messages activate when outputs fail validation or when instructors operate in non -AI mode (Aldrich, 2005). This bounded application introduces meaningful variation across simulation runs and supports empathy-building, all while the deterministic mechanics remain fully intact. Figure 1 The Phone Message Interface Displays AI-Generated Communications from Family Members and Service Providers. Design principles traced to practice The following principles emerged from the documented failures and institutional constraints above, and we trace each to its originating episode (Wang & Hannafin, 2005). Separation of deterministic and generative components arose because AI -generated cost s tructures produced inconsistencies that undermined learning objectives. Educator authorship of core mechanics resolved this while confining AI to a role where variability adds value and fairness is preserved. Trauma- aware content governance emerged from en counters with AI outputs that stereotyped justice-involved families. Instructor override, scenario review, and explicit content boundaries ensure that every version of the simulation actively interrogates these patterns. Privacy-conscious architecture responded to institutional review board concerns, and the minimal state approach transmits only current meter values and recent decisions (Pardo & Siemens, 2014). Redundancy and fallback systems became essential after pilot-session technical failures disrupted engagement, so pre -authored alternatives for every AI feature ensure continuity. Reflection over scoring prioritizes metacognition because early testing revealed that competitive scoring distracted students from systemic insights (Li et al., 2024). Conclusion Life Happens demonstrates that AI can enhance educational simulations when carefully bounded by pedagogical goals and equity commitments. The most consequential design decisions centered on preserving educator authority over content touching systemic inequality, trauma, and identity. These transferable principles confirm that thoughtful AI integration remains accessible across diverse educational settings when guided by clear learning objectives. 2866 References Aldrich, C. papers.title: Toward a Socio-Cognitive Framework for AI Literacy in K–8: Integrating Cognitive Science and Learning Sciences Perspectives
papers.authors: Jessica Vandenberg
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping the civic, social, and educational landscapes that children inhabit. While calls for K –8 AI literacy are expanding globally, the field lacks coherent theoretical grounding for how children learn to understand and r eason about AI systems. This paper proposes a socio-cognitive framework that integrates cognitive science and Learning Sciences perspectives to conceptualize AI literacy as a process that is both individually constructed and socially situated. The framework highlights how cognitive mechanisms (such as analogy, metacognition, and reasoning about uncertainty) emerge through collaborative, participatory learning contexts. By positioning cognition within designed social ecologies, this framework provides a foundation for designing equitable, developmentally appropriate AI literacy experiences. We argue that understanding how children make sense of AI requires integrating cognitive and sociocultural theories to advance design, research, and practice in AI education.

papers.title: Wordless Books as Tools for Language, Identity, and Voice
papers.authors: Arlen Nava, Christine Lee
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This paper is led by a dual language kindergarten teacher and presents insights on a multi-year participatory research study on wordless books. We discuss how wordless books can support emergent dual language learners by fostering literacy through storyte lling and creative expression. The paper highlights a case study on how wordless books can empower children to see themselves as competent readers. We argue for a broader definition of literacy that values and includes students’ linguistic and cultural resources, and position wordless books as a tool for equitable access to reading for all children. Objectives of our practice-oriented paper Over the past three years, Arlen and Christine , a dual language kindergarten teacher and a university researcher, have collaborated on a participatory design -based research study (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) examining the potential of wordless books for young dual language learners. Our paper examines how wordless books can serve as a powerful tool for dual language literacy, empowering young learners to take agency in their oral storytelling and reading. When we think of literacy instruction in primary grade levels, it tends to focus solely on phonics, accuracy, and decoding words. This experience can provide a narrow view of literacy, and it views children as passive recipients rather than active meaning makers (Freire & Slover, 1983). It also doesn’t leave ro om for student-driven creative expression, like storytelling. For emergent dual language learners, the act of learning to read in a new language can present an extra level of pressure, setting expectations that they have to somehow quickly master both languages. Wordless picture books offer a different kind of entry point into literacy. It can remove the pressure to perform and instead invite children to build their own narratives using a variety of resources like language, tone, gestures, and imagination. Our paper shows wordless books as a resource to support children’s identities as lifelong readers and empower them by giving children agency in their storytelling. We argue that we need to move away from deficit thinking by highlighting the immense skills children already bring to the world of reading. This means that we must ultimately expand the definition of literacy by exploring ways of being a lifelong literate human being, and help children form a relationship with literature that extends beyond merely decoding words. In this paper, we present a case study that shares how a student with limited Spanish, in a dual language classroom, can communicate powerfully to tell stories when given the tools and space to do so. We follow a kindergarten student (5 year old) who used wordless books to tell stories in both English and Spanish over time. Her storytelling showed how young children can express meaning in complex and personal ways, even when their vocabulary in a second language is limited and still dev eloping. Therefore, we wonder, how can wordless picture books support student autonomy in storytelling for emergent dual language learners? Wordless books Wordless books are picture books with little to no written text. Thus, readers rely on the illustrations and images to read and tell stories. These visual stories invite readers to interpret meaning and construct narratives using their own imagination, lived experiences, and cultural knowledge (Lee, et al., 2025; Razfar & Gutierrez, 2003; Vygotsky, 1978). Our case study draws on literature that positions literacy as a meaning- making social activity. Freire and Slover (1983) argue that literacy is not a mechanical skill to be mastered, but a process of consciousness formation where learners first “read the world” before they “read the word.” His conception of reading was that it was a critical, experiential, and transformative act (Crawford & Hade, 2000). Therefore, reading is inherently social, reflective, and tied to identity, power, and context (Vygotsky, 1978). We argue wordless books can support storytelling, language development, and creative expression, and offer young learners the opportunity to reflec t on their own experiences and prior knowledge (Arif & Hashim, 2008). Wordless books open up storytelling for all children, regardless of their reading level or language proficiency. They invite students to navigate meaning using gesture, tone, facial expression, and oral language across multiple languages (Alvermann, 2002; Dehghani et al., 2013). In doing so, wordless books position students as active participants in the meaning- making process (Freire & Slover, 1983), rather than passive recipients of a fixed and scripted narrative. Wordless books also offer space for children still developing language to engage with complex ideas and express personal insights through their own narrative decisions (Arif & Hashim, 2008; Goriot et al., 2024) . For emergent dual language learners, wordless picture books offer inclusive, flexible, and linguistically accessible 2147 entry points into literacy. Children may even feel freer to communicate authentically by lifting the pressure of correctness and allowing for fluid, spontaneous storytelling. Because the narrative is not fixed by written words, students are free to interpr et and reframe the story in ways that reflect their multilingual and multicultural experiences (Crawford & Hade, 2000). This makes wordless books especially powerful in culturally and linguistically diverse classrooms, where children can exercise autonomy and agency in meaning-making, without being confined by rigid, traditional models of literacy instruction that often feel limited at a young age. Each child, regardless of language or fluency, is encouraged by the pictures in wordless books to construct their own meaning of the story, offering beneficial possibilities for use in all-inclusive learning settings. Designing wordless books into literacy curriculum The design and implementation of wordless books into our literacy curriculum came from a multi -year collaboration between Arlen and Christine. We began the work by searching for and reading research on wordless books in early literacy. We then introduced wordless books to our kindergarten (5- 6 years) classroom, and immediately realized the potential these books had for emergent readers, especial ly as a way to equitably engage and provide access to literacy regardless of the child’s background. Our initial observation of students exploring wordless books was that these books can be a powerful tool for voice and agency. This is important for dual language classrooms and multi-lingual learners because many children in a dual language classroom can often be positioned as “being academically behind” in their literacy or language skills. We took these preliminary observations and focused on designing a learning experience for children with wordless books where they can see themselves as creative meaning-makers, where they can author their own stories, and come to form a solid identity as a reader early on. In Table 1, we outline how we designed our literacy curriculum to incorporate wordless books over the academic school year. Table 1 Outline of Wordless Books in our Literacy Curriculum. Timeline Goals Description of Goals September Exposure and exploration of wordless books Children freely explored wordless books. October-November Sequence of events and details from illustrations Students did picture walks and were encouraged to pay close attention to the details in the illustrations. Based on their observations, students made conjectures about what the story was about and where they thought the story was going. December-January Perspectives in storytelling Students explored how narration and dialogue shape a story. Tried on and played with different voices for different characters. Discussed and practiced how stories can be told in first, second, or third person. February-June Wordless books as part of regular reading practices Wordless books became a regular reading activity that sparked creative and playful conversation. Students regularly chose to read wordless books during their reading time. Case study Arlen teaches in the dual language program, and Christine is a university researcher. Our research was conducted in an elementary school in Southern California, and the case we present in this paper is from Arlen’s dual language (10% English instruction and 90% Spanish instruction) kindergarten classroom. Our focal student, Camila (pseudonym), was a five year old emergent bilingual learner who primarily spoke English at home and was newly acquiring Spanish through the school's dual language program. To explore Camila's storytelling across languages, 2148 we video-recorded her storytelling with wordless books. In November 2024, Camila narrated the wordless picture book Good Dog, Carl (Day, 1985) in English, and in March 2025, she narrated The Girl and the Bicycle (Pett, 2014) in Spanish. When we look at Camila’s number of words spoken across the two video recordings (Table 2), it is no surprise that the total words spoken in English while reading Good Dog, Carl is much higher than when she read The Girl and the Bicycle in Spanish. Table 2 Total Words Spoken when Reading in English and Spanish English (Good Dog, Carl) in November 2024 Spanish (The Girl and the Bicycle) in March 2025 Total Words Spoken 261 111 Average Words Spoken per Page 8 words per page 3 words per page In both recordings, Camila is reading the wordless books to two of her classmates who were attentively listening to the story by her side. We transcribed both video- recorded reading sessions and organized the transcripts by page to arrange her narration with the visual content of the book. Together, we analyzed the two transcripts and found two emerging themes that we present in this paper (Braun & Clarke, 2022). Theme 1: Emotional expression as a storytelling strategy Across our transcripts, Camila demonstrated that emotional expression can be a powerful tool for storytelling. Throughout the Spanish storytelling transcript, Camila relied on her vocal tone, pauses, facial gestures, and nonverbal sounds (like dramatic sighs) to convey a character's or narrator's feelings. The transcript of her Spanish reading of the wordless book was rich with these emotional expressions and was a crucial part of her storytelling. Camila expressed deep understanding of the story even when her Spanish vocabulary was limited, showing how emotional gestures, prosody, and tone can support meaning- making when verbal language is still developing. In her English narration of Good Dog, Carl , Camila primarily used sentences with consistent pacing and a neutral tone. For example, she said, “Carl looks out the window. The baby sneaks out, and the dog comes by”. While this sentence is descriptively accurate of the story, her delivery and oral t elling of it resembled the cadence of classroom read-alouds, where students are taught to prioritize clarity and linear sequencing rather than emotional interpretation and creative storytelling. In contrast, her Spanish narration of The Girl and the Bicycle had nonverbal elements like tone, gesture, and diverse pacing to convey emotional depth. Earlier in the story, she asked, “¿En dónde está mi dinero? ¿Aquí? ¿Aquí?” with a rising intonation while using her whole body to mimic the action of searching for something. Her rising intonation and repetition of “¿Aquí?” created a sense of urgency and concern, as she embodied the character's anxious search for money to buy a bicycle. Later, Camila captured the character’s disappointment by using a different tone to interpret and communicate the emotional arc of the story. She paused and sighed dramatically before saying “Poquito triste,” meaning “a little sad” as she embodied the character’s emotions when she found out the bicycle was gone. Camila effectively communicated the sadness of the moment through her tone shift, softly stating “Poquito triste”, dramatic pause, and pacing. These emotional expressions added depth to the statement, expressing a feeling that extended beyond the image itself and making listeners understand the heavy moment in the story. Therefore, Camila’s use of semiotic resources effectively communicated the feelings and emotional depth of the story despite speaking fewer words – illustrating the true power of embodiment and emotional connections in rich storytelling. Theme 2: Narrative perspectives Camila's storytelling across the two transcripts also revealed a shift in narrative perspectives. When she read Good Dog, Carl in English, her point of view was in the third person, and when she read The Girl and the Bicycle in Spanish, it was in both the third person and first person perspectives. For example, in Good Dog, Carl, she said, “They open the door, and went to the Mommy and Daddy's room, and they played with makeup”. Camila stayed in the third person, narrative perspective throughout her entire reading of the story as she orally described the events of the story. 2149 In contrast, Camila's narration in Spanish showed more fluidity. Rather than sticking to a single point of view, she moved between third person and first person to tell the story. For example, on page 8 of The Girl and the Bicycle, Camila said “No tiene más money, no tiene más monedas,” meaning “She doesn’t have any more money, she doesn’t have any more coins,”. But later, on page 13, she exclaimed, “Ven con yo! No! ¡No quiero, no gracias!” meaning “Come with me! No! I don’t want to, no thank you!”, steppi ng into the character’s voice and embodying what the character would excitedly say in the story. Camila exercised narrative autonomy, shaping the story in deeper ways that felt meaningful to her in the moment. Her inventive dialogue and expressive stance reflect how learners construct meaning by using their voice and lived experience. Instead of simply retelling the events, Camila authored a story that reflected her understanding, feelings, and agency. Concluding remarks One of the most powerful lessons learned from observing students engage with wordless books is how quickly they are able to see themselves as competent readers. Even at a young age, children can step into stories with confidence and agency before they’ve mastered decoding text. They also don’t need to rely on others to access these books. This accessibility gives them the opportunity to take ownership of their reading. As a dual language teacher, this was powerful for students because it encouraged them to take risks and play with language. It was wonderful to see young children feel empowered with their reading, as if they could grab a book and tell a story all on their own. As a result of this work, a parent thanked Arlen for our work with wordless books because her son had a hard time feeling confident while decoding text. However, she mentioned that with wordless books, he was never discouraged and always saw himself as a storyteller and reader. Recently, Arlen saw this parent on campus again, and she shared that her son now reads books and loves being a reader. She attributed his journey and growth as a reader to wordless books because they made him feel like a competent reader as he learned to decode text. As a dual language teacher, A rlen also learned that wordless books encourage emerging dual language students to take risks. While there is clearly a story to tell, wordless books have no script; thus, there is no strict expectation of what students must say. Instead, students are able to freely use the words they already know or play with new and unfamiliar words in their storytelling. Through their experimentation with storytelling, they are able to stretch themselves in a low -stakes and playful way. This feeling of agency and creative freedom is what creates space for incredible growth. We also realized that wordless books served as a tool for equity because the stories welcome every child, no matter their background knowledge. Regardless of the child’s dominant or target language, wordless books provide everyone an opportunity for conversation, making literacy accessible across all learners. The books create a space of inclusivity and allow students to connect, share, and learn from each other. Thus, every child’s unique voice is honored through expression filled with emotion, because although children are reading the author’s art and images, they are ultimately telling their own stories. When children are able to bring aspects of themselves into the classroom, such as their home language or family stories, they naturally create a space f or cultural representation through wordless books. This affirms their identities as competent and agentic storytellers and makes them visible within the classroom setting. Wordless books become a universal resource for students. Institutionalized education often lacks opportunities for every child to be heard and valued. Wordless books remove these barriers, allowing every child to be seen. Throughout our research partnership, we came to realize how intertwined research, teaching, and learning are. Before becoming a teacher, Arlen studied with Fred Erickson, whose work with teachers showed Arlen the power in positioning educators as co-constructors of knowledge. In our work, we made decisions about how wordless books would be integrated into the curriculum and how to collect and analyze our data together. We respected and made space for our intellectual insights and curiosities in this work. Not only has this made our research stronger, but it has also given Arlen the confidence to speak to other educators to reform literacy programs, especially for elementary dual language classrooms. The collaborative participation in research gave Arlen the data and the tools to communicate and share the importance of wordless books in this paper, which invites other teachers to engage in this work as a way to transform and grow our teaching practices. papers.title: A “Co-Design Intervention” with AI analytics to Support the Academically Productive Talk of Title 1 School Math Tutors and their Students: A Comparative Interrupted Time Series Analysis
papers.authors: Amirpasha Zandieh, Jeffrey Bush Tayne, Chelsea Brown, Jennifer Jacobs, Sandra Sawaya
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines whether a co- design-based professional learning intervention for tutors, supported by an AI feedback tool, influenced students’ Academically Productive Talk (APT) within a high-dosage algebra tutoring program in Title 1 schools in an urban U.S. school district. Using a comparative interrupted time series (CITS) design, we analyzed 9,037 tutoring sessions over the 42 weeks of one academic year, comparing tutors who participated in a nine - week co-design process with those who did not. Tuto rs in the intervention co -designed an AI interface called the “Talk Trees”, visualizing student talk patterns to guide student reflection on collaborative discourse. Results show short -term, positive shifts in students’ relating to academic ideas of their peers following the intervention, with modest, non- significant gains in instances of students making claims and providing reasoning. These findings highlight co- design’s potential to foster dialogic pedagogy in the context of boundary-crossing professional learning. They also demonstrate how CITS methods can evaluate AI-mediated interventions in authentic educational contexts.

papers.title: Collaboration and Competition in Educational Gameplay: Strategic Student Decision -Making
papers.authors: Tianyu Ma, Jennifer Kahn
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines how middle school students engaged in strategic decision- making when collaboration and competition were tightly intertwined in an educational gameplay setting. Drawing from a design-based research study of an afterschool program, six students played Isles of Ilkmaar, a multiplayer game designed to support data science learning. Using Activity Theory as an analytic lens, we traced how students mobilized tools, interpreted rules, and negotiated roles in the game’s diner competition. Analysis of three gameplay episodes showed students adapting in real time, moving from tool learning to contested claims and finally to rule negotiation. Findings highlight that collaboration and competition were not separate modes of activity but operated together, with conflicts often catalyzing adaptation and role change. This work contributes to CSCL by showing how collaborative learning can be sustained under competitive pressures, offering implications for the design of educational environments that integrate both cooperative and adversarial elements.

papers.title: “A Makerspace is a Lousy Place to Do School In”: Studying Student-Driven Sociocultural Shifts in a Classroom Makerspace
papers.authors: John F. “Trey” Smith, Colin Hennessy Elliott
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This paper investigates longitudinal shifts in sociocultural activity in a K-8 classroom makerspace in the United States. Using cultural historical activity theory (CHAT) as a theoretical framework and practitioner reflections over three years as a primary data source, a school-based practitioner researcher and university -based researcher identify key shifts in activity and tensions that emerged when making was both enabled and constrained by school . Findings illustrate the central role that students’ acts of self-determination can have on shifting a classroom makerspace activity system, particularly when a teacher is attuned and receptive to those acts of self -determination. Key tensions emerged related to teacher as central node for facilitating activity, even as the system shifted with student-directed activity.

papers.title: From Implementation to Innovation: Re-imagining the role of Practice in Research
papers.authors: Linette Victor
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Reverse Translation (RT) is a conceptual framework repositioning educational practice as a generative source of knowledge. Drawing from Design-Based Research (DBIR), Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs), and Improvement Science (IS), RT challenges the conventional theory-to-practice pipeline by beginning with practitioner-identified tensions and insights. It offers a structured process for elevating practitioner insights into theoretical discourse, fostering reciprocal learning, and context-specific innovation. This model is especially relevant for knowledge mobilizers, such as instructional coaches and teacher leaders, who often support others ’growth without sustained opportunities to develop their own practice. RT contributes to the learning sciences by expanding methodologies for practice-initiated inquiry, deepening commitments to equity, and strengthening the relevance and adaptability of contextually grounded interventions. Using vignettes and applied examples, this paper identifies how RT can inform professional development and research design, bridging the research- practice divide in more effective ways.

papers.title: Knowledge Links in the Wild
papers.authors: Kathy L. Schuh, Mandy Dunphy, Faiaz Rahman, Ricardo Domingues
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study explores learning processes in an outdoor experiential learning opportunity to understand how learners may use their prior knowledge in these settings . Grounded in constructivism and generative learning, we operationalized students’ meaning making through knowledge construction links, capturing the links between what students already know and what they are learning via a system of cues and trajectory dimensions. Using qualitative methods, we observed and recorded interactions of students from three sixth -grade classrooms while they attended School of the Wild. Students also participated in follow -up interviews and a writing activity. Findings indicated that while knowledge links in this outdoor environment were similar to those in classrooms document ed in prior research , differences included a more robust definition for the function cue, the enactment of elements from students’ media trajectories, and the juxtaposition of prior learning with historical artifacts that problematized their learning task.

papers.title: Learning to Deconstruct AI/ML Systems: Scaffolds to Support Learners in Critically Evaluating
papers.authors: Luis Morales-Navarro, Yasmin B. Kafai, Olli Hilke, Nicolas Pope, Matti Tedre, Daniel J. Noh, Rotem Landesman, Jayne Everson, Jean Ryoo, Ole Sejer Iversen
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Historically, the learning sciences have emphasized how computing construction activities can support learners in building relationships between old and new knowledge in interactions with others while creating artifacts of social relevance. With the ubiquity of socia l media and AI/ML, researchers have turned their attention to the social and ethical implications of computing, proposing that deconstruction—the process of critically examining and understanding how meaning and intentionality are encoded into computing systems and practices that impact people’s lives and the environment —is equally important. In this symposium we bring together researchers investigating how to design deconstruction learning activities in which young people critically evaluate AI/ML systems of social relevance. We present different perspectives on how to design activities and scaffold learners to examine the socio-ethical implications of AI/ML systems. We discuss the role of deconstruction in computing education and its relation to construction activities. Symposium overview The learning sciences have been concerned with how involving learners in the construction of socially relevant computing applications for and with other people can support knowledge construction (Kafai, 2006; Holbert et al., 2021). This interest in construction can be traced back to Papert’s work on constructionism (see Papert, 1991), which argued that knowledge structures are built through the creation of personal and socially relevant artifacts, centering on the connected nature of knowledge with its personal and social dimensions. Today, many tools and educational efforts have embraced constructionism, positioning young people as designers of applications, from commercial products such as Nintendo’s Game Builder Garage and Roblox to educational tools and curricula that have made designing applications a mainstay in most K-12 computing education initiatives (Kafai & Burke, 2014; Oleson et al., 2020; Waite & Sentance, 2021). 2203 Yet, with the ubiquity of social media and AI/ML and their ethical, environmental, and societal implications (Ko et al., 2020), coupled with the political or critical turn in the learning sciences (Politics of Learning Writing Collective, 2017), researchers have turned their attention to the equally important process of deconstruction. Iversen and colleagues (2018) define deconstruction as the process of “critically examining and understanding how meaning and intentionality are encoded into digital artifac ts and practices that impact upon our everyday lives.” Deconstruction involves describing, evaluating and reflecting on the values and intentions embedded in sociotechnical systems used in everyday life while considering their possible implications (Dindle r et al., 2020; Schaper et al., 2023). We argue that such practices can contribute to learners' development of both ethical and functional understandings of AI/ML systems. This involves assessing the properties of a system in terms of its inputs, outputs and materials (e.g., data); inquiring about the intended use and actual use of a system; foregrounding the values, worldviews, and assumptions embedded in the system; and investigating how the system impacts individuals, communities and the environment (Dindler et al., 2023). In this symposium, we bring together researchers taking different approaches to deconstruction to address the following research questions: How can we design activities that scaffold learners to deconstruct AI/ML systems? How does deconstruction support learners in developing their functional and ethical understanding of AI/ML systems? Contributions include presentations about tools and activities that foster deconstruction, participatory approaches that involve teachers in the design of deconstruction acti vities, and insights into learners' thinking processes when investigating socio- ethical issues. Furthermore, we discuss how deconstruction relates to construction and their role in computing education. This session is organized in three sections: (1) the chairs will introduce the topic and participants (~10 min); (2) participants will have seven minutes to share their work; (3) our discussants Jean Ryoo, a learning scientist and computing education researcher that has advocated for equity and inquiry-oriented computing, and Ole Sejer Iversen, a child-computer interaction and activity theory researcher that proposed the term deconstruction, will synthesize and reflect on findings (10 min), followed by a Q&A with the audience and presenters (~15 min). Presentation 1 — Deconstructing machine vision with breakable machine Olli Hilke, Nicolas Pope, Matti Tedre Many K–12 education initiatives use “Teachable Machine” -type tools to let students build simple models, but these activities face difficulties preparing students to interrogate or critique the complex commercial AI -driven systems they frequently use. The AI - and data-driven systems from major companies can often produce biased or misleading results, but when they fail, it often happens in subtle and unpredictable ways —and because they are proprietary black boxes, it is nearly impossible to see why they failed. Yet, understanding that AI systems are not neutral or infallible requires exposing their brittleness, hidden biases, and human design choices. Breakable Machine (Hilke et al., 2025) (spoof.gen- ai.fi) offers students an accessible entry point into scaffolded critical inquiry and analysis of construction, use, values, and consequences of AI systems. It is a multiplayer, browser-based classroom game that lets students destabilize and probe an image classifier in real - time while competing with one another. papers.title: Dignity-Affirming Music Pedagogy: Reframing Music as Relational Design in Learning Spaces
papers.authors: Melanie West, Shirin Vossoughi, Michael Horn, Melita Morales, Samual Carrol
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: In K -12 education settings, music is often framed as an enrichment activity, overlooking its deeper role in shaping dignity -affirming learning spaces and in organizing interaction among community members. We examine music as interactional infrastructure, asking how it makes dignity observable in learning environments. Using Rhythmic Interaction Analysis (RIA), we analyze a drum circle interaction to examine how participation unfolds through rhythmic turns. We trace how vulnerability, attunement, and agency emerge as participants respond to one another, illustrating how dignity can be made visible through coordinated, embodied interaction. Problem / reframe Within K -12 education settings, music is often invoked to motivate participation, support memorization, or improve testable skills (Bhide, Power, & Goswami, 2013; Governor, Hall, & Jackson, 2013; Ashley & Timmers, 2017; Kumar et al., 2022). Such framings risk eclipsing music’s relational, historical, and identity work (Blacking, 1973; Small, 1998; Robinson, 2020; Hess, 2019). At the same time, dignity- affirming education (DAE) calls for learning environments that center learners’ full humanity—supporting vulnerability, agency, and meaningful participation through relational practice (Espinoza, et al., 2020; Vossoughi, et al., 2018; Keifert, et al., 2021). This perspective shifts attention from outcomes alone to the conditions under which learners are recognized, supported, and able to contribute. We take up this shift by approaching music as an epistemic and affective partner that co-organizes learning. In this view, meaning- making unfolds as a collective process of “rhythmic attunement” —people sensing, responding to, and adapting with one another, much like players in an ensemble. Grounded in DAE, ethnomusicology, and sociocultural theories, we ask: How can music -infused pedagogy—listening, speaking about music, and making music together —cultivate learning environments that affirm students’ dignity and agency while expanding relational forms of participation? Conceptual orientation: Dignity as interaction Rhythm has long been understood as a structuring feature of social interaction, shaping how participants coordinate attention, timing, and response (Erickson, 1982; Bassetti & Bottazzi, 2015). We examine how rhythmic interaction organizes participation itself. As participants coordinate through rhythm, they make space for one another’s contributions —creating conditions where participation can be recognized, supported, and sustained. From this perspective, dignity is not an abstract quality of a learning environment, but something enacted in time, as participants recognize, respond to, and sustain one another’s contributions. We ground this work in dignity-affirming education, which frames learning as a relational practice enacted through everyday interaction. To make this construct analytically tractable, we focus on three observable dimensions: vulnerability—moments where participants take risks (e.g., initiating a contribution); attunement—moments of alignment (e.g., synchronized timing or coordinated response); and agency—moments where participants shape the direction of activity.

papers.title: Bodies, Participation, and Power: Learning as a Site of Inclusion, Exclusion, and Resistance
papers.authors: Morgan Vickery
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Youth bring diverse ways of knowing, communicating, and creating meaning to school, yet classrooms often privilege a narrow slice of these practices—treating difference as deficit and leaving many disabled, neurodivergent, queer, or trauma-impacted youth at the margins of participation. These exclusions affect belonging and access to civic, community, and disciplinary life. My research investigates how to design asset-oriented, participatory, and body- inclusive learning environments for young adolescents, where questions of identity and belonging are especially acute. Drawing on sociocultural and critical learning theories, participatory design-based research, and social models of ability and the body, I examine how multimodal repertoires can be recognized and leveraged as learning resources. This agenda advances three strands focused on designing multimodal learning environments that prioritize learner and educator dignity: (1) expanding conceptions of adolescent participation and literacy, (2) designing inclusive multimodal technologies, and (3) positioning youth as co-designers and co-theorists of their learning. Strand 1: Expanding conceptions of youth participation This strand is grounded in my experiences and those of current adolescents regarding secondary schools’ narrow conceptions of participation. Secondary schooling has privileged print and verbal literacies while devaluing embodied, affective, and multimodal avenues for meaning-making. These framings disproportionately exclude multiply-marginalized adolescents and reinforce deficit orientations and hegemonic norms. In my previous work, I employ a social model of disability to explore how schools ‘disable’ and ‘enable’ certain bodies, calling for researchers to shift responsibility for student performance away from the individual and onto the design of the system in which they operate (Vickery, 2023). In my dissertation, I introduce a five- dimensional inter-theoretical framework that conceptualizes the body as simultaneously thinking, feeling, observed, politicized, and autonomous. I also provide methodological guidance for conducting humanizing, dignity-affirming research with youth living in non-normative bodies (Vickery, 2025a) and employ critical resistance narrative analysis to examine how adolescents navigate and resist normative embodied expectations in schools (Vickery, 2025b). Moving forward, I expand normative notions of participation in youth civic education. I extend this work into civic and technical domains—motivated by the current sociopolitical climate. Such work demands multidisciplinary and multimodal competencies that cannot be siloed within individual subject areas. To these ends, I hope to support adolescents’ learning of media, data, digital, and scientific literacies through engagement with culturally relevant issues. Building from epistemic practices in science and engineering education (e.g., evidence evaluation, systems reasoning, modeling), I see opportunities to extend these into literacy/language education (rhetorical device usage, media & data literacy, interpretation of misinformation), social studies/history (complex sociopolitical systems, causal mechanisms), and computing education (engineering ethics, data privacy, transparency, ethical AI adoption). As political systems increasingly disenfranchise multiply-marginalized youth, these literacies become not abstract skills but conceptual and tangible tools for civic and social change. A society of care must acknowledge and design against these barriers. Strand 2: Designing inclusive multimodal technologies This strand is rooted in my experience as a UX designer and researcher, where access and inclusion were often addressed retroactively rather than prioritized from the start. In educational technologies, this reinforces deficit- oriented assumptions about learners whose practices do not align with normative expectations. This work centers on learners’ histories, needs, and desires in the edtech design process, ensuring technologies are proactive, responsive, and adaptive to learners’ needs. In my recent work (Vickery & Danish, 2025), I share my rapid design and iterative refinement of a mixed-reality embodied learning environment for a reverse-inclusion summer camp for youth with moderate-to- severe disabilities, aimed at identifying and addressing barriers to expression and participation. In my 2024 work o n the GEM-STEP project (Vickery et al., 2024; NSF Grants #1908632 & #1908791), I led my team in integrating trauma-informed pedagogies into the facilitation and evaluation of mixed-reality embodied activities (where students use motion-tracking technologies to collaboratively model complex scientific phenomena), demonstrating how centering comfort, choice, and agency can amplify students’ capacities for participation. In Zhou et al. (2025), we investigate how elementary learners' group-divergent embodied practices afford opportunities to learn about complex scientific phenomena. As a Visiting Research Scientist funded by the Engage AI Institute, I design and develop narrative-based, AI-scaffolded, gamified experiences for middle school students that are context-relevant and engage learners in critical thinking about food and environmental justice (Humburg et al., 2025). I build on my dual background in software engineering and UX design to critically engage with how ‘cutting-edge’ technologies such as AI, XR, and asynchronous learning tools are implemented at scale. My prior work has often relied on retrofitting inclusion into technologies – moving forward, I hope to (1) establish trusting partnerships with schools and communities, (2) conduct on-the-ground needs assessments, (3) co-design contextually grounded solutions with these needs prioritized at the onset, and (4) iteratively evaluate implementation. Access and inclusion are not endpoints but baselines; innovation must be defined by—and accountable to—those most impacted. Strand 3: Positioning youth as co-designers and co-theorists of their learning This strand addresses a tension across education and research alike – that too often, youth are positioned as passive users of and participants in designs they had no role in shaping. Thus, these designs (which here include pedagogies, activities, tools, communities, and theories) fail to provide the necessary scaffolding for youth to thrive and learn within them. My work takes an asset-oriented stance, treating adolescents’ perspectives and repertoires of practice as valuable resources for designing more sensitive, equitable, and emancipatory experiences for youth who would otherwise be forced to (at best) change themselves for the sake of compliance. In prior work, I’ve offered autoethnographic accounts of how my traditional notions of research-practice partnerships were challenged and remade in a collaboration with local paraprofessionals, special educators, and youth with disabilities (Vickery & Peabody, Under Review). In my dissertation Article 2 (Vickery, 2025c), I drew on Vygotskian notions of mediation and affect to understand what affective, sensory, and lived experiences are activated for youth with non-normative embodied experiences in the presence of various instructional design elements (i.e. various activity/task framings, technologies, proximity of embodiment, sensory demands, forms of movement, & participation structures). Further, Article 3 positions youth as co-theorists of a framework for dignity-affirming, body-inclusive embodied learning environments (Vickery, 2025d). This strand responds to a recurring theme across my projects—that “grown-ups just don’t get it.” This perceived ignorance strains opportunities for authentic educator–youth relationships and deepens youth distrust of educational systems. To address this, I aim to develop organized, protected “designer spaces”—digital and physical—for youth to co-design community-facing projects and professional development for educators and youth-service providers. Theoretically, this strand validates youth knowledge as legitimate civic and pedagogical insight; methodologically, it redefines youth’s role in research beyond that of participants to that of educators and researchers with the means to help adults “do better.” References Humburg, M., Danish, J., Kim, Y., Hmelo-Silver, C., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., Ryan, Z., Glazewski, K., & Lester, J. papers.title: Exploring the Affordances and Challenges of Participatory Co-Analysis of Clinical Interviews
papers.authors: Hedi Jaza, Marta Kobiela, Amna Fleeh
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Clinical interviews have long served as a method to learn about individual’s thinking and reasoning in mathematics and science education. Yet, analysis of interviews has often relied solely on researcher interpretations. In this methodological paper, we s hare an alternate approach in which we engaged in co -analysis with research participants. We focus on co- analysis sessions conducted with one preservice teacher (the third author) following her engagement in a task -based clinical interview about s patial rotation. We examine how the co- analysis provided additional insights into the participant’s spatial reasoning and the challenges that arose for both the researchers and participant. Our findings suggest the potential of co- analysis for providing greater understanding of participants’ use of gesture and language.

papers.title: How Simulation Design Shapes Academically Productive Talk: An Epistemic Network Analysis of Teacher Discourse in Middle-School Physics
papers.authors: Wei Jia, Kexin Li, Gaowei Chen
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Dialogic teaching, through Academically Productive Talk (APT), enhances student learning. While digital simulations are common in science education, their specific impact on teacher discourse patterns remains underexplored. This study examines how simulation design, Multiple Representations (MR) versus Single Representation (SR), shapes whole -class discourse structure and teachers’ use of APT moves. One teacher and 99 eighth-grade students from two classes in Western China participated. Using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) and discourse analysis of 147 teacher talk turns, we compared APT patterns between two conditions. ENA revealed distinct strategic repertoires: the MR condition showed an integrated, collaborative network centered on reasoning and building on ideas, involving more students in shorter, focused turns. The SR condition exhibited a linear, teacher- guided pattern dominated by elicitation and challenge, with longer explanations from fewer students. Overall, simulation design relates to teacher facilitation and student participation, suggesting that multiple representational tools may afford more collaborative-dialogic classrooms.

papers.title: Toward Expansive Teacher Imagination: Design Principles from a Review of Speculative Education Literature
papers.authors: Brit Claiborne
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Speculative imagining—the act of envisioning a future beyond the constraints of the present—is at the core of a growing body of research in the learning sciences. The aim of this literature review is to analyze the limited subset of this research that engages teachers and teacher educators in speculative imagination in order to identify the qualities of learning environments that support the complex imaginative work of speculation for teachers. Out of the analysis of these qualities, I propose four design principles for designing learning environments for teacher speculation. These principles have utility for guiding future speculative learning experiences for teachers, as speculative activities are growing in their use in teacher education and professional development. The personal, historical, creative, and collective resources that come together across the four proposed principles coalesce to outline a path for designing for teacher speculation that challenges the systemic constraints of the education system.

papers.title: Speculative Learning Through Conference Participation: On the Affordances of Rogue Poster Sessions
papers.authors: Colin Hennessy Elliott, Peter J. Woods
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: While some education researchers have begun to explore the learning that happens at academic conferences, this work largely examines the praxes of sanctioned participation (e.g., presentations, organizing, networking). In response, we use this paper to explore the learning that occurred during “rogue” poster sessions that the authors conducted at the 2025 ISLS annual meeting focused on a poster conceptualizing learning at the conference itself. Analyzing video recordings of four rogue poster prese ntations, we iterate a model of speculative and participatory learning that builds from the content of the poster to reimagine the borders of the learning sciences and the conference itself. Beyond our analysis of learning within (familiar) poster presentations, w e propose the embrace of unsanctioned conference participation as a means to amplify marginalized voices and ways of knowing in the field while also acknowledging the inherent barriers that come with challenging social norms in this way.

papers.title: From Solo to Collaborative: Design Affordances in Multi-User Immersive VR Simulations for Transforming Science Learning
papers.authors: Michelle Lui, Sunnie Gong, Chloe Lok
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) shows promise for science learning by enabling visualization of microscopic phenomena and dynamic processes. However, research has focused predominantly on individual learning experiences, overlooking the social nature of learning. This study investigates the collaborative affordances of multi -user IVR for science education through participatory design, involving six teams of undergraduate students and educators who co- created IVR learning simulations. Findings revealed seven science learning affordances: microscopic visualization, spatial relationships, scale traversal, representational connections, perspective-taking, temporal phenomena, and procedural skills—which multi-user IVR amplified through embodied communication, role -taking that grounds collaborative discourse, and distributed perspectives that require coordination. Analysis of designs highlights how narrative structures establish group- worthy joint tasks, fostering six collaborative activity types. Variations in structuring collaborative processes emerged from play- level scripts with undifferentiated roles, and scene -level scripts with defined roles enhanc ing interdependence. Results provide design insights for leveraging IVR ’s spatial and embodied features in collaborative science learning.

papers.title: Stories, Futures and Histories: Co-design Routines to Center Community Knowledge for Environmental Education in India
papers.authors: Gautam Bisht, Vishesh Kumar, Pankaj Dev, Jyoti Tiwari, Ankit Bhatt, Lata Upreti, Kiran Pant
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Centering co-design as a site of social justice, we analyze a collaboration between learning scientists and local teachers from a non-profit organization in the Himalayan region of Uttarakhand, India. We ask, what design routines support the emergence of c ommunity-driven ideas for ecological education, and how do they build on each other to deepen cultural, imaginative, and historical engagement? Data for this paper comes from the initial phase of collaboration, which consisted of six online meetings, each two hour long. We conducted thematic analysis along to identify three interconnected routines: (i) autecology narratives surfaced ecological connections grounded in community and personal rituals, (ii) speculative futuring opened imaginative engagement with communication, technology, and markets; and (iii) interactions with community elders supported the development of critical historicity. Together, these routines illustrate a co -design approach which fosters collective sense -making integrating cultural, imaginative, and historical dimensions of community life .

papers.title: Integrating the Learning Sciences into Technical Infrastructure for the Future of AI in Education
papers.authors: Jeremy Roschelle, John Whitmer, Rene Kizilcec, Xin Wei
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly influential in education, attention must extend beyond AI applications to the technical infrastructure on which those applications depend. Datasets, models, benchmarks, and governance mechanisms are already shaping the future of educational AI, yet these foundational resources are often developed without sufficient engagement with the learning sciences. This workshop explores how learning scientists can contribute to the design of such infrastructural public goods in ways that better reflect what is known about learning, while also addressing concerns related to safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. By bringing together researchers working at the intersection of AI and learning, the workshop seeks to identify promising lines of work, articulate key tensions, and stimulate future collaboration on learning-science-informed AI infrastructure. Overview The learning sciences offer strong conceptual foundations for the design of educational AI, drawing on longstanding research on scaffolding, feedback, self-regulation, and collaboration (Quintana et al., 2004; Hattie & Timperley, 2007; Järvelä et al., 2016; Sawyer, 2022). Yet these principles still only lightly shape the datasets, benchmarks, and model documentation on which AI systems depend. Training data rarely reflect what is known about productive learning interactions; benchmarks tend to measure task completion or factual accuracy rather than the quality of scaffolding or the depth of learner understanding; and model documentation seldom describes how a system's design relates to evidence on how people learn. Recent work by major AI developers signals growing interest in grounding educational AI in learning sciences principles (Jurenka et al., 2024; LearnLM Team, Google, 2025), but without more intentional integration into underlying infrastructure, educational AI risks prioritizing efficiency or engagement over meaningful support for learning. As past waves of "personalized learning" have shown, technology that optimizes for engagement without attending to how learning works can reproduce rather than address longstanding inequities in educational opportunity. This challenge is particularly pressing as new efforts seek to build openly shared educational AI resources as public goods. The K–12 AI Infrastructure Initiative, a five-year, $26 million effort led by Digital Promise and a coalition of partners, is funding the development of tutoring interaction corpora, learning-aligned benchmarks, and model documentation frameworks that embed pedagogical principles by design (Digital Promise, 2025; Roschelle et al., 2025). For such resources to genuinely advance learning, learning scientists must be actively involved in their co-design alongside AI engineers, education practitioners, and policymakers — contributing not only domain knowledge but also the critical perspectives needed to navigate questions of safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. This workshop therefore explores how the learning sciences can be systematically integrated into these infrastructural public goods. It brings together learning scientists, AI developers, education practitioners, and funders to examine where and how learning sciences expertise is most needed in the development of technical infrastructure for educational AI. Its goals are to inform participants about emerging infrastructure efforts and the role learning sciences can play in shaping them, create space for participants to share current work and articulate concerns, identify promising directions for future research and investment, and stimulate the formation of cross- sector collaborations. Building on recent ISLS programming on AI and education (International Society of the Learning Sciences, 2022, 2024), the workshop positions the learning sciences not only as a field that evaluates AI applications after they are built, but as one that can help shape the foundations on which educational AI is constructed. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108776462 GoGoData Participatory Sensing: Students, Educators and Researchers Building Collaborative Data Networks Charles Pimentel charlespimentel@ufrj.br Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) Vithoria Cabreira vithoriacabreira@gmail.com Federal Technological University of Paraná (UTFPR) Walter Akio Goya, Paulo Blikstein, Renato Russo aag2197@tc.columbia.edu, paulob@tc.columbia.edu, renrusso@gmail.com Teachers College, Columbia University Arnan Sipitakiat arnan.s@cmu.ac.th Chiang Mai University Abstract: In this half-day workshop, participants will engage with GoGoData, an open learning plugin that connects the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) communication, and the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) to support participatory sensing and collaborative exploration of real-time data. Beyond experimenting with the plugin’s features for data collection, transmission, and interpretation, participants will analyze GoGoData as a design case that integrates constructionist principles with learning sciences perspectives on data literacy. Participants will, in turn, extend these theoretical and design lenses to examine how collaborative data networks can foster critical engagement with data in their own educational and research contexts. Proposers/Organizers Charles Pimentel Charles Pimentel is a Research Fellow at the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, supporting the documentation of the GoGo Board and the development of data-focused learning activities. She supports the development of digital tools and web technologies for educational and research projects. Her interests include software development, web platforms, and the creation of digital solutions that improve user experience. Vithoria is currently strengthening her technical skills through practical projects and experimentation with new technologies. Akio Goya Akio is an Educational Technology Designer for the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, coordinating the design, implementation, and documentation of GoGo Boards in Brazil, as well as the implementation of makerspaces in public schools. Akio holds a Master’s degree in Instructional Technology and Media from Teachers College, Columbia University (USA) and a Master’s and a Bachelor’s degree in Computer Engineering from University of Sao Paulo (Brazil), and a Teacher Licensure in Mathematics (Middle and High School) from FIAR (Brazil). Paulo Blikstein P aulo Blikstein is an Associate Professor at Teachers College and an Affiliate Associate Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, where he directs the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab and the Lemann Center for Brazilian Studies. His research focuses on how new technologies can transform the learning of science, engineering and computation. Paulo is the co-inventor of the GoGo Board, co-leading its research and development since 2001. Paulo has a Ph.D. from Northwestern University, a MSc. from the MIT Media Lab and an M.Eng. and B.Eng. from the University of São Paulo, Brazil. Renato Russo Renato is a doctoral candidate at the Technology, Media, and Learning program at Teachers College, Columbia University and a researcher at Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. In his research, Renato explores how learning technologies can promote critical and emancipatory knowledge construction practices. Renato earned a MA degree in Learning, Design and Technology from Stanford University Graduate School of Education. Arnan (Roger) Sipitakiat Arnan (Roger) directs the Teaching and Learning Innovation Center (TLIC) at Chiang Mai University in Thailand. As a faculty and researcher at the Computer Engineering Department, he also directs the Learning Inventions Laboratory (LIL). Arnan is the co-inventor of the GoGo Board, co-leading research and development on the toolkit since 2001. Arnan focuses on designing technologically-rich learning tools, such as the GoGo Board, that have allowed students to explore areas including robotics, interactive art, games, agriculture, and community development. Arnan earned his MSc. and Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and B.Eng. from Chiang Mai University. Intended audience This workshop is intended for graduate students, educators, and researchers interested in exploring participatory sensing, critical data literacy, and learning technology design through hands-on experimentation. It particularly welcomes those studying or developing tools that connect physical computing, IoT, and real-time data exploration to promote collaborative inquiry and learning. More broadly, the session is open to all participants interested in integrating constructionist and learning sciences perspectives into the design of educational technologies. (Note that GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP are open-source platforms.) Duration of the event Half-day (3-4 hours, flexible depending on conference scheduling demands). Description of the event The GoGo Board was invented in 2001 as a low-cost and learner-friendly robotics and scientific sensing platform. In the years since, the project has undergone several design iterations, each affording new possibilities for students across diverse ages and backgrounds to explore powerful ideas in computing and STEM. In this workshop, participants will also engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that connects the GoGo Board to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data communication and visualization. CODAP, developed by the Concord Consortium, has a long-standing history as an open-source environment for data analysis and modeling that supports inquiry-based learning. Together, GoGoData, the GoGo Board Kit version 7, and CODAP create a participatory sensing ecosystem that enables students to collect, share, and interpret live data while examining the learning sciences principles underlying the design of these tools [1-3]. Workshop Format The workshop will be organized into five main activities. I - Historical framing. Participants will begin with a brief discussion on the evolution of tangible interfaces within the Learning Sciences and basic education contexts. This discussion will be situated alongside the rise of big data practices and participatory or crowd sensing, showing how learner-generated, real-time data from distributed sensors can reshape inquiry, evidence making, and classroom discourse. The framing will surface design lessons on openness, transparency, and agency, linking data practices to issues of provenance, privacy, and ethics, and highlighting how collaborative data networks can support critical engagement and community action. II - Exploring the GoGo Board 7 / GoGoData / CODAP. Participants will explore the core features of the GoGo Board version 7 and the GoGoData plugin, examining how each component emerged from research data and i terative design decisions. Using onboard controls, they will visualize sensor values, directly before connecting to a computer to interact with GoGoData and its integration with the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP). Through this connection, participants will experience how real-time sensor data can be collected, transmitted, analyzed, and explored within CODAP’s interactive environment. Facilitators will highlight how each feature embodies specific design principles that link tangible experimentation with data-driven inquiry. III - Participatory sensing exploration. Participants will collaboratively select a variable to measure, such as temperature, luminosity, pollution, or sound level, using a GoGo Board 7 kit sensor. Working in small groups, they will connect the GoGo Board to CODAP through the GoGoData plugin and deploy sensors in different internet-connected areas across the UCI campus. Each group will collect and share real-time data through the open-source plugin integrated with the data analysis platform, contributing to a collaborative network of distributed measurements. As data accumulate, participants will analyze emerging patterns across locations, drawing inferences about environmental or contextual factors. The activity will conclude with a collective discussion where groups interpret their findings, reflect on methodological decisions, and connect their insights to broader perspectives on participatory sensing, open data collaboration, and critical data literacy in education. IV - Conclusion and gallery walk. Participants will share and discuss the outcomes of their activities, reflecting on the lessons learned and insights gained throughout the workshop. The session will conclude with a collective show-and-tell, allowing groups to present their findings, highlight key observations from the participatory sensing exercise, and connect these experiences to broader questions about learning, design, and data literacy. V - Post-workshop interaction. Optional follow-up opportunities will be provided for participants who wish to continue collaborating after the session. These interactions may include online discussions, exchange of design ideas, and updates on future developments of the GoGoData platform. Participants will be invited to share reflections, resources, and potential research connections that extend the learning and collaboration initiated during the workshop. Throughout the workshop, facilitators will guide discussions connecting the design of GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP to learning sciences and constructionist frameworks, emphasizing how participatory sensing and data exploration are enhanced by open-source ecosystems. The session will highlight how openness, transparency, and accessibility in these tools empower learners and researchers to collaboratively collect, analyze, and interpret real-time data. Rather than serving as a technical training, the workshop offers a hands-on exploration of how open, theory-informed technologies developed through over twenty years of design-based research can foster agency, collaboration, and critical engagement with data. Participation requirements No requirements. We invite to join all participants interested in tangible interface design, educational robotics, and data science, irrespective of skill or experience levels. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past The author team conducted an NSF-funded project at the New York Hall of Science in collaboration with Teachers College, Columbia University, using the GoGo Board in data science camps for middle school students under the AISL program. We also did a physical computing workshop at ISLS 2024. Facilities and equipment required Facilities: ● Projector / screen for workshop facilitators ● Wifi connectivity Equipment: ● Gogo Boards Kits (board and sensors - we will provide them) ● Participants will be asked to bring their laptops with an available USB-C port. Minimal and maximal number of participants expected 8 - 15 participants Draft call for participation C alling all researchers, designers, and educators interested in exploring the power of participatory sensing to connect learning, data, and design. In this half-day workshop, you will engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that links the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, and Internet of Things (IoT) communication to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data exploration. Together, these tools create a participatory sensing ecosystem where learners and researchers can collaboratively collect, share, and interpret live data (Figer 1). Beyond experimenting with the platform’s features, you will analyze GoGoData as a design case informed by constructionist and learning sciences perspectives, building on over two decades of iterative design research with the GoGo Board. This workshop offers a unique opportunity to experience how open-source technologies can empower communities to transform local data into meaningful insights and to apply these theoretical and design perspectives to your own educational research and development projects. Workshop format The workshop is planned for in-person delivery, with the option of hybrid participation if necessary. The program will include interactive, hands-on activities supported by remote contributions from members of the international workshop team, ensuring collaboration and engagement across locations.
