papers.title: Playful Learning in the Community: An interactive tour of community based early learning installations
papers.authors: Andres S. Bustamante, Maria J. Anderson-Coto, Karlena D. Ochoa, Annelise Pesch, Julie Salazar
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Playful Learning Landscapes (PLL) transforms everyday community spaces like parks, bus-stops, and grocery stores into conduits for caregiver-child interactions and early learning. During this workshop, attendees will visit a series of PLL installations in Santa Ana, CA, which were co-designed by researchers from UC Irvine and Temple University, and families from the Santa Ana Early Learning Initiative, a local grassroots non-profit community organization. Attendees will engage with the PLL installations and learn about the design process and impact of the installations on community members and caregiver child interactions at PLL sites. The session will also demonstrate how this project was conducted in partnership with the City of Santa Ana’s Parks and Recreation and Public Works departments who own and maintain the installations and have begun to replicate them using public funds in other community spaces. Challenges, lessons learned, plans for sustainability, and practical and theoretical insights will be discussed. Playful learning in the community: An interactive tour of community based early learning installations Informal learning environments like children’s museums, zoos, and maker spaces are powerful contexts for supporting young children’s science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) learning and identity. Unfortunately, children from low-income families have less access to these spaces due to a variety of barriers like admission prices, transportation challenges, or even an awareness of their existence. In addition to these barriers, linguistically and ethnically minoritized families can feel alienated in these spaces which rarely center their languages, cultural values, and practices. Playful Learning Landscapes is an international initiative that brings informal learning installations to everyday spaces like parks, bus-stops, grocery stores, laundry mats, medical clinic waiting rooms, sidewalks, and walls (Hassinger-Das, 2018; Bustamante et al., 2019). Playful Learning Landscapes promote the caregiver-child conversations and interactions that decades of developmental and learning sciences research suggest lead to learning, such as conversational turns, STEM language, and hands-on engagement (Bustamante et al., 2020; Hassinger-Das et al., 2021; Pesch et al., 2025). In addition to designing PLLs based on the latest research in developmental and learning sciences, they are also designed in partnership with local families, so the installations build from families’ values, routines, and cultural practices (Bermudez et al., 2023). Understanding learning as a cultural process situates family’s participation in learning environments and design as dictated by values, routines, and cultural practices (Bang & Medin, 2010; Rogoff et al, 2007). Leveraging cultural assets, practices, and values can therefore increase relevance and significance for families, in turn increasing inclusivity, sustainability, and engagement. Partners The PLL work in Santa Ana, CA, is conducted in the context of a long-term research practice partnership between the Santa Ana Early Learning Initiative (SAELI), the University of California Irvine, and the City of Santa Ana. SAELI is a grassroots non-profit community organization bringing together local families, non-profit organizations, and leadership from the Santa Ana Unified School district to support families with children between 0-9 years of age. SAELI is led by director Wendy Gomez and uses a multigenerational approach through which promotoras (e.g., Chen et al., 2023) promote wellness through initiatives on child development, connecting families with resources, and local advocacy projects. On the university side, these projects are led by UC Irvine S chool of Education Professors Andres Bustamante and June Ahn and Temple University Psychology Professor Kathy Hirsh-Pasek. This research team brings expertise in child development, early education, participatory design, and research practice partnerships. The City of Santa Ana supported the project through their Parks and Recreation Department and Public Works Department, with support from the City Manager’s Office, Mayor's Office, and City Council. Other organizations and businesses included in this work were Northgate Gonzalez Market grocery chain, the Santa Ana Unified School District, First Five Orange County, and Orange County Health Care Agency. In this RPP, we endeavored to center families’ voices in all phases of the process from designing the installations, to deciding their locations, to the evaluation research, and dissemination of the findings. Importantly, trust and relationship-building with families were central to the design sessions. Personal stories and family values were shared through informal conversations over meals. These informal opportunities to connect allowed trust to be built over time, which uniquely positioned researchers and families as equals. We believe this allowed families to share openly and addressed traditional power dynamics between researchers and families. Decisions were taken jointly through parallel conversations with partners and interested parties, requiring transparency, trust-building, multiple channels of communication, rapid problem-solving, adaptation, and other forms of invisible relational labor. However, tensions emerged throughout the process particularly when navigating the intersection of large bureaucracies including federal funding, university systems, and city government. The project faced multiple challenges, including changing project timelines and material constraints, changes in organizational leadership, physical limitations of the public spaces designated for installations, and the complex social and political contexts of the community. Given existing power differentials between governmental partners and community stakeholders, our university team played a critical intermediary role, advocating on behalf of the community in certain cases. Whereas in other cases, our community partners stepped up and advocated for the project using their influence as voting constituents and activists in their community. Ultimately, the political capital of all stake- holders was necessary to bring this project to fruition. Research design in the community The Santa Ana PLLs were supported by an Advancing Informal STEM Learning (AISL) award from the National Science Foundation. The project began in 2020, and due to the pandemic, all design sessions in the first year of the project were held on Zoom. We held seven 90-minute co-design sessions where we learned about families histories and experiences with their community spaces, and used participatory design activities such as bags-of- stuff, photo-elicitation, story boarding, and storytelling to encourage families to share their goals and routines in their community spaces (for a detailed description of design process see Bermudez et al., 2023; Garcia et al., 2022; Chew et al., 2022). Through an inductive thematic analysis of these co-design sessions, we surfaced community values, practices, and aspirations such as promoting intergenerational learning, and increasing family time. As part of these themes, we also surfaced ways in which families' own routines and practices already involved STEM concepts and practices. We iteratively combined these themes and existing practices with the science practices and crosscutting concepts from the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) and principles from developmental science for creating high-quality early learning environments that are active, engaging, iterative, social, meaningful, and joyful (Hirsh-Pasek et al., 2015). While a single design could not meet all the criteria, we sought balance across community values, developmental principles, and science learning goals (see Bermudez et al., 2023 for more detail). Further, we were intentional to align these practices with SAELI’s three step design model that included engaging parents in discovery & dreaming, designing, and creating a sustainability plan. Using these design goals and guiding frameworks, we conducted prototype ideation sessions with SAELI families and then subsequent sessions where we created low-fidelity mock-ups of the prototypes for play testing and iteration during the second and third years of the project. Children and parents were interviewed to hear their feedback on the designs and learn about their experiences playing with the physical prototypes. These sessions were key to evaluate factors from usability to how and if families’ interactions aligned with their values and practices. These sessions were held in person at their local Community Center, started with a shared meal, followed by a design activity, reflections and share outs. Through these sessions we iterated and refined the prototypes until they were ready to be shared with our fabrication partners. Fabrication and launch For fabrication, we contracted a Los Angeles based museum installation design shop. We worked closely with their engineers to adapt the co-designed prototypes for durability, usability, safety, cost efficiency, and regulation compliance. All designs were reviewed by City of Santa Ana Parks and Recreation or Public Works departments and UC Irvine’s Facilities Management department. We worked collaboratively with the City of Santa Ana and S AELI to decide where the installations would go, taking advantage of existing city renovation efforts to save costs and create efficiencies when possible. We also worked with legal representation from UCI and the City of Santa Ana to execute a Memorandum of Understanding that the PLL installations were being donated to the city by UCI and the City of Santa Ana would own and maintain them. This process took approximately two years from the beginning of the fabrication process to installation in public spaces. The installations were implemented between Fall 2024 and Spring 2025 with a grand opening ribbon cutting ceremony held on May 10th, 2025, as part of the NSF’s 75th anniversary celebration and Mother’s Day in many Latin American countries. The ceremony was hosted at Madison Park in Santa Ana and attended by the Mayor, Director of Parks and Recreation, several city council members, and the Dean of the UCI School of Education. Data collection Our data collection protocol included baseline observations of STEM language and caregiver child interactions at each of the five installation sites pre-installation as well as a matched comparison site (e.g., for a bus-stop installation we observed a comparison bus stop in the same neighborhood). We also trained SAELI parents to collect surveys at all PLL and control sites of caregiver’s self-efficacy in teaching STEM to their children, perceptions of safety and learning opportunities in their community spaces, and attitudes around the connection between play and learning. We then performed the observational and survey data collection protocol post- installation to examine the impacts of the PLL’s on caregiver child interactions and experiences in community spaces. While post-installation data collection is on-going we expect to present findings from these analyses at the ISLS workshop in June 2026. For a more detailed description of our analytical plans please refer to our project pre-registration on the Open Science Framework. Workshop details The tour will be hosted by UCI Associate Professor and project PI Andres Bustamante, UCI Professor and project Co-PI June Ahn, SAELI Director Wendy Gomez, and several SAELI parents who participated in the design and data collection processes. The hosts will offer insights into the project’s co-design approach, the partnership with the city (challenges and opportunities), parents’ roles as designers, data collectors, and project advocates, impact results, and future plans for policy agenda towards sustainability and scaling. The timetable of activities and sites to be visited are shown below (Table 1). We will also discuss several cross-site design considerations, including Playful Learning Principles, culturally responsive design, the use of public spaces as learning environments, multigenerational engagement, attention to accessibility, and low-burden participation that aligns with families’ everyday routines. Table 1 Timetable of Activities Hour Activity 8:00 am Meet at the conference hotel at 8am PST on June 15th, 2026. We will depart on a charter bus to tour the five PLL sites in Santa Ana. 8:30 am Arrive at Santa Ana, touring the 5 different sites (see text below). 11:30 am End of the tour. The charter bus will be taking people back to the conference hotel. Site 1: Madison Park. Madison Park features the largest of the Santa Ana PLL installation, Parkopolis, the life-sized board game for math and science learning. Parkopolis is a giant board game where children spin life sized dice and advance around the board completing math and science games like playing patterns on musical pipes, and measuring how far you can jump on a giant ruler. Through the co-design process, we learned about games like Basta, a category game that many SAELI families play, and integrated them into Parkopolis games. During the co-design sessions, many families expressed concerns about visiting their neighborhood parks and cited the bathroom facility in the back of Madison Park as a hotspot for illicit activities like drug use and prostitution. In response, the city demolished those bathrooms replacing them with new bathroom facilities in another part of the park, and we constructed Parkopolis where the old bathrooms were transforming a hot spot for criminal activity into a hub for early learning, a powerful example of community voice leading to impact in public infrastructure. Site 2: Abacus bus stop. T he giant abacus at the bus stop on the corner of Main Street and McFadden Avenue in Santa Ana invites families to engage in conversations around numeracy and arithmetic. Many families in our design session reference using an abacus to learn math when they were children in Mexico and other countries in Latin America and wondered why their children’s schools didn’t use an abacus. This installation is a powerful symbol of scalability because it was not funded by our NSF grant. The city of Santa Ana was renovating bus stops in this area and due to the awareness of our projects, leveraged existing funds to execute the design. Site 3: Northgate Gonzalez market. Northgate is a family owned local grocery chain that many of the SAELI families shop at. During our co-design sessions, we used families stories about grocery shopping with their parents growing up or with their children now to develop signage that promote math and science interactions. Examples include a conversion chart between pounds and kilos at the deli and using your senses to pick out the best fruits and vegetables in the produce section. This installation is unique because it demonstrates how local business and the private sector can engage and support this work. Site 4: Angels Park. Angels Park features two PLL installations, La Lotería which is a giant version of the bingo style game that is very popular with local families, and How Tall Am I? which is a statue where children can measure their height in comparison to California animals. Both of these installations are a great example of intuitive design and leveraging existing knowledge to create engaging STEM learning experiences. How Tall Am I? invites immediate engagement through its visual design and integrated measurement markers, requiring only minimal instruction in the form of a single guiding question. Similarly, Lotería is among the most popular family games in this community, lengthy instructions are not necessary. Instead, we simply embed short STEM activities into the playing cards for families to integrate into the game play. In addition to supporting informal STEM learning, both of these installations were co-designed with the intention of supporting intergenerational learning which is a core value of Latine families. Site 5: Washington elementary school. The last stop on the tour will visit the Yo Veo (I See) Mural, an interactive art exhibit where children look for hidden objects that reflect local cultural and community activities. This is another example of a local institution adopting a project design. This mural was funded by the Santa Ana Unified School District, who were renovating this school and directed funds for murals. This school also features a different project, Fraction Ball, a redesigned basketball court for math learning. Future directions During the May 10th ribbon cutting event, the City of Santa Ana made an official proclamation that May will be Early Childhood Education month in the city in recognition of this innovative work. Building on this momentum, we are working with city officials on a resolution to integrate PLLs into the city’s on-going process for new public amenities leveraging existing budget from local institutions. We plan to position SAELI as drivers of future PLL efforts where they engage local community members in a design process of new public amenities that center early learning and build from local families’ funds of knowledge. This work represents a scalable and community centered vision for designing public infrastructure to promote child development and civic engagement. Invitation to ICLS participants This session examines the evolution of a project and partnership from initial creation through implementation, using this project as a live case study to surface challenges, lessons learned, and future directions from different points of view. In doing so, we demonstrate how partnering with purpose can generate meaningful community impact and offer useful insights for other scholars and initiatives seeking to engage in collaborative, community- centered work. papers.title: Participatory Design for AI in Teacher Education: From Top-Down Directives to Teacher Empowerment
papers.authors: Ekta Shokeen, Ane Vielandt Jensen, Ole Sejer Iversen, Christian Dindler, Marianne Graves Petersen
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: Empowering teacher educators to lead technology integration is essential for creating context-sensitive educational futures. This study examines how participatory design workshops can support educators in collaboratively developing sustainable capacity for integrating AI into teacher education. Drawing on a series of three participatory design workshops, the analysis focuses on the collaborative learning processes involved and the professional outcomes they produce. Structured around exploration, co- creation, and reflection, these workshops enabled educators to critically engage with the pedagogical, ethical, and institutional dimensions of AI, fostering both ownership and transformative agency. The findings demonstrate how participatory design can function not only as a design methodology but also as a framework for professional learning. A key contribution of this paper is the demonstration that participatory design supports sustainable AI integration by building e ducators’ capacity for change through the design process.

papers.title: Can Critical Pedagogy Survive Algorithmic Constraints?
papers.authors: Mariana Lederman Edelstein, Carolina Sotério, Andréia Maria de Lima Assunção, Paulo Blikstein
papers.design_stakeholders: Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Educational researchers increasingly explore social media as learning spaces, yet platforms are often shaped by logics of visibility, brevity, and algorithmic amplification rather than sustained dialogue. This paper examines an educational experiment on I nstagram that intentionally adopted Freirean design principles (e.g., posing generative questions, organizing content into editorial lines) to cultivate dialogical participation. By qualitatively analyzing 1,056 user comments for epistemic moves (reinterpretation, testimony, comparison) and comparing emergent themes with one year of platform metrics, we identify traces of dialogical engagement emerging alongside platform design changes. This study foregrounds tensions between critical pedagogies and algorithmic social media environments, raising questions about their suitability as learning environments and how learning is designed, enacted, and constrained beyond formal educational settings.

papers.title: Co-design as a Catalyst for Becoming: Identity, Practice, and Learning Trajectories in Undergraduate Science
papers.authors: Sunnie Gong, Michelle Lui, Aidyn Intykbekov
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Co-design is a collaborative methodology for creating educational innovations involving researchers, educators, and developers. While research -practice partnerships in the Learning Sciences have historically co-designed with teachers, recent developments have begun involving students. However, research on students’ experiences of co- design remains limited. This study explores what students learn from engaging in co-design through a situated learning framework linking learning to identity formation. Using a multiple case study methodology, the relationships between the identities, learning, and participation of six undergraduate science students were examined in a co -design project for creating educational virtual reality simulations. Findings reveal that identity, practice, and learning exist in dynamic and reciprocal relationships within co -design contexts. Students’ existing identities informed their co- design engagement. Through practice, students developed collaboration skills and learned about themselves which led to diverse identity development trajectories. These findings suggest engaging students as co-design partners creates unique opportunities for integrated learning and identity development.

papers.title: Exploring Learner Engagement in an LLM-Supported Simulation Environment for Complex Systems Understanding
papers.authors: Amit Nair, Man Su, Tomohiro Nagashima
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Understanding complex systems is challenging, as learners often rely on linear reasoning and struggle to recognize decentralized and emergent processes. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to support inquiry in simulation- based learning, yet how learners engage with these tools and how such engagement relates to learning outcomes remains underexplored. In this study, we investigate learner engagement within a theory- informed, LLM -supported simulation environment, based on an exper iment with 69 postsecondary students that varied parameter control and questioning agency. Focusing on questioning agency, we examine how interactions with an LLM -based tutor and engagement with exploratory instructional regions relate to posttest performa nce. Results show that greater engagement with the tutor, particularly through content-focused interactions, is associated with higher learning gains. Time spent in exploratory regions also significantly predicts performance. These findings highlight the i mportance of fostering meaningful engagement with both conversational tutors and interactive features in LLM-supported environments.

papers.title: Teacher Agency in Learning Sciences Co-design: Dubious or Undocumented?
papers.authors: Abigail A. Williams, Sam H. Ross, R. Benjamin Shapiro
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Frequent mentions of co- design in the learning sciences (LS) reflect an increasing effort to create resources through partnerships where researchers and educators share agency. Whether these partnerships meaningfully lead to new, teacher -shaped innovations depends on the dynamics of cross-role collaborations, including who gets to make design choices. We use Bratteteig and Wagner’s (2016) conceptual framework for the types of decision- making in co- design to evaluate LS research that involves co -designing with teachers. Our review reveals substantial gaps in descriptions of teacher decision- making, indicating either insufficiently described or insufficiently empowering co-design practices. We advocate for more transparent and egalitarian approaches to co- design at all phases of the design process, to increase the equity, robustness, research contributions, and potential real-world impact of co-design.

papers.authors: Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Marcelo Worsley, Michael Alan Chang, Chelsea Chandler, Sierra Rose
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: As AI technologies become increasingly integrated into schools, questions arise about what students should learn about AI and how AI-powered tools can support collaborative learning. This symposium reports on the Institute of Student-AI Teaming (iSAT), which designs AI partners and curricular activity systems to promote AI literacy and collaboration. Unlike most classroom AI tools designed for 1:1 interactions, iSAT develops AI partners as social collaborators that both facilitate group learning and serve as objects of inquiry —helping students “look under the hood” of AI systems. Our multi -year co-design process across three U.S. states engages teachers, students, and parents to build integrated systems of curriculum, technology, and professional learning. The symposium’s six posters span AI design, infrastructure, curriculum, and teacher learning, illustrating how AI can be productively embedded within classroom collaboration. Together, they advance understanding of how AI systems can meaningfully support and transform collaborative learning. Objective of the session As AI technologies become increasingly embedded in education (Reich & Dukes, 2024), so do questions about what students should learn about AI systems (AI literacy) and how AI -powered tools may support (or hinder) student learning. While there is growing excitement about AI’s potential to transform education, decades of research highlight repeated failures of earlier innovations to do so. Scholars argue these failures often stem from underappreciating the infrastructural nature of technology and overestimating its power to drive change in classroom practice (Roschelle et al., 2010). First, technology is infrastructural in that its value lies not in its particular content but in its ability to generate new representations of disciplinary ideas and create opportunities for students to engage more deeply in those ideas (Hegedus & Kaput, 2003). Second, like previous technologies, today’s AI tools will not transform education on their own. Their success depends on how curriculum activity systems—teacher professional learning (PL), instructional materials, and technology —work together to reshape learning environments (Vahey et al., 2013). Their success also depends on how teachers and students work together within the system to support learning. This symposium reports on work from the Institute of Student-AI Teaming (iSAT), an institute that aims to design AI -powered tools and curricular activity systems that promote collaborative knowledge building and student learning around AI -literacy specifically (D’Mello et al., 2024, OECD, 2025). Our project intentionally combines both AI -literacy and AI as a tool for collaborative learning in ways that will enable the AI -partner to serve simultaneously as a collaboration support and an object of inquiry as students think critically about how the AI works. That is, our AI partners play a dual role of supporting student collaboration and as a tool for “looking under the hood” at how AI systems work. Supporting collaborative learning is a longstanding goal of both the ISLS and CSCL community, and is crucial because we know that learning is inherently a social process. Yet, the dominant approach to incorporating AI inside K-12 classrooms focuses on 1:1 interactions between students and AI systems. iSAT’s approach is radically different: we aim to develop AI as a social, collaborative partner that works alongside students and teachers to deepen their engagement with one another. This goal has required that our team engage in multi -year co-design processes to better understand the needs and desires of multiple users 556 and stakeholders (e.g. teachers, students, parents) as we work to develop and refine AI partners, curriculum materials, and professional development to support the development of AI literacies. Over the past five years, our work has involved working with stakeholders in districts across three U.S. states to conceptualize, develop, enact, and refine our curricular activity system. This session will focus on the design of iSAT’s curricular activity system to deepen the field’s conversation about the role of AI -systems in supporting collaborative learning. Across the posters, we will describe how our co- design practices, back -end models, classroom pilot studies, professional learning, and curricular routines and designs worked toward our emerging understanding of the utility of these tools for supporting collaborative learning. Overview of the symposium The 6 posters that constitute the symposium represent our collective efforts to take seriously what it means for AI systems to partner within the curricular activity systems of secondary schools. Poster 1 will detail the trajectory of co-design for our first AI partner, the Community Builder (CoBi) and how the ongoing design, implementation and analysis of the co- design space informed the values of our institute. Poster 2 will present on the design, development, and pilot studies of our second Jigsaw Interactive Agent (JIA) in secondary classrooms and how productive uncertainty was leveraged to design the AI partner interventions to suppo rt small group jigsaws. In Poster 3, we will report on the architecture and analytic pipeline that underlies our two existing AI partners, documenting how the pipeline infrastructure, state detection and dialogue policies inform the AI- partner outputs and interventions. Posters 4-6 address how we built both curriculum materials and teachers’ capacities to leverage them so that the AI partners could be meaningfully integrated into everyday classroom activities. In Poster 4, we examine how curricular routines can support students' sensemaking of their own collaborative practices. In Poster 5, we show how our PL design supported teachers’ learning about AI, our AI literacy curriculum and pedagogical approaches that center student sensemaking. Finally, Poster 6 describes the design and refinement of our curriculum materials that focus on AI literacy, a process guided by co- design, adaptation and refinement with teachers in their classrooms. Scholarly significance This session is both timely and essential. First, AI tools are becoming increasingly embedded in schools and in our world. At the same time, few teachers are currently prepared to teach about AI, use AI -enabled tools, and adopt student-centered, collaborative pedagogies—what we call a triple innovation challenge . We also know that external forces (e.g. social and news media) shape students’ understanding of AI, and that schools/educators play a less significant role (OECD, 2025) This session highlights a new approach to supporting AI literacy through the design of curricular activity systems where AI Partners are meaningfully embedded to support AI literacies through collaborative learning. Structure of the session The symposium will be organized as a structured poster session. The chair of the session will first provide a brief overview of the session (4 mins). Each presenter will give a one -minute elevator pitch to introduce their project (6 mins). Presenters will then move to their respective posters; participants can view posters, demos (if applicable) and engage in discussion. We will invite participants to engage in two “rounds” of poster-viewing (30 mins each), so that co-presenters have a chance to view other s’ posters . Our discussant will synthesize the posters and pose questions for the audience to discuss, focusing on the challenges and affordances of AI -powered systems in supporting collaborative learning in schools (20 minutes). CoBi Origins: Co-design narratives as boundary objects to translate Co-design findings into interdisciplinary implementation Michael Alan Chang Objectives Collaborative and participatory design is increasingly used to inform the design and implementation of AI -Ed tools that are responsive to the needs and lived experiences of interest holders (Ravi et al., 2025). An AI -Ed research team hosts a co -design context, completes an analysis of it, and then responds to the co- design efforts through implementation. While this sequential and linear process simplifies the already complex and interdisciplinary process of building AI-Ed tools, it can constrain both the types of analysis that can be conducted within the co-design context and the ways in which stakeholders can engage in the ongoing design of AI-Ed tools 557 (Chang, under review). Here, I share our efforts in iSAT, where there were parallel, longitudinal efforts to (a) develop and analyze a three- year co-design study with high school youth to surface their hopes and concerns around the use of AI in schools and (b) respond to the findings of those co- design studies to develop AI partners and curricular activity systems that surround the use of the technology. Here, I ask: how does the ongoing design, implementation, and analysis of co- design spaces shape the des ign activities of an interdisciplinary research institute? Perspectives Here, I view stories about co-design activities as an evolving boundary object that guides how large-scale AI-Ed implementation teams take on co-design findings (Star & Griesemer, 1989). Boundary objects are conceptualized as “how artifacts can fulfill a specific function in bridging intersecting practices” (pg. 134, Akkerman & Bakker, 2011). As Star (2010) clarifies, a boundary object is characterized by interpretive flexibility across different contexts, allowing each context to tailor the object to its own needs locally. Finally, boundary objects follow particular trajectories within organizational contexts; once created, boundary objects evolve through local tailoring, standardize over time, and, finally, fade away as the standardization practices begin to constrain possible local adaptations. In turn, new boundary objects are then created.

papers.title: Designing with Care: Exploring the Embodied and Affective Dimensions of Collaborative Noticing
papers.authors: Shivani Davé, Lindsay Lindberg, Ananda Marin
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper brings together three cases to examine the question, what happens when we approach the design of research contexts to explore professional noticing with care? Through video-based interaction analysis, a pattern emerged within the researcher -participant interactions. When researchers engaged with care, research contexts became sites of collaborative sense- making that supported participants to come to new insights about their practices. Essential to the development of these research contexts was the emic nature of the researchers’ connections to the partnerships–each researcher had a personal connection to the professional practice. Together, these insights point to possibilities for the study of a researchers’ noticing practices, which we argue is integral to the analysis and design of future research partnerships and contribute to meaningful and care-full learning and research.

papers.title: Developing K-12 Teachers’ Ethical Competencies through Cognitive Dissonance of Gameplay
papers.authors: Ming Ma, Zhichun Liu, Gary K.W. Wong
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Students & Learners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: As AI literacy becomes increasingly integrated into K–12 education, teachers require robust ethical competencies to effectively teach AI ethics in classroom instruction. To address this need, we developed Responsible AI CAB, a scenario- based tabletop role -playing game designed to immerse teachers in real -world ethical dilemmas and foster collective ethical reasoning. Eight technology teachers participated in the gameplay. We employed bipartite epistemic network analysis (ENA) methods to examine teachers’ discourse. Results highlighted that gameplay -induced cognitive dissonance facilitated the development of teachers ’ ethical competencies. This was evidenced by their adoption of multiple stakeholder perspectives under role pressures, their comprehension and application of responsible AI principles in group ethical reasoning through peer challenges or arguments, and their critical evaluation of new information to challenge existing beliefs. These findings inform the design of professional development programs seeking to cultivate the ethical competencies essential for K–12 AI literacy education.

papers.title: “You Can Actually Do Something”: Shifts in High School Computer Science Teachers’ Conceptions of AI/ML Systems and Algorithmic Justice
papers.authors: Daniel J. Noh, Deborah A. Fields, Yasmin B. Kafai, Danaé Metaxa
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: The recent proliferation of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) systems highlights the need for all people to develop effective competencies to interact with and examine AI/ML systems. We study shifts in five experienced high school CS tea chers’ understanding of AI/ML systems after one year of participatory design, where they co- developed lessons on AI auditing, a systematic method to query AI/ML systems. Drawing on individual and group interviews, we found that teachers’ perspectives becam e more situated, grounding their understanding in everyday contexts; more critical, reflecting growing awareness of harms; and more agentic, highlighting possibilities for action. Further, across all three perspectives, teachers consistently framed algorit hmic justice through their role as educators, situating their concerns within their school communities. In the discussion, we consider the ways teachers’ perspectives shifted, how AI auditing can shape these shifts, and the implications of these findings on AI literacy for both teachers and students.

papers.title: AI Tools in Arts Learning: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Jaycee Sansom, Safinah Ali
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students
papers.abstract: With the proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in art making, AI knowledge and skills have made their way to arts learning. However, an assessment of the current state of AI tools in arts learning is lacking. This study used scoping review methodology to identify current research trends in AI applications in arts learning, and what gaps exist for future research. 58 papers were reviewed revealing four trends and five gaps and opportunities.

papers.title: Middle School Student Science Practices in a Justice-Oriented Wildfire Science Unit
papers.authors: Spencer Eusden, Li Ke
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Middle School Students; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: The growing impacts of climate change -driven disasters and environmental issues on communities create a compelling case for using these issues as anchoring phenomena to support both science learning and disaster resilience. This poster shares results from a co - produced middle school wildfire science unit. Results include 1) How self-situation in localized data sets shaped student conclusions and 2) How students incorporated knowledge of their community when analyzing data and constructing evidence -based arg uments about wildfire resilience. Poster proposal Climate change-driven disasters and environmental issues (CCDDEI’s) such as wildfires, hurricanes, and extreme weather are increasingly disrupting the lives of both students and their communities (Benvolenza & DeRignez, 2019; Lambrou et al., 2023). Moreover, the impacts of these issues, especially wildfire, are likely to become more severe and unjust in the coming decades (Davies et al., 2018; Méndez et al, 2020; Qui et al., 2025, Smith et al., 2020). Youth are vulnerable to trauma from increasingly destructive wildfires (Brown et al., 2019) and missed school days from school closures due to hazardous air quality (Santana et al., 2021). However, youth can play needed roles in addressing wildfire-related (Codreanu et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2019) and other environmental justice issues through participatory action learning (Ballard et al., 2017; Morales-Doyle & Frausto, 2019). There is potential for using CCDDEI’s as both anchoring phenomena for science learning and pathways to support youth and community resilience to these issues. However, how instructional materials incorporate such phenomena shapes whether the materials help equitably support student learning (Penuel et al., 2022) and resilience to these disruptive issues (Condreau et al., 2014; Park et al., 2024) or reinforce existing inequities in both education (National Academies, 2025) and disaster resilience (Lambrou et al., 2023). This poster draws on the socio-spatial justice work of Tan et al. (2022) to explore how analysis of the spatial aspects of wildfire risk can be used to support students’ engagement in justice- oriented science learning. Empirical research on how students construct arguments and use da ta science practices in instructional materials that blend science learning and community resilience goals can further discussion on effective student learning in these contexts. This paper shares results from a co-produced curriculum pilot that blends western scientific knowledge of wildfire and justice-oriented data sources that center students' perspectives on the impact of wildfire on their community. Research question: How do middle school students construct evidence-based arguments and use data science practices in a justice-oriented wildfire science unit?

papers.title: Prolepsis ’Till Infinity : Designing STEM Futures Through Play, Media, and Imagination
papers.authors: Kareem Edouard
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Prolepsis ’Till Infinity calls for an education that recognizes imagination as infrastructure. Dr. Kareem Edouard invites us to rethink how we build STEM spaces that honor culture, creativity, and care as the foundation of learning. His research at the ILLEST Lab challenges systems that reward compliance over curiosity, asking what becomes possible when play, storytelling, and design are treated as serious forms of knowledge, particularly for those most marginalized in STEAM, Black boys. Drawing from his design practices across learning, children’s media, and informal STEAM environments, Dr. Edouard examines how learners develop identity, agency, and understanding through participatory, culturally responsive experiences, highlighting key insights from the learning sciences. For example, in co-design projects with educators and youth, students engage in creative problem-solving and media production, positioning them as knowledge-makers whose ideas actively shape the learning environment. These collaborative partnerships demonstrate how purposeful engagement between educators, researchers, and communities fosters equitable and imaginative learning outcomes. Dr. Edouard envisions an educational future where play, imagination, and community are essential for liberation. This keynote invites us to build toward proleptic, possible, and connected futures already in motion, where creativity and meaning-making shape how we learn, teach, and thrive together. By treating play, imagination, and community as foundational, Dr. Edouard shows how learning and partnership are inseparable in designing educational spaces that cultivate curiosity, empowerment, and cultural relevance. Bio: Dr. Kareem Edouard is an Assistant Professor of Learning Technologies at Drexel University’s School of Education and Co-Director of the Informal Learning Linking Engineering, Science and Technology (ILLEST) Lab. His work explores how design, as a cultural, creative, and communal practice, intersects informal STEM education and children’s media to promote meaningful knowledge transfer across learning spaces. He examines how storytelling and co-creation cultivate belonging, purpose, and imagination in environments shaped by inequity. Through initiatives like the Black Male Animation Lab, Dr. Edouard redefines STEM as a space for cultural creation and collective care, empowering Black boys as designers, storytellers, and innovators. He focuses on Black boys because their experiences sharpen the stakes of equity work in STEM: to support those most marginalized by systemic exclusion is to test whether design can truly be liberatory. His liberatory co-design framework examines how collaborative creation transforms educational systems and expands equity and representation. In the Sneaker Lab, design, material science, and cultural expression are explored for their impact on identity and innovation. The GRIND initiative further investigates how sports, data, and technology can foster community-driven STEM engagement. Dr. Edouard integrates his co-liberty design framing vision into children’s STEM media. This approach combines his experience as a former music video and commercial director with his academic research. As Executive Producer of MayNERD’s Wild World of Science (YouTube Kids), Built From Scratch, and Creative Producer of Work It Out Wombats! (PBS KIDS), he uses media as a conduit to share STEM learning and engagement, which remains at the heart of his work with children’s media. https://drexel.edu/soe/faculty-and-staff/faculty/Edouard-Kareem https://www.linkedin.com/in/kareemedouard https://www.olegreensgroup.com/home Special Session

papers.title: AI as a Collaborative Partner: EMPA’s Role in Supporting Reflective Teamwork Learning
papers.authors: Aparajita Jaiswal, Ashish Ashish
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students
papers.abstract: Teamwork requires students to reflect on their practices, yet individualized mentoring is often limited. While AI tutoring systems increasingly support learning, most position AI as external evaluator rather than collaborative partner. We present EMPA, an AI - based collaborative partner that scaffolds teamwork learning through case studies, activities, and videos. Grounded in Schön’s reflection -in-action and reflection -on-action, EMPA encourages students to adapt strategies during tasks and analyze experiences afterwards. Students engage with scenarios and activities while EMPA prompts real -time reflection, then receive personalized summaries and complete surveys that consolidate learning. Early deployment with undergraduates shows EMPA’s potential to help learners examine assumptions, recognize cultural dynamics, and develop strategies for improving collaboration. This study operationalizes Schön’s framework via AI-supported mentoring, positioning AI as a reflective partner to scale practice and strengthen teamwork.

papers.title: Participatory Narratives for AI Learning: Integrating Self-Efficacy, Agency, and Ethical Reflection
papers.authors: Jessica Vandenberg, Bradford Mott, Carlos Penilla, James Lester, Elizabeth Ozer
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This work presents a theory-driven design framework grounded in Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) and informed by participatory learning perspectives to support middle school students’ AI literacy and career interests. Implemented in a narrative- centered game- based learning environment, the framework connects SCT’s motivational constructs ( self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and goals ) with participatory mechanisms such as role -based engagement, consequential decision-making, and ethical reflection. Findings from a pilot study with middle school students illustrate how narrative participation supports the development of self-efficacy, AI understanding, and emerging career awareness.

papers.title: Teachers Bridging Technical and Reflective Stances in K–9 AI Education
papers.authors: Ane Vielandt Jensen, Inger Malene Surrow, Ekta Shokeen, Line Have Musaeus, Yu- Yu Liu
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students
papers.abstract: As AI tools enter K -9 classrooms, teachers face the challenge of supporting both technical understanding and critical reflection. This study examines how lower secondary teachers integrate technical and reflective stances of AI through participatory lesson design with simplified Large Language Model activities. Analysis of classroom enactments, lesson plans, and interviews shows that : First, technical and reflective stances can be bridged in discrete, well-structured activities. Second, teachers stress technical insights before critical reflection. Third, abstract reflection concepts can cause classroom detachment, and fourth, bridging technical and reflective stances requires more than explanation. Additionally, these findings lead us to suggest implications highlighting awareness of teachers’ assumptions, deliberate activity scaffolding, and pedagogical strategies to support teachers in balancing technical and reflective stances of AI literacy.

papers.title: Vulnerability and Expertise in Intergenerational STEM: Teachers Negotiating Learner Identities in EMPWER
papers.authors: Assyria A. Chambers, Carrie D. Allen
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This short paper examines how two high school science teachers responded to invitations to position themselves as learners within an intergenerational program focused on environmental justice and data literacy, called E MPWER. Drawing on Holland et al.’s (1998) notion of figured worlds and Goodwin’s (1997) concept of interactional expertise, we traced how teachers negotiated identity and expertise within EMPWER as science educators, learners, and community members. A comparative case analysis showed that both teachers struggled with and resisted learner identities in different ways throughout the year-long project; however, one teacher was able to author a learn er identity more consistently, while the other resisted learner positioning. Our findings speak to how teacher learning identities are shaped by prior figured worlds of school science and social expectations associated with expertise. We argue that intergenerational designs should support teacher vulnerability, share authority, and create conditions for purposeful partnership that build collective agency across generations.

papers.title: Dialogue, Design, and Reflect: Partnering with Teachers to Transform Education
papers.authors: Gayithri Jayathirtha, Joanna Goode, Gail Chapman, Taghrid Elmeligui, Elaine Griggs, Tangela Crocker, John Ottina, Don Yanek, Jennifer Parr
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Teachers have the potential to be transformational agents of change. And yet, fewer accounts from practice illuminate the process of teachers becoming transformational agents. In this paper, we present a composite counterstory developed with six high school teachers to demonstrate how they and their colleagues evolved as transformational intellectuals through their participation in professional activities over the years, including inquiry -based teacher professional development (PD) sessions, co- designing a justice -oriented computing program, and reflecting on their experiences . Drawing from thematic qualitative analysis of video recordings of five reflective sessions with teachers at the end of a three -year-long codesign work, we answer: How did teachers develop as transformational intellectuals through co- designing a justice -oriented computing curriculum alongside inquiry- based professional development and reflective practice? The counterstory highlights themes that emerged from the analysis, showing that teachers developed trusted relationships , agency, and solidarity through critical historical analysis and reflectivity.

papers.title: How Transnational Youth Make Sense of Multiscalar Citizenship Towards Climate Justice
papers.authors: Batoul Y. Abdallah, Wisam Sedawi, Rachel Sherwin
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study investigates how transnational youth make sense of climate change across personal, local, and global contexts. Drawing upon critical participatory design-based methods, we bear witness to how youths’ embodied experiences, including transnationa l identity and cultural, ecological, and geopolitical positioning, become onto- epistemological resources for climate sense-making. Through a case study, we illustrate how one youth connected scientific climate knowledge to war experiences, framing war as climate catastrophe encompassing increased carbon footprints and ecological devastation, displacement, cultural erosion, and trauma. Youth draw on their vulnerability to deepen understanding of climate causes and consequences, while fostering empathy-driven solidarity and advocacy. They amplify silenced voices and call for collective responsibility in confronting intertwined climate and geopolitical injustices. Youth’s multiscalar experiences constitute legitimate knowledge that expands and critiques dominant climate narratives, offering onto -epistemological testimony that reframes climate justice scholarship and pedagogy.

papers.title: Amplifying the Voices of High School Graduates with Special Education and Neurodiversity Experiences to Shape GenAI Practices in Education
papers.authors: Gina Tesoriero
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This qualitative study explores how GenAI Use Case Scenarios spark critical dialogue about GenAI in education among high school graduates with special education and neurodiverse experiences. Drawing on Cultural -Historical Activity Theory (Engeström & Sannino, 2010), justice -driven inclusive education (Waitoller & Artiles, 2013), and DisCrit (Annamma et al., 2013), this study positions youth as philosophers of technology (Vakil & McKinney de Royston, 2022) and co-designers of AI policy. Findings reveal the critical insights marginalized voices bring to conversations about responsible GenAI use in schools.

papers.title: Advancing a Learning Sciences Approach to Quantum Information Science in K-12
papers.authors: Raquel Coelho
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: My research examines learning in complex, rapidly evolving technological domains, particularly quantum information science. Bridging multiple theoretical perspectives, I am currently pursuing two directions: designing learning environments that make ultra-complex STEM accessible to K-12 learners; and theorizing quantum computational thinking to identify concepts, practices, and perspectives that distinguish quantum from classical reasoning. Research agenda and theoretical framing In my research, I am committed to understanding how emerging technologies shape and support learning. I pursue this understanding both via conceptual inquiry and via the design of learning environments that help learners navigate complex, rapidly evolving domains. While some of my previous (e.g., Coelho & McCollum, 2025) and ongoing work involves empirical investigations using AI and NLP technologies to support teaching and learning across K-12 and post-secondary contexts (e.g., Coelho et al., 2025a), this submission focuses on my research in K-12 quantum information science (QIS). My scholarship is primarily grounded in learning sciences traditions that view learning as situated and mediated by material and social interactions (e.g., Cole, 1998; Moll et al., 2006; Pea, 1985, 1993a, 1993b; Rogoff, 2003). I adopt an integrationist stance (Danish & Gresalfi, 2018), deliberately examining learning across one or more interrelated planes (Rogoff, 2008), while critically attending to the analytic affordances and limitations of this approach and maintaining a commitment to understanding the dynamic interplay among learners, social interactions, and context. I also draw on complementary perspectives that have traditionally emphasized the individual – such as constructivism (Kafai, 2012; Papert & Harel, 1991; Wilensky, 2020) – and cognitive sciences (e.g., Bandura, 2010) as generative for understanding and supporting meaning-making, agency, and motivation. I utilize these complementary perspectives to inform my conceptual and empirical contributions to K-12 quantum information science education as described in the subsequent sections. Thereafter, I discuss future directions centered on studying and designing for quantum computational thinking. Current work When I began reviewing the literature on K-12 quantum information science education (Coelho et al., 2025b), I was surprised to find that learning sciences researchers, who have spent decades studying how students understand complex scientific concepts, were almost entirely absent from the conversations. This absence seemed particularly striking given that learning quantum information science requires learners to grapple with ideas that defy classical intuition and mathematical formalisms that create barriers to accessibility even at the college level, let alone in K- 12 settings. These are precisely the kinds of challenges that learning sciences researchers have developed expertise in addressing: making complex, abstract concepts accessible through appropriate representational tools, scaffolding, and cultural practices that support new ways of thinking. And just as this expertise is most needed, national initiatives are pushing for quantum education to begin in middle and high school (NSF, 2020). While computer science and physics education researchers (e.g., Franklin et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2022) have begun important work in this space, the conversations have yet to substantially engage with learning sciences frameworks and methods that could complement and extend these disciplinary efforts. Our review also showed that both theoretical grounding and design conjectures in K-12 QIS education research remain limited. Many initiatives simply ask, “Does it work?” in a Thomas Edison exploratory framework (Stokes, 2011), without interrogating why or under what conditions learning occurs, risking innovations that engage learners but do not reliably support deep understanding. My position paper (Coelho et al., 2025d) argues for a bidirectional opportunity that neither field has fully recognized. QIS education could leverage learning sciences expertise in design-based research to iteratively develop quantum learning environments. This includes principled approaches for creating new representational infrastructures (Wilensky, 2020) that make quantum phenomena accessible while preserving mathematical integrity, as well as participation structures that allow learners to collectively make sense of quantum phenomena, negotiate meaning through shared representations, and transform their participation in disciplinary practices (Lemke, 2001; Pea, 1992; Rogoff et al., 1995). But equally important, and perhaps more provocative, is what q uantum information science offers the learning sciences: a domain that pushes us to reconsider our theories of conceptual change, representation, and learning at the boundaries of human intuition. To put these conceptual arguments into practice, my recent empirical work (Coelho et al., 2025c) investigates how collaborative game making (Fields & Kafai, 2018) leveraging distributed expertise (Pea, 1993) can support students in developing initial mental models of quantum information science concepts and practice while cultivating curiosity, confidence, and identity – early pathways toward a “competent outsider” stance (Sandoval et al., 2025). We found that designing quantum-themed board games created accessible entry points supporting participation without requiring advanced formalism, though supplementary social and material support will also be incorporated in future iterations of the work. Throughout this process, groups mobilized diverse expertise and resources to materialize quantum ideas, illustrating how even quantum-adjacent activities can drive motivation, sensemaking, and participation in ultra-complex STEM domains. Future work Building on my prior work in K-12 quantum information science education, I have begun to articulate a tentative framework for quantum computational thinking (QCT), extending classical computational thinking to the distinct concepts, practices, and perspectives of quantum information science, while attending to the ethical, societal, and justice-related dimensions of access to quantum technologies (Coelho et al., 2025e). This exploration identifies key concepts (e.g., randomness, interference, superposition), practices (e.g., designing probabilistic algorithms, leveraging amplitude amplification), and perspectives (e.g., understanding computation as materially grounded, designing under indeterminacy) that distinguish QCT from classical computational reasoning, while also emphasizing equitable participation and the social and ethical stakes of access to quantum technologies. Conceptually, this work considers how engagement with QCT might prompt learners to develop non-classical intuitions, reason under uncertainty, and approach computation, abstraction, and scientific problem-solving in fundamentally new ways. Looking forward, my K-12 research agenda focuses on two interrelated directions. First, inspired by the STEM novice/expert research literature (Bransford et al., 2000; Erickson et al., 2006) and Science-Technology- Studies investigations of laboratory life (e.g., Latour, 2005; Latour & Woolgar, 1986), I aim to ground a QCT framework in empirical studies of how quantum information scientists think and work, examining the concepts they use, the practices they enact, and the perspectives they bring to reasoning with quantum phenomena and technologies. Second, I plan to build on these insights by designing and iteratively refining K-12 learning environments that scaffold engagement with QCT, leveraging new representational infrastructures and collaborative practices that invite students into developmentally appropriate, quantum-adjacent forms of authentic inquiry. Such activities may include designing games, music, or visualizations that incorporate principles like amplitude amplification or probabilistic reasoning, enabling learners to make abstract quantum ideas tangible, expressive, and personally meaningful. While practical quantum computers remain on the horizon, progress toward them is uncertain and uneven (Eisert & Preskill, 2025). They are not expected to replace classical systems; instead, future systems will likely integrate both paradigms (Preskill, 2018). The field is already shaped by substantial financial investment to address the enormous hardware challenges. Yet an even greater obstacle lies in identifying problems for which quantum approaches provide decisive advantages, beyond those canonical examples discovered decades ago. How we approach quantum reasoning and learning today will influence not only who gets to participate in shaping this emerging field, but also what kinds of problems we even recognize as solvable. The learning sciences contribution, then, is not auxiliary to quantum computing’s development; rather, it is central to its realization. References Bandura, A. (2010). papers.title: Examining Youth Authority in Community Member Interviews during the Co- Design of an Environmental Engineering Curriculum
papers.authors: Yuxi Huang, Symone Gyles, Aakriti Bisht, Rossella Santagata, Hosun Kang, Sara Ludovise
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study examines youth authority in interviews with community members during a series of environmental engineering curriculum co -design sessions. Seven high school students, together with teachers, university researchers and informal environmental educators, participated in this multi- session task. The study aimed to understand how youth articulate, realize, and negotiate authority throughout the process. The qualitative analysis of audio recordings from co -design group discussions, formal interviews, reflections, and end- of-year interviews yielded three themes. First, youth authority drew from different sources across different activities. Second, facilitated activities scaffolded youth to realize epistemic and deontic authority. Third, youth authority emerged through adapting and challenging tasks. These findings extend the previous macro-level analyses of power dynamics and suggest that a balance between scaffolding and autonomy is critical to allow youth to exercise authority. This work also contributes to broader literature on power, authority, and equitable youth engagement in curriculum design.
