papers.title: Conceptualizations and Mechanisms of Teachers’ Learning to Notice
papers.authors: Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Elizabeth van Es, Alf Coles, Sigal-Hava Rotem, Thorsten Scheiner, Heather
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This symposium brings together a set of posters that focus on science and mathematics teachers’ learning to notice. Teacher noticing is a core construct of teaching, and refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making amidst the “blooming, buzzing confusion” of classr oom interactions. The goal of the session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” is conceptualized and unpack mechanisms that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Symposium overview: Goal, structure, and highlights Teacher noticing, a core construct of teaching (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023), broadly refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making of classroom interactions (Jacobs et al., 2010; Sherin et al., 2011). With the growing recognition of noticing as a core practice of teaching, there is an expanding line of research that seeks to understand how to support teachers’ learning to notice (Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021). Prior research shows that well -designed professional learning opportunities can foster teachers’ learning to notice students’ thinking and teaching in interaction with student learning (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa et al., 2018; Warshauer et al., 2023). As this knowledge has grown, it has prompted scholars to investigate what constitutes learning of noticing. In this symposium, we pause and ask: How do we think about what constitutes learning to notice? While efforts to support teachers’ learning to notice is evolving, less is understood about the mechanisms of teacher learning to notice (Walkoe & Luna, 2020). Some research investigates how video tagging tools focus teachers’ attention on particular features for further analysis (e.g., Walkoe et al., 2020). Others have considered how different kinds of video clips are selected and situated in professional learning and how collaborative analysis of particular types of clips can shape teachers’ learning (e.g ., Sherin & Dyer, 2017). Recent work has pointed to the role of discourse as a mechanism of teachers’ learning to notice (van Es et al., 2024). However, there is more to be understood about how teachers come to notice complexities of teaching and learning, and designs to better 2318 support that. Going beyond the descriptive account of noticing, in this symposium, our work collectively explores: What drives teachers’ learning to notice? All in all, the goal of our session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” has been conceptualized, and unpack the "mechanisms" that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Using multiple methods such as participatory design research approach and typological analysis of artifacts of teaching , these studies document shifts in teachers’ learning to notice, factors that contribute to teachers’ learning of noticing, and the design choices in facilitating teachers’ learning this complex practice. T he studies identify mechanisms of teachers’ learning to notice such as coding schemes that serve as epistemic mechanisms and collective sensemaking of the complexity of teaching through analysis of classroom videos in professional learning contexts. While some papers zoom in on noticing subprocesses that different video processes afford, others seek to understand teachers’ learning to notice when teachers worked on making links to socio-ecological issues relevant to their lives. Together, these papers advance theory on teachers’ learning to notice, while also considering the situated and relational features of teacher learning. At the same time, they offer methodological tools and frameworks to advance research on learning to notice across math and science. This 90-minute structured poster session will consist of a brief introduction to the session by the session co-chairs (5 min), followed by the interactive discussion of 10 posters (60 min), 10-minutes of commentary from a discussant, Adam Lefstein from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, who brings expertise on teachers’ learning in professional development. We will conclude with 15-minutes of questions and discussion. The discussant will consider commonalities and differences across these studies, surfacing the considerations and tensions for supporting teachers’ learning to notice and mechanisms that drive learning of noticing among math and science teachers across the trajectory of teaching careers. Poster 1: Grounding prospective mathematics teacher noticing in socio- ecological issues: learning to notice in turbulent times Alf Coles, Sigal-Hava Rotem This study addresses the gap between current turbulent times and the seeming ‘objectivity’ of mathematics. We explore what constitutes prospective teachers (PTs) of mathematics learning to notice, during a time of war, the links they make to socio- ecological (Coles et al., 2024) issues of relevance to their lives, and the role of the mathematics teacher educator. Following van Es and Sherin (2002), we conceptualize teacher noticing as attending to and interpreting students' mathematical thinking. Following Mason (2002), we emphasize attention to event details for in -depth interpretation. We focus on “critical events” - moments when teachers notice students' mathematical thinking has potential for deepening. We also bring a notion of “authenticity”, which relates to teachers’ task design choices, and the extent to which tasks include social or ecological issues of relevance to their lives and the extent to which the mathematics includes opportunities for generalization. The study was conducted during wartime, heightening turbulence and data significance. We employed a case study methodology, to research a year- long problem-solving course in a B.Ed. mathematics program. The course focused on a reform in mathematics educati on emphasizing "mathematics in everyday life" and incorporated two design-teach-reflect cycles where participants: 1) photographed and discussed socio- ecological concerns (photovoice method); 2) designed mathematical tasks; and 3) taught and reflected on critical events they identified. Among 23 participants, we focus on Nadin (Bedouin community member) as an illustrative case. Our analysis examines shifts in her articulation of event details, interpretations, the social- ecological issue's authenticity and the role of the teacher educator. The analysis revealed three key findings. First, Nadin was able to bring a highly relevant socio-ecological issue to her classroom, surfacing deeply held beliefs and engaging with students about their beliefs. Secondly, Nadin wrote in great detail and we observed subtle and shifting relationships between detail and interpretation in her accounts, which is of significance to how noticing might be supported. Thirdly, in examining the role of the teacher educator, we uncover the significance of the way space w as offered on the course for PTs to discuss and work on socio-ecological issues of relevance to their lives. Through examining the particulars of one case, our findings offer an example of how teacher preparation, during a time of war, can still support the noticing of prospective teachers, in connecting mathematics to relevant socio-ecological issues. We tentati vely point to a role for prospective teachers’ sharing stories from their lives, and to the power of engaging in design-teach-reflect cycles, in supporting their noticing. 2319 Poster 2: Learning to notice students’ strengths: Coding schemes as epistemic mechanisms in design-based teacher education Thorsten Scheiner This investigation addresses a critical challenge in teacher education: developing teachers’ capacity to recognize and build upon students’ strengths rather than defaulting to deficit -based orientations. While research demonstrates that strength -based noticing practices foster more equitable learning environments (Louie et al., 2021), significant gaps remain in understanding the mechanisms through which teachers develop these sophisticated ways of seeing. This study examines how structured coding schemes function as epistemic tools that bridge cognitive and socio- cultural dimensions of professional learning, offering insights into design -based approaches for transforming teacher noticing practices. The study advances an integrated framework synthesizing professional noticing theory, transformative learning mechanisms, and frame analysis. Professional noticing encompasses attending to critical aspects of student reasoning, interpreting student thinking, and deciding how to respond instructionally (Jacobs et al., 2010). Frame analysis illuminates how interpretive schemas shape what teachers notice and value in student work (Sherin & Russ, 2014). Transformative learning theory provides mechanisms for frame shifting through critical reflection and conscious reorientation of perspective (Mezirow, 2000). The framework positions coding schemes as mediating artifacts that operationalize frame orientations while scaffolding transformative professional development through the dynamic interplay of cognitive restructuring and socio-cultural meaning-making. This exploratory study used a participatory design research approach within an intensive professional learning context. Prospective teachers engaged in three iterative cycles of analysis using a structured coding scheme distinguishing deficit-based, strength-based, and uncommitted orientations across noticing practices. Each iteration incorporated fine -grained examination of transformative mechanisms through structured reflective prompts targeting frame awareness, conscious reframing, and progressive integr ation. Data collection utilized standardized noticing tasks, complemented by reflective journals documenting participants’ evolving interpretive frameworks. Analysis combined quantitative tracking of orientation patterns with qualitative mapping of transformative processes. Analysis revealed three primary mechanisms driving teachers’ learning to notice strengths. First, epistemic visibility emerged through the coding scheme’s dual function as analytical tool and pedagogical scaffold, rendering implicit interpretive frames explicit and actionable. Participants demonstrated systematic shifts from deficit- based toward strength- based noticing practices. Second, collaborative meaning -making facilitated frame shifting through structured protocols that created social spaces for negot iating alternative interpretations of student thinking. Third, reflective reframing supported progressive integration of strength-based orientations through systematic comparisons of deficit-based and asset-oriented perspectives. The iterative design revealed how these mechanisms operated synergistically, with cognitive restructuring mediated by socio-cultural practices of professional discourse and collective analysis. The findings illuminate coding schemes as powerful epistemic mechanisms that render interpretive frames both visible and actionable in teacher education. By functioning simultaneously as analytical tools and pedagogical scaffolds, structured coding schemes support the cognitive work of frame identification while creating social spaces for collaborative meaning -making. This dual functionality bridges individual cognitive transformation and collective professional development, revealing how participatory desi gn research can systematically develop teachers’ capacity for strength- based noticing. The study contributes methodological insights for designing equity- oriented professional learning experiences that leverage the sophisticated interplay between cognitive and socio-cultural dimensions of transformative practice. Poster 3: From noticing to navigating: Pre-service teachers' expansive sensemaking in science instruction Heather Johnson, Tara Barnhart Teacher noticing—especially of student thinking—has become central in teacher education research (Weston & Amador, 2023). Noticing can be cultivated during teacher education (van Es, 2011), but connecting it to student - centered instruction requires space to reflect on the interplay between interpretations, decisions, and institutional contexts (Schwartz et al., 2021). In this study, we explore what pre -service teachers apply from their noticing of expansive sensemaking in videos of accomplished teachers to video analysis tasks in which PSTs design and enact student-centered science experiences. We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who 2320 share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We conducted a typological analysis (Miles et al., 2014) of written coursework and fieldwork from PSTs enrolled in a secondary methods course prior to student teaching. Data included their planning documents, video analysis templates, and written reflections for four video tasks: one around an accomplished teacher’s classroom and three around their own teaching. Analysis of what teachers noticed in their own and others’ videos was guided by the Expansive Sensemaking framework (Bautista & Davis, 2024). By applying this framework, the study illuminates how PSTs bridge noticing of student thinking with enacting responsive science teaching. Accomplished teacher video When analyzing videos of accomplished teachers, PSTs attended to how classroom culture shaped student participation. They noticed who was given access to share ideas publicly, how ideas were taken up by the teacher and peers, and how norms and structure supported collaborative learning. PST Videos In their own lesson planning, PSTs designed inclusive tasks that positioned students as epistemic agents and included multimodal participation strategies. They also aimed to expand what "counts" as science and promote diverse ways of knowing. However, enac ting these plans surfaced asset -oriented, equity- oriented, and participation-oriented challenges. Though each PST intended to empower students, their enactments did not always lead to the anticipated engagement. These realizations revealed a gap between in tention and impact, especially in balancing student agency with institutional constraints such as pacing guides and test preparation. Equity-related challenges emerged as PSTs attempted to make lessons culturally relevant. Some PSTs reflected on how their examples did not resonate as expected. PSTs also identified challenges in fostering student-to-student interactions. They reflected on classroom dynamics, noting the need for psychological safety and clearer norms. Importantly, they attributed participation issues to instructional design, not student deficits—demonstrating asset - oriented thinking. Prior work on noticing student thinking has presumed that teachers will apply what they learn to notice in coursework to their own practice. These results support this hypothesis while also highlighting the challenges of responsive instruction and affirming the importance of reflection and collaboration in preparing teachers to sustain asset-based noticing through opportunities to analyze their own artifacts of practice and contribute to the research base for preparing teachers to teach responsively in diverse, authentic contexts. Poster 4: Noticing in college mathematics: Development of noticing discourse in a video-based professional development Patricia Fuentes Acevedo, Christina Kimmerling, Rossella Santagata, Alessandra Pantano, Roberto Pelayo College mathematics classrooms can be marginalizing spaces, particularly for women and students of color (Riegle-Crumb & King, 2010). Persistent inequalities motivate the call for more responsive and equity- oriented college teaching. Teacher noticing is at the core of responsive teaching, with substantial research primarily conducted in K-12 settings (Santagata et al., 2021). Building on K-12 evidence, we developed and tested a video- based curriculum for instructors and graduate and undergraduate teaching a ssistants that fostered expansive noticing of students' mathematical thinking and participation (Santagata et al., 2025). Recent work has emerged suggesting that evidence of learning to notice includes uptaking a particular form of discourse (van Es et al. , 2024). We seek to unpack the relationship between participants' discourse during PD sessions and observed changes in the groups' noticing. We ask: What are the features of participants’ discourse around video- based noticing tasks? Except for a few characterizations of exemplary cases (e.g., Louie et al., 2021), little is known about how educators can learn to notice for equity. We adopt a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000) and draw on van Es et al.’s (2024) work on learning to notice by engaging in discourse-rich spaces where educators collectively make sense of instruction. Their model characterizes discourse practices that enable participants to learn how to attend to and interpret student thinking. We extend this to student participation. The authors define features of generative noticing for the different purposes that the discourse practices serve. 2321 Participants include three college instructors, five graduate and four undergraduate assistants. They engaged in whole and small group discussions around video clips during four PD sessions. For this study, we selected all segments where small groups discussed noticing prompts after watching a video clip (20 in total) and subsequent whole-group discussions. We portioned the transcribed data into conversational turns and idea units and created analytical memos. Finally, two of us deductively coded the data using van Es et al.'s (2024) features of noticing discourse (Table 1), allowing for emergent codes as well. Table 1 Features of Noticing Discourse Feature of a Noticing Discourse Definition of Feature Negotiating noteworthy phenomena A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending activity, defining what is and is not worthy of attention, and supports learning to decide what to call out and what to ignore. Problematizing and puzzling over objects of teaching and learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support interpreting and sense-making activity, which is adopting an inquiry stance toward objects of focus, such as offering conflicting viewpoints of what is observed or grappling over intent and meaning. Creating moments for further inquiry of objects of attention A collection of discursive practices that intend to support shaping interactions to gather more information for further attending and interpreting. Being accountable to evidence A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending and interpreting activity by supporting one’s claims with concrete observations, using artifacts of teaching and learning to advance an idea, and elaborating one’s ideas with more specific and precise explanations. Positioning students’ ideas and actions as resources in learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending, interpreting, and shaping activity by requiring an openness to seeing what might appear as mundane, or correct/incorrect, as something important and meaningful that can be figured out and used toward understanding. Connecting to their experiences of teaching and learning (emergent A collection of discursive practices that intend to extend the discussion from what was observed in the video to their own past experiences when teaching and/or learning, or with potential future teaching scenarios. Participants discussed aspects related to student thinking and participation, primarily focusing on problematizing objects of teaching observed in the clips, and less frequently engaging in negotiation of noteworthy phenomena. An emergent and predominant feature of their noticing discourse was making connections to their own experiences, which included extending the observed episode to past or potential future teaching scenarios. Additionally, although there is little evidence of positioning students' ideas as resources, participants maintained an asset-based perspective as required by the facilitators. The identified features in our data provide evidence that PD video prompts supported productive noticing discourse among participants and shed light on the processes through which their collective sensemaking contributed to their learning to notice. Our findings reflect the PD emphasis on noticing as multidimensional and are encouraging as they suggest tangible implications for participants' future instruction. This work contributes to the limited literature on how mechanisms for learning to notice take place at the college level. Poster 5: Attending, interpreting, and shaping: How varied ways of working with video connect with subprocesses of teacher noticing Jennifer Richards, Miriam Sherin, Sarah Larison 2322 Research has documented how video- based environments can provide rich opportunities for teachers’ learning, including learning to notice student thinking (e.g., Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021). Further, advancements in video-related technology have expanded how teachers can engage with video — moving beyond watching and discussing videos to filming and editing their own clips. In this poster, we extend a prior exploration of how teachers noticed student thinking as they engaged in multiple video processes (Richards & Sherin, 2025) by specifying ways in which these video processes map onto posited subprocesses of teacher noticing, contributing to understandings of potential drivers for noticing. The framework we animate specifies several interrelated subprocesses of teacher noticing — attending, interpreting, and shaping (van Es & Sherin, 2021). “Attending” refers to what teachers focus on in classrooms, acknowledging that humans cannot pay attention to everything. “Interpreting” refers to how teachers reason about classroom events. “Shaping” refers to what teachers do in order to support their noticing during or after instruction. While these subprocesses dynamically interact with and influence one another, we think they also reflect important opportunities for learning in their own right. Data come from three iterations of an online, video- based course for early elementary teachers in the United States on mathematical argumentation (Lomax et al., 2017). Twenty -nine in-service teachers participated in the course, in which they engaged in four sequential video processes — recording video in their own classrooms, watching and reflecting on the video, editing clips to share in the course, and interacting with others around their clips. Data sources included interviews and think- alouds with teachers about these video processes and video annotations on clips. Our prior analysis explored the affordances and constraints of each video process for teachers’ noticing of student thinking (Richards & Sherin, 2025). Here, we build on this prior analysis to characterize the noticing subprocesses that different video processes seemed to afford. When teachers recorded video in their classrooms, all three noticing subprocesses seemed to be in play as teachers iteratively focused on student ideas that required attention, sought to make sense of them in real time, and shaped interactions to test working interpretations and gather more information. Watching and reflecting on the video tended to afford continued “interpreting” and “shaping,” as teachers primarily used the video as a tool to make sense of and gain more evidence about student ideas that had intrigued them. Editing clips , in contrast, afforded “attending” with some further “interpreting” as teachers selectively identified moments of student thinking to make visible to colleagues. Finally, when interacting with others around clips , all three subprocesses were again in play as teachers highlighted specific student ideas to consider, discussed varied interpretations, and at times reviewed the video to seek more information. These findings suggest potential implications for targeted video-based designs to facilitate specific noticing subprocesses (e.g., cultivating teachers’ attending by providing multiple opportunities to edit clips). Further research could deepen understandings of how engaging with varied sequences of video processes drives teachers’ learning to notice over time. Poster 6: Developing professional vision through negotiating understanding of videorecorded whole-class talks in mathematics Håvard Johnsrud Evang, Inga Staal Jenset Supporting teacher candidates’ development of ambitious and equitable mathematics teaching is a key challenge in teacher education (Louie, 2018) and requires that teachers adapt their instruction in response to students’ content-specific ideas and ways of participating in the talk (Jacobs & Empson, 2016). Prior research has studied this situation -specific competence through concepts such as ‘noticing of students strengths’ (Jilk, 2016) and ‘equitable noticing’ (Louie, 2018) demonstrating how video- anchored activities may support candidates developing this capacity (Jenset et al., 2024). Building on a recent socio- cultural turn in noticing research (Scheiner et al., 2026), the present study extends this work by investigating how teacher candidates’ professional vision develops as they engage in discussions of video-recorded mathematical classroom talk in Grade 8 settings. This study draws on Goodwin’s (1994) concept of professional vision, defined as the ability to construct relevant knowledge through socio-historically developed practices of highlighting and coding. This framework is used to examine how teacher candidates interpret students’ utterances and actions within recorded episodes of classroom discourse. Adopting a socio- cultural perspective, the study assumes that cultural frames —that is, culturally and historically shaped interpretive lenses regarding school mathe matics, mathematical teaching, and learning (Goffman, 1974; Scheiner, 2021) —function as mediational means that shape these practices. Consequently, the negotiation and adaptation of cultural frames to make sense of students’ mathematical contributions are understood as mechanisms that drive the development of teachers’ professional vision. The study investigates how video- anchored discussions contribute to the development of mathematics teacher candidates’ professional vision. Data consists of approximately 30 hours of video recordings from five 2323 seminars integrated into an existing mathematics-didactics course across one academic year (24 candidates). The seminars were structured to progressively broaden candidates’ highlighting and coding practices, with the goal of fostering increased attention to students’ diverse mathematical reasoning and forms of participation. Candidates’ discussions were scaffolded through an observation rubric and prompts encouraging them to focus on the qualities of students’ contributions, rather than on perceived defici encies or errors. Through reflective thematic and discourse analysis, the study examines how these practices evolved over time and how cultural frames informed candidates’ interpretations of students’ mathematical work. The study yielded three insights into candidates’ professional vision development: (i) a shift from “glossy” to complex understanding of students’ participation, (ii) an expanded understanding of students’ multiple mathematical competencies, and (iii) pers istent privileging of an authoritative view on valuable mathematical outcomes. Video-anchored discussions supported candidates develop richer framing of students as valuable resources in building mathematical knowledge. However, persistent cultural frames constrained candidates’ appreciation of student’s mathematical thinking (Louie, 2018) highlighting the need for teacher education to explicitly challenge these frames to support the development of professional vision for ambitious and equitable teaching. Poster 7: Teacher-designed cases as a tool to support pre-service teacher noticing Tracy E. Dobie, Liza Escobar Aquino, Bailey N. Ondricek, Raven Burton, Angela Warnock Extensive research illustrates the value of supporting teachers’ noticing of student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010). We respond to the call for more research that investigates learning to notice from an equity frame (van Es et al., 2017) by examining cases (Shulman, 1992) as a tool to support pre-service teachers’ noticing for equity. Teacher noticing is commonly described as having three components – attending, interpreting, and responding (Jacobs et al., 2010). Research on noticing for equity explores various facets of this construct including noticing of individual student histories, anti-deficit discourses, and status and positioning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2017). Challenges include supporting pre -service teachers (PSTs) to attend to individual students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and notice more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Cases are written narratives describing authentic and complex teaching situations (Shulman, 1992) that can be intentionally designed to investigate certain themes (Dobie et al., 2024). We use cases to help PSTs grapple with the challenges of enacting equitable mathematics and science instruction —or leveraging students’ multiple strengths, honoring students’ diverse lived experiences, dismantling classroom power and status hierarchies, and challenging dominant perspectives (e.g., Aguirre et al., 2013). We partnered with local U.S. teachers, who designed cases exploring themes such as assumptions about multilingual students, inequitable group dynamics, and school structures that disadvantage minoritized students (Dobie et al., 2024). Data include PSTs’ written responses (N=1,036; 224 PSTs) to prompts for six cases that were implemented 2 -4 times each in an elementary math or science methods course. Our team deductively and inductively developed a coding scheme (Miles et al., 2014) capturing a) case details (what PSTs attended to), b) equity-oriented interpretations (PSTs’ reasoning), and c) solutions (ideas about how to respond). Two coders coded every response, and discrepancies were resolved. We highlight three findings: 1) Cases support PSTs to attend to details about students and their actions, 2) Cases and prompts can be designed to support PSTs to make wide-ranging equity-oriented interpretations, and 3) Case prompts elicit solutions that include in-the-moment actions, changes for future instruction, and advocacy- based actions including gathering data and research. We offer frequency counts across the dataset, PST quotes, and case comparisons. As an example, we explore how a subtle difference in prompts influenced PSTs’ breadth of interpretations in two similar cases focused on group dynamics: In one case, 83% of responses offering equity- oriented interpretations focused on a general imbalance in group dynamics; in the other, PSTs reasoned about a general imbalance in group dynamics (39%), as well as the roles of friendship (46%), language (43%), prior school experiences (24%), and gender (15%). Cases have significant potential for supporting PSTs’ noticing for equity including details of specific students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Questions remain about trajectories of noticing over time and the impact of noticing in cases on noticing in classrooms. 2324 Poster 8: Accounting for teacher learning in a video club: Learning a noticing discourse Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Elizabeth van Es, Melissa Luna Video-based professional development has been shown to support mathematics and science teachers’ learning to notice for responsive and equitable instruction (Santagata et al., 2021). This vision of teaching calls on teachers to attend to the substantive contributions students make toward the learning goals and adopt an inquiry stance to validate and interpret student thinking to position students’ ideas as resources for their own and others’ learning. What is less understood is how and why these settings support teacher learning. Thus, we ask what might be mechanisms of teacher learning to notice in the context of video- based professional development centered on noticing student thinking? We conceptualize video-based professional development as complex activity systems in which the video clips, the norms for participation, and the cultural and historical practices of professional development all coordinate to influence teachers’ opportunities to learn in these settings (Barnhart, 2021). Our research is informed by an often overlooked feature of complex activity systems of professional development that may be supporting teachers’ learning to notice: the nature of talk that takes place in video- based professional learning contexts. Professional discourse plays a central role in teacher learning (Lefstein et al., 2020), yet less is known about the character of talk that results in teachers’ learning to notice. Data include video recordings and transcripts from two video clubs to support teachers to learn to notice the complexity of teacher -student learning interactions. Video club facilitators prompted teachers to explore the details of student thinking, potential interpretations of their ideas, in relation to teaching. One video club included nine 4th and 5th grade mathematics teachers that met ten times for about one hour over the academic year, approximately once a month. The second video club focused on supporting six middle school science teachers’ learning to notice student thinking and teaching in seven hour -long sessions throughout an academic year. We analyzed an early and late video club meeting for both groups to identify features of a noticing discourse that were present in each meeting (van Es et al., 2024; Table 1). To account for teachers’ learning a noticing discourse, we coded the video club data and wrote analytic memos for evidence and disconfirming evidence of the noticing discourse features, also noting who enacted the talk moves that represented the noticing discourse features. Findings show that both groups shifted in their enactment of a noticing discourse over time. Both groups shifting their talk to highlight more ideas represented in the clips as worthwhile for noticing (i.e., negotiating noteworthy phenomena), pursue these ideas as objects of inquiry for the group to analyze (i.e., creating moments for further inquiry), anchor their analyses of student thinking in classroom evidence (i.e., being accountable to evidence), and demonstrate an openness to explore students’ ideas as resources for learning. Moreover, teachers demonstrated an accountability to the learning community by enacting talk that balanced respecting and honoring teachers' practice represented in the video, while also pressing on what was going on to further understand student thinking and teaching. This finding offers additional insights into features of talk that are enacted to support teachers’ learning to notice, which we argue represents the importance of collective sensemaking as a critical component of noticing discourse in professional learning. Looking across both video-clubs, this study provides evidence for a noticing discourse as key to teachers’ learning to notice, and has implications for design features, such as creating moments for further inquiry, to make video club discourse generative for teacher learning. Poster 9: Science teachers’ learning to notice expansively Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Jennifer Richards There is growing agreement in the field that teacher noticing is critical in ambitious forms of teaching that center students (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023). Joining other scholars in exploring the complexities of noticing (e.g., van Es et al., 2022), our ongoing work considers the multidimensionality of teachers' noticing for facilitating students’ sensemaking in science classrooms (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). However, there is much to learn about what supports teachers to develop multidimensional noticing practices. In this study, we explored whether a group of science teachers shifted their noticing through engaging in a specific video- based professional learning (PL) design. Briefly, with multidimensional noticing, we bring together key threads from prior work on noticing, such as the importance of noticing student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010) as well as pedagogy connected to student thinking (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa & Stein, 2015), and working toward anti -deficit ways of noticing disciplines and 2325 students (e.g., Louie et al., 2021). Taking a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000), which emphasizes learning through interaction in activity systems, we sought to embody these noticing practices in PL tools and routines (Greeno, 2006; Sandoval, 2014). This study was conducted within the context of an NSF -funded project, Implementing Practices of Ambitious Teaching for Complex Assessment Tasks (IMPACT). IMPACT PL is centered around the implementation of science performance assessments, providing a laboratory for teachers to work with students’ ideas. Five 8th -grade science teachers from different schools in a large urban district in the United States participated. Teachers engaged in collaborative analysis of performance assessment video clips intentional ly selected to highlight relations between student thinking and ambitious teaching principles (Windschitl et al., 2018) and were consistently asked to focus first on student thinking, then aspects of teaching that seemed to support student thinking. To explore changes in teachers’ noticing, we analyzed teachers’ baseline and exit interviews during which they were asked to share what they noticed and how they might respond to events in a ~7- minute video clip. We separated teachers’ interview transcripts into idea units and coded each idea unit with respect to teachers’ noticing, using the multidimensional noticing framework as an analytical lens (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). At the end of the IMPACT PL, there was growing attention to student thinking among all five teachers. When they noticed student thinking, they began to see what students were saying or appeared to be thinking as valuable, taking an asset-based frame. Moreover, in the exit interviews, teachers focused more on ways to work with students' ideas as opposed to only correcting those ideas. In short, the video- based PL tools and routines seemed to hold promise for supporting shifts in multiple dimensions of teache rs’ noticing in concert with each other. Future research can elaborate on the dynamics of teachers’ noticing practices throughout the PL, particularly how teachers iterated among noticing student thinking and pedagogy. Poster 10: A learning to notice for equity framework Jose Mendez, Elizabeth A. van Es Descriptive accounts of teachers’ noticing for equity contribute to theorizing the complexity of teachers’ in the moment attention and sensemaking to advance responsive and equitable instruction (e.g. Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). What is less understood is how teachers learn to notice for equity. Teacher noticing for equity is characterized by teachers ’ attention to multiple dimensions of the classroom environment including linguistic resources, power dynamics, relational interactions, social i dentities, and sociopolitical narratives (van Es et al., 2022). We theorize that learning to attend to equity involves the ability to name these classroom dynamics and see them as interconnected (e.g., Rubin & van Es, 2025). The second dimension involves the development of an interpretive practice , which entails continuously engaging with evidence to better understand and support students’ needs (Sherin & Russ, 2017). The third dimension involves embodied engagement , drawing on recent noticing-as-embodied c onceptualizations that highlight the nuanced and multi -sensory aspects of noticing (Mason, 2002; Scheiner, 2021). Embodied engagement of one’s noticing includes both actions, such as shaping, to position oneself to notice more expansively, and choosing to ignore particular aspects of classroom interactions that are less generative for student learning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). Embodied engagement that disrupts inequities is a reflection of developing one’s noticing for equity (Scheiner, 2021). We qualitatively analyzed data from a research practice partnership that explored whether and how co - designing and analyzing practical measurement data could provoke a mathematics teacher’s learning to notice for equity (Mendez & van Es, 2025). We adopt sociopolitical perspectives to theorize teachers’ learning to notice as tied to their personal histories and the power -laden environments they teach in (Louie et al., 2021). We also theorize learning as a progression that can support teachers and teacher educators formatively documenting changes in teachers’ noticing over time (e.g., van Es, 2011). Data included transcripts of co- design meetings to develop a survey as a form of practical measurement data and data discussions of iterative cycles of survey implementation. This poster will present a framework for learning to notice for equity that consists of four levels. Each level is characterized by shifts in noticing along the dimensions of attending to equity, interpretive practice, and embodied engagement. As the case study teacher shifted in his noticing for equity, he came to see noticing as multidimensional and integrated, shifting frames to interpret events from an asset- and evidence-based stance. He also made connections to his practice and considered how to disrupt persistent inequities to create a responsive classroom through shaping noticing interactions focused on students’ ideas and patterns of participation. This framework moves from descriptive accounts of teacher noticing for equity to characterize the prog ression of learning to noticing from an equity lens over time. In doing so, this tool offers a framework to study teachers’ 2326 learning to notice for equity, while also providing guidance for designing experiences to support teachers’ expansive noticing. papers.title: How Teachers Learn by Designing AI-Ethics Scenarios Using an LLM-Supported Authoring Tool
papers.authors: Jeanhee Lee, Sieun Park, Yue Wang, Kyuwon Kim, Yeji Ko, Hyo-Jeong So
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study investigates how teachers learn by designing AI ethics scenarios using a customized LLM-supported authoring tool. Seventeen pre - and in-service teachers engaged in dilemma-based scenario design within the Learning by Design framework through int eractive dialogue with the LLM. Data from prompt logs, think- aloud sessions, surveys, interviews, and reflections revealed diverse prompting patterns. Teachers alternated between seeking guidance and generating, evaluating, and refining ideas. Through this process, they developed a deeper understanding of AI ethics, greater confidence, and more student -centered perspectives, viewing AI as a collaborative design partner. The findings suggest that iterative prompting and scenario design provide an effective pathway for teacher learning and highlight the potential of LLM-supported environments for professional growth in AI-integrated education.

papers.title: Bloom’s Waterfall
papers.authors: Jonan Phillip Donaldson
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This poster, a conceptual contribution, reframes Bloom’s Taxonomy’s pyramid model, proposing a waterfall frame where creation is the generative source. Higher -order thinking cascades downward, naturally engaging lower -order skills. Grounded in constructionist learning theory, this model suggests learning starts with complex creation, not remembering or even understanding. It challenges traditional instructional design sequencing and offers a new perspective for designing rich learning environments that better reflect how humans naturally develop deep, contextualized enactive knowledge and skill. The problem with pyramids Bloom's Taxonomy has been a foundational framework for educational design since its introduction in 1956 (Bloom, 1956) and subsequent revision in 2001 (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001). The traditional pyramid representation creates persistent misconceptions about how learning unfolds in authentic contexts. The pyramid suggests a hierarchical climb from simple recall to complex creation, implying that learners must master lower - order skills before attempting higher -order thinking. This bottom -up interpretation is at odds with established learning sciences principles that view knowledge as enacted and learning as a situated, participatory, and tool - mediated process (Fischer et al., 2018; Nasir et al., 2020; Sawyer, 2022). Several scholars have critiqued this pyramidal structure (Crawford & Smith, 2015; Murtonen et al., 2017; Wineburg & Schneider, 2010), arguing that it misrepresents the dynamic and interconnected nature of cognitive development, yet none have proposed a learning-theory-grounded alternative. When learning designers treat the taxonomy as something to climb, they often design learning experiences that isolate knowledge and skills from meaningful contexts. They assume that learners must spend considerable time memorizing facts and practicing decontextualized procedures before being allowed to engage with complex, authentic problems . This is in tension with what learning sciences research suggests about the nature of learning (Donaldson & Allen-Handy, 2019, 2023; Schank, 2016). A waterfall reframing of Bloom’s Taxonomy This conceptual poster proposes an alternative visualization of Bloom's Taxonomy as a waterfall (see Figure 1), with “Create” positioned not as the pinnacle, but as the generative source of all learning. Figure 1 Bloom’s Waterfall with Domains in the Center, Potential Impacts on the Left, and Practices on the Right In this model, higher- order thinking naturally demands and develops lower -order skills as integrated practices. The waterfall metaphor captures how creation flows through evaluation and analysis, gathering force 2626 as it activates and develops remembering, understanding, and applying along the way. Water flowing down a waterfall gains momentum and power as it descends to the pool at the bottom, just as learners engaged in creative and analytical work naturally develop knowledge and skills. The waterfall model challenges conventional instructional sequencing by suggesting that learners should begin with complex, generative tasks rather than working their way up from basic recall. When students create artifacts, evaluate designs, or analyze systems, they must necessarily remember information, develop understanding, and apply concepts. These lower -order skills emerge organically within meaningful contexts rather than requiring separate instructional time. This reframing is grounded in constructionist learning theory ( Kafai, 2006 ; Papert & Harel, 1991), which argues that deep learning occurs when people construct external artifacts that serve as tools for thinking. Constructionism naturally emphasizes the Create level of the taxonomy, positioning making and building as primary learning activities rather than culminating achievements. The theory suggests that learners develop their most robust and transferable knowledge through the process of designing, constructing, and refining tangible or digital objects. Implications for learning design The waterfall model carries significant implications for how researchers and practitioners design learning environments. Rather than sequencing instruction from simple to complex, designers should create rich problem spaces that invite learners to engage i mmediately with high-level cognitive work. This approach does not mean throwing students into deep water without support. Instead, it means structuring activities so that scaffolding and guidance help learners succeed at complex tasks while developing enactive knowledge (Newen et al., 2018 ) in context. Project-based learning exemplifies this approach. When students tackle authentic problems that matter beyond the classroom, they must create solutions, evaluate alternatives, and analyze complex systems. The project naturally integrates all levels of the taxonomy, with creation serving as the driving force that pulls other cognitive skills into play. This also clarifies the mechanism behind knowledge building communities (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2022), where the collective goal of creating new ideas naturally requires members to remember, apply, and synthesize information in service of that higher-order goal. In these environments, students collectively work in generative modalities to advance community knowledge through sustained inquiry. They create theories, evaluate evidence, analyze explanations, and synthesize ideas. The community's shared epistemic goals situate lower-order cognitive work within the higher-order work of knowledge creation. Students remember information because they need it for their theories, not because remembering was specified as a learning objective. The model also suggests reconsidering how we write learning objectives. Traditional instructional design often generates separate objectives for each taxonomy level, treating them as discrete competencies and often requiring objectives targeting the bottom two levels before addressing higher levels. The waterfall model advises writing learning objectives around high- level outcomes. Achieving these complex outcomes will inherently require the development of supporting skills. An objective might specify that students will design and evaluate a solution to an engineering challenge, with the understanding that this work requires applying concepts, understanding principles, and remembering relevant information. Challenges and considerations Implementing waterfall-based design requires significant shifts in educational practice. Assessment systems built around recall and comprehension must evolve toward complex and holistic enactment or performance-based evaluation at the individual level, or collective evaluation at the activity system level (Engeström, 2022). Learning facilitators need professional learning opportunities to develop facilitation skills for supporting students engaged in open- ended creative work. Institutional structures like pacing guides and standardized curricula may need redesign to allow time for sustained, complex projects. The model also requires careful attention to scaffolding and support structures. Starting with creation does not mean removing guidance or structure. Research on productive failure (Kapur, 2008) demonstrates that struggling with complex problems before receiving instruction can enhance learning, but this requires thoughtful design of the problem space and strategic timing of support. Learners need access to resources, models, and feedback that help them succeed at challenging work while developing expertise. The learning sciences community has long emphasized authentic activity ( Papert & Harel, 1991 ), legitimate peripheral participation (Lave & Wenger, 1991), and learning through designing (Kolodner et al., 2003). The waterfall model of Bloom's Taxonomy offers a way to connect these theoretical commitments to a widely recognized framework. The metaphors we use for learning shape how we design for it ( Donaldson & Allen-Handy, 2023), and repositioning creation as the source rather than the summit of cognitive work can help us design learning environments that better reflect how humans naturally develop deep, contextualized expertise. 2627 References Anderson, L. papers.title: Youth Climate Storytelling as Transformative Learning: A Scoping Review of Designs, Contexts, and Digital Practices
papers.authors: Asli Sezen-Barrie, Yuxi Huang
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This scoping review synthesizes 30 peer -reviewed studies (2014– 2024) on youth storytelling in climate change education, illuminating how storytelling approaches foster transformative climate change learning. Findings reveal that storytelling functions as relational infrastructure while relating climate complexity into lived experience, cultivating eco - emotional awareness and agency, and sustaining Indigenous and community knowledge. Across formal and informal settings, educators and youth partnered to co- create stories that merged data, emotion, and cultural meaning. Digital tools such as participatory video, multimedia, and augmented reality expanded access and impact but also raised questions of equity and authorship. By mapping designs, scaffolds, and digital practices, the review offers design implications for research -practice partnerships that nurture belonging, imagination, and civic participation through climate storytelling. The need and the goal As the climate crisis intensifies, educators face an urgent challenge: how to cultivate young people’s capacity to understand, feel, and act in relation to a rapidly changing world. Traditional climate change education often privileges scientific facts, da ta, and predictive models but rarely engages the emotional, cultural, and ethical dimensions necessary for sustained transformation (Walsh, 2022 ). Transformative climate change education reframes learning as an ethical, relational, and action -oriented process that centers justice, hope, and collective capacity (Leite, 2024; Sezen -Barrie et al., 2025). Within this reframing, storytelling emerges as a powerful pedagogical and epistemological approach that binds scientific sense-making with identity, emotion, culture, and community (Gottschall, 2012). Storytelling makes climate data meaningful, futures imaginable, and collective agency possible (Bentz & O’Brien, 2019; Bloomfield, 2024). It allows youth to relate abstract climate concepts into local experiences and shared narratives of resilience, repositioning them as authors of change rather than passive recipients of information. Yet, despite growing interest, the field lacks a compr ehensive synthesis of how storytelling is designed, scaffolded, and studied across learning contexts. Moreover, as digita l media and participatory technologies proliferate from personal storytelling platforms to augmented reality, the need for design frameworks that ensure equity, authenticity, and purpose becomes more pressing. This review addresses a central gap in the learning sciences: the absence of an integrated understanding of how storytelling, across diverse designs, pedagogical functions, and digital practices, shapes transformative climate learning. While storytelling is increasingly recognized as a catalyst for connection, agency, and inclusion, its implementation remains fragmented across specific areas of social science research. Drawing on 30 peer - reviewed studies (2014– 2024), this scoping review was guided by the following research questions: (1) What research designs and learning contexts characterize studies on youth storytelling in climate change education? (2) How do storytelling function and are scaffolded to support climate change education? (3) In what ways do digital tools and frameworks support engaging in storytelling related to climate change? Conceptual framework: Storytelling in climate change education “We are the authors of our lives. We compose our self -narratives and we are composed by them” (Gottschall, 2012, p. 147). In The Storytelling Animal: How Stories Make Us Human, Gottschall (2012) argues that stories are not only how we communicate experiences but also how we construct meaning, identity, and belonging. Storytelling, the structuring and sharing of lived or imagined experiences through narrative form, is thus foundational to human cognition, culture, and communication (Gottschall, 2012). Within education, storytelling functions as both an epistemological and pedagogical approach : a way of knowing the world and of teaching it. In climate change education, it extends beyond communication to become a transformative learning practice , weaving scientific understanding with emotional relations, ethical inquiry, and socio-cultural meaning. Mainstream climate change education often privileges technocratic and positivist paradigms, emphasizing data, models, and prediction (Krasny & Schneider, 2021). While such approaches are essential for understanding biophysical mechanisms, they rarely foste r the emotional, ethical, or civic engagement necessary 1877 for meaningful transformation. Storytelling intervenes by humanizing climate knowledge while translating complex systems into situated experiences and relationships. By embedding abstract concepts in personal or community narratives, it deepens comprehension and fosters empathy (Bloomfield , 2024). In this sense, stories “relocalize” climate learning, situating it within histories of place, culture, and justice rather than abstract global metrics. Storytelling aligns with transformative climate change education frameworks (Sezen-Barrie et al., 2025; Leite, 2024), which highlights attention to learning across epistemologies and improving emotional well -being. Climate stories , especially those from marginalized or Indigenous communities , which operates as counter- hegemonic discourses that challenge dominant narratives of progress and environmental relationships (Leite, 2024; Tuck, McKenzie, & McCoy, 2014). These narratives open epistemic space for lear ners to question assumptions about development, responsibility, and belonging in the Anthropocene. Through engagement with such stories, learners cultivate more pluralistic and justice -oriented understandings of socio- ecological systems. Indigenous storytelling traditions exemplify this transformative potential. In many Indigenous epistemologies, story is both method and ethic: a means of transmitting knowledge and sustaining reciprocal relationships among humans, nonhumans, and the land (Whyte, 2017). Integrating Indigenous storytelling into climate curricula enacts decolonial praxis, repositioning learners as participants in relational webs of care rather than as detached observers of climate data (Tuck et al., 2014). Empirical research reinforces the pedagogical value of storytelling. Pahl et al. (2019) found that climate messages conveyed through stories were significantly more effective at fostering emotional engagement and pro- environmental intentions than statistical presentations. Educational research further shows that storytelling supports identity work: when students create or analyze stories about climate change through oral narratives, filmmaking, or digital media, they articulate their roles, values, and hopes within broader ecological systems (Leite, 2024). In sum, storytelling is far more than a communication tool; it is a transformative framework for learning. It bridges the cognitive, affective, and ethical domains —helping learners think, feel, and act with relational awareness. By integrating storytelling into climate change education, educators can nurture imagination, agency, and care, cultivating learners who are not only informed about the planetary crisis but also empowered to participate in r eimagining its futures. Storytelling, in this sense, becomes both pedagogy and praxis —a way of composing more just and livable worlds.

papers.title: Infrastructuring for Climate Justice in STEM-Rich Making
papers.authors: Wisam Sedawi, Edna Tan
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents
papers.abstract: This study employs critical participatory design- based research to investigate how integrating infrastructuring practices into a community- based STEM-rich maker program supports youth in responding to urgent, felt challenges of climate change through their making, while also promoting sustainable communities. Grounded in the experiences of middle school youth participating in a year -long, community -centered program, our findings highlight how infrastructural resources (material, relational, social /emotional, and intellectual) enabled youth to engage in meaningful, climate-focused making. These resources became a site for incubating ways of knowing and being, as they emerged as connective tissue linking people, practices, and contexts through acts of making for change. They fostered solidarity and shared responsibility by positioning youth as active agents in generating educative, solution- oriented artifacts for climate justice and reorganizing physical spaces using maker materials. We argue that int egrating infrastructural resources into community-based STEM-rich making supports youth-led responses to climate change and advances justice-oriented outcomes.

papers.title: Entities Detonating Potentials: Interuniversity Design Workshop TiUD as an Exploratory Lab for Actants of the Futures
papers.authors: Inés Alvarez-Icaza, Claudia Garduño-García, Edrei Ibarra-Martínez, Reneé Harari Masri
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: The Interuniversity Design Workshop is an exploratory laboratory that promotes the study of design activism, sustainable design, and transition design. The seventh edition of the workshop aimed to visualize the organizations, institutions, or companies that must be created to enable Mexico City to reach its potential for social well-being. The object of this educational experience is to enable design students to discover new ways to promote social activation through design as a professional activity. A group of 60 undergraduate design students from five high education institutions (HEI,’s) analyzed their own contexts, emphasi zing the identification of potential sources of wellbeing; later, they were given the task to design interactions, including giving shape to the agents that would make them possible. Their projects revealed three key findings: (a) that students are able to identify potentials through contextual observation; (b) that the creation of new actors can potentially activate new realities; and (c) the proposed entities hint potential future roles of designers in Latin American contexts. This study contributes to the field of design, looking towards a fairer, more pluralistic and diverse future .

papers.title: A Tale of Two Rivers: Pedagogical Implications Learned Through the Co- Design of an Environmental Engineering Curriculum
papers.authors: Taryn Williams, Symone Gyles, Hosun Kang, Rossella Santagata, Yuxi Huang, Aakriti Bisht, Teresa Hachey, Jennifer Long, Erick Valdez, Sara Ludovise
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: As the impacts of climate change intensify, it is critical to support high school students in developing Critical Science Agency (CSA) and Systems Thinking (ST) to leverage science learning to address environmental concerns in their local communities and beyond. This study is part of a project involving a collaboration between university researchers, informal science educators, and high school students and teachers to codesign a place - and community- based environmental engineering curriculum. We explore pedagogical implications surfaced through the analysis of teacher and student codesign experiences and reflections that focus on community- embedded and relational environmental learning. Findings highlight the importance of physical presence to support critical and informed socio-ecological understanding of place.

papers.title: Collaborative Lore Development as a Mediational Bridge Between Material and Playworlds
papers.authors: JC Leapman, Lee Martin
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Youth & Adolescents
papers.abstract: This study examines how playful, collaborative development of project -related lore can mediate learning in a making-focused STEM learning environment. We present a case study of two intersectionally -marginalized seventh -grade girls who initially distanced themselves from STEM-related materials and practices but came to create a robotic character, “Mr. Evil French Cheeto”. To understand the evolution of their participation, we employ a Vygotskian perspective on play, extended by theories of storytelling, ima ginative world -building, and identity-resources. Through a microethnographic analysis of video and audio data from a ten- week in -school maker program, we explore how lore — the evolving narrative about the character and his world —generated iterative exchanges between the girls’ imaginative playworld and the constraint-laiden material world. Our findings suggest that collaborative lore development can be a promising avenue for supporting agency, authorship, and problem- solving, and may have the potential to open up expansive pathways for equitable participation in STEM-related learning environments.

papers.title: An Unstructured Way: How Students Learn to Provide Feedback in a Reading Club
papers.authors: Shiyao Wei, Xiang Li, Zhichun Liu
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: While peer feedback is beneficial for students’ learning, students a re not always ready to provide constructive feedback to their peers. Prior studies have used cognitive scaffolding, such as review forms , to support students ’ feedback provision, yet the social context of learning has been overlooked. In the current study, we investigate how students naturally learn to provide feedback within a reading club. Over ten weeks of participation in receiving and giv ing feedback, students’ feedback became more specific and targeted to their peers’ work. By participati ng in community activities, students sha red perspectives and knowledge with their peers and found their own ways to provide constructive feedback.

papers.title: Designing the Next Generation of Computational Modeling and Learning with AI
papers.authors: Tamar Fuhrmann, Line Have Musaeus, Ole Sejer Iversen, Paulo Blikstein
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: As generative AI rapidly transforms how humans interact with computation, it challenges the foundations of many educational technologies designed to teach coding, modeling, and computational thinking. Systems that were once built around writing or arranging code—whether block-based or text-based—now coexist with tools that generate programs through natural language. This workshop invites the learning sciences and design research community to collectively explore how educational technologies that include coding must be re-envisioned in light of these shifts. What will it mean to “code,” “debug,” or “model” when AI becomes a co-author? How might our existing environments—like MoDa, a block-based modeling platform, or text-based NetLogo simulations—need to be rethought for an era where learners reason through prompts, outputs, and model interpretation rather than syntax and structure? Our goal is to identify key design principles, challenges, and opportunities to guide the next generation of AI-powered computational learning environments. Theoretical background and significance Integrating computational thinking (CT) into science education equips students with powerful tools to explore scientific phenomena, foster deeper conceptual understanding, and engage in authentic scientific practices. The interdisciplinary potential of this work empowers students and practitioners to engage meaningfully with emerging local and global challenges (Barr et al., 2011; Weintrop et al., 2016). Existing literature identifies several core CT practices: abstraction, generalization, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, and debugging (Caeli & Yadav, 2020). Computational modeling, including agent-based modeling (ABM), has long been recognized as a valuable tool that can simultaneously support students' science learning and CT (e.g., Wilkerson et al., 2015; Musaeus et al., 2023; Musaeus et al., 2022). Recently, however, developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have introduced new possibilities for how learners and educators may interact with computational models (Chen et al., 2023). In the future, it may no longer be necessary to write code to create scientific computer models, putting learners in the role of collaborators with generative AI. For decades, coding has served as both a tool for learning and a language for thinking (Papert, 1980; diSessa, 2000). Block-based and text-based environments embody constructionist ideals, empowering learners to express, test, and refine ideas through computation. Yet today, this paradigm is shifting. AI’s ability to generate executable code from natural language redefines what it means to “speak computation.” As we transition from programming languages to prompting, foundational concepts—such as loops, conditions, and agents—risk becoming invisible. At the same time, new epistemic practices emerge: prompt engineering, iterative interpretation of AI outputs, and ethical reasoning about algorithmic agency. This timely workshop for the field of learning sciences demands that we rethink not only curricula, but also what fundamental concepts in programming that we still need to teach and how to design the tools themselves; how they mediate learning, distribute agency, and scaffold understanding when code is no longer the learner’s sole artifact of construction. Organizing team Line Have Musaeus leads research at the Center for Computational Thinking & Design, focusing on computing education, computational modeling, and STEM learning. Her work explores how integrating computational thinking into school subjects supports both student learning and teacher development. She co-designed CoTinker and has extensive experience organizing workshops on computing and AI in education. Tamar Fuhrmann leads research at the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab at Teachers College, Columbia University. She is a founding leader of the MoDa project, focusing on computational modeling in science education. Her work integrates STEM, AI, and constructionist approaches, and she regularly leads professional development and international collaborations. Paulo Blikstein is an Associate Professor at Columbia University and director of the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. His research focuses on using technology to t ransform learning in STEM and AI. He founded the FabLearn program and has received major awards, including the NSF CAREER and AERA Early Career Award. Ole Sejer Iversen is a professor at Aarhus University and director of the Center for Computational Thinking & Design. His research focuses on computational empowerment, helping young people become active creators of technology. He works at the intersection of participatory design, computing education, and policy, leading large-scale international projects. Workshop goals and intended audience This workshop is designed for researchers, designers, and educators in the learning sciences, computing education, and educational technology who are exploring the future of computational learning in the age of AI. It will particularly interest those developing or studying coding-based environments—such as block-based, text-based, or modeling tools—and those investigating how generative AI transforms students’ epistemic, creative, and design practices. Participants with backgrounds in design-based research, computational modeling, or AI in education will find opportunities to share perspectives, contribute to collaborative redesign activities, and help shape a research agenda for rethinking the role of coding and modeling in AI-mediated learning environments. Outline of planned activities and facility requirements The four-hour workshop (plus one hour for lunch and coffee) will begin with an opening and framing session (20 minutes) introducing key tensions in AI-integrated coding environments. This will be followed by case study provocations (40 minutes), during which participants engage with two computational modeling environments: MoDa, a block-based agent-based modeling tool, and CoTinker, a collaborative modeling environment. Participants will explore and design models while considering how these tools might evolve as learners use AI to generate, modify, and explain models. In the collaborative design challenge (60 minutes), small groups will reimagine an educational technology that includes coding, redesigning it to integrate AI while preserving learners’ epistemic and creative engagement. This will lead into a group synthesis and discussion (40 minutes), during which participants share insights, identify emerging principles, and surface tensions, producing a poster as the group outcome. The workshop will conclude with a closing reflection (20 minutes), focusing on articulating open research questions and opportunities for future collaboration. Participation requirements Participation is open to researchers, designers, educators, and graduate students interested in computational modeling, coding education, or AI-supported learning environments. No specific technical expertise or prior experience with educational learning environments is required. We would like to support a dynamic, collaborative environment in which multiple perspectives on the redesign of coding-based educational technologies can emerge. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past Over the past several years, ISLS conferences have hosted numerous workshops and symposia exploring computational modeling, data science education, and AI-supported learning, for example, Kafai et al., 2025; Wagh et al., 2024; Fuhrmann et al., 2022; Fuhrmann et al., 2024; and McElhaney et al., 2020. These events advanced theoretical and design frameworks for integrating computational practices into science and engineering education. However, few have directly addressed the implications of generative AI for redesigning the educational technologies that include coding, particularly how block-based and text-based modeling environments must evolve when learners can construct programs through natural language. This workshop builds on that lineage but reframes the central question: not how to teach coding, but how coding itself—and the tools built around it—should be reimagined for an AI-mediated future. By convening researchers working at the intersection of computational modeling, design-based research, and AI in education, the session extends ongoing ISLS dialogues toward a new design agenda: understanding how AI reshapes the epistemic and pedagogical foundations of computational learning tools. Expected outcome and outputs The workshop will strengthen a community of practice focused on designing tools that preserve human sense- making and agency alongside AI assistance. It will generate open-ended questions that help rethink computational educational technologies in an AI-mediated context, and build a shared vocabulary around emerging hybrid practices where coding, prompting, and modeling intersect. Rather than defining what the future of coding should be, the session aims to open a dialogue on how our tools—and our field—must evolve to meet it. papers.title: Creating Artifacts for Expansive Science Teaching through Art-Based Collaboration
papers.authors: Deborah Dutta, Miwa A. Takeuchi
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: The need for newer ways to enact human- nature relationships calls for educational practices to expand their boundaries of learning. Several educational initiatives have engaged in integrating arts -based practices with science learning to broaden the scope and aims of learning. However, the creation of artifacts that mediate the processes by which science educators can expand their pedagogical repertoire to engage with the emergent possibilities of arts-based practices has received less attention. This study describes collaborative processes between an artist and a pre-service teacher, Becca, which inspired her attempts to reimagine her teaching aims and practices, as part of a summer camp research –design partnership on a community urban farm. The study highlights how the evolution of pedagogical artifacts through collaborations made space for emergent learning anchored in embodied experiences.

papers.title: Design-Based Approaches to Co-Analysis in Collaborative Research
papers.authors: Kylie Peppler, June Ahn, Maggie Dahn
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) and design- based implementation research (DBIR) emphasize co-design with stakeholders, yet approaches for collaborative data analysis remain underdeveloped. This paper examines how design approaches can scaffold quali tative and quantitative inquiry for diverse partners in co-analysis processes. We present two working examples: the TRACE Project, which developed a community -driven taxonomy of arts program outcomes through collaborative classification with 26 community arts organizations, and the Whole Child Analytics Project (WCAP), which employed AI -assisted reflection tools to measure college and career readiness competencies through teacher and student co-design in a large, urban school district. Through these cases, we illustrate methods for creating spaces that afford meaningful engagement from all partners while honoring multiple perspectives, voices, and worldviews in the analysis process.
