papers.title: Mentorship Approaches for Establishing Communities of Practice in Constructionist Learning Spaces
papers.authors: Ashita Bawankule, Mike Tissenbaum, Santiago Ospina-Tabares, David Hopping, Blake Danzig, Nathan
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Constructionist spaces encourage learners to create artifacts and, in the process, engage with others who hold diverse knowledge, skills, and expertise, thus creating a community of practice. This can lead to the development of and need for mentorship – often taking the form of peer and near -peer mentorship. In this structured poster symposium, we present a collection of implementations and studies within diverse contexts of constructionist learning spaces to discuss how mentorship practices support the development of communities of practice. Drawing from a variety of contexts and approaches, we seek to understand how to implement mentorship, what it means, its benefits, and the different forms it can take.

papers.title: Speculative Interaction Geography: Imagining How Embodied Interactions Take Shape Beyond AI Prediction
papers.authors: Ben Rydal Shapiro, Deborah Silvis
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Recent advances in qualitative data visualization are expanding how researchers and educators analyze interactions among people and things across learning environments. Yet , these tools remain primarily retrospective , representing what has already occurred from data such as video. Bridging traditions of interaction analysis with research centering affect and speculative design, this paper explores how qualitative data visualization tools can also serve as speculative instrument s for creating data to imagine possible interactions in learning spaces. Specifically, we extend a method called interaction geography through two illustrative cases that demonstrate new technical capabilities. These capabilities enabl e researchers and practitioners to sketch imagined interactions and spatial configurations, reconfiguring interaction geography as both an analytic and speculative practice. We propose the notion of speculative interaction geography and show how speculative data visualization can serve as a human-centered counterpoint to AI-driven prediction in the learning sciences, with implications for areas like teacher education and participatory design.

papers.authors: Madison Allen Kuyenga
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: My research examines how cultural practices (e.g., barbering, cosmetology, fashion design) and epistemologies (i.e., ways of knowing) can be learned and sustained while acquiring computer science (CS) skills. I draw on ethnocomputing and leverage heritage algorithms— hybrids of computing and culture—to create simulations of cultural practices using algorithms. These simulations can be used to teach cultural ways of knowing and making as well as CS skills. Overall, my research focuses on sustaining cultural making practices and cultivating the creative aspects of CS education through community-based participatory design research. In this statement, I share my previous work in CS education and ethnocomputing and situate future strands of my work in STEAM and the learning sciences.

papers.title: From Practice Partner to Co-Learning: Designing Role-Fluid AI Partnership for Skills Development
papers.authors: Fengfeng Ke, Xin Yuan, Nuodi Zhang, Chaewon Kim, Alex Barrett, Rosalyn Shin
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Building on research in human– AI collaboration and appropriate reliance, we propose a conceptual design model of a role -fluid, AI -driven practice– learning partner to support novices’ skill development in dynamic, context-dependent tasks. The model integrates LLM-generated personas with agent -based modeling. Using a multiple -case, mixed-methods approach, we examined its implementation and feasibility across three domains: responsive teaching, transitional care, and multimodal qualitative data coding. The findings inform the design of novice –AI collaborations that promote learning and sustained skill development, rather than merely cognitive offloading or short-term task completion.

papers.title: Revisiting Wise and Schwarz’s Provocations for CSCL: Partnerships for Transformation and Educational Change
papers.authors: Breneil Malcolm, Marcela Borge, Alyssa Wise, Marcelo Worsley, Sebastian Simon, Tanner Vea
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: In 2017, Wise and Schwarz proposed eight provocations for the field of CSCL following their interactions and analyses with scholars within the field. We broaden the call to the entire LS community to once again pause, reflect, and discuss a vision for the next 10 years of opportunities, challenges, and impacts we seek to make. This collective ambition is not simply to be responsive to technological changes but also to inform their design and use. Towards this end, we invited researchers from the ICLS and CSCL communities to propose new provocations for us to consider and discuss that focus both on the changing technological landscape and the need to ensure that diverse perspectives and viewpoints are brought into the forefront of technology-enhanced collaboration in meaningful ways.

papers.authors: Kathy H. Zhou, Robin Michel, Rubina Khan
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Youth & Adolescents
papers.abstract: T races of Transformation: An Artist-in-School-Community Project Traces of Transformation is a co-created artist-in-school-community project emerging from Fall of Artica (FoA), developed through a partnership between Artivition Projects (represented by artist Kathy H. Zhou) and the interdisciplinary Art and Design course (IDC) at University of Toronto Schools, led by teacher Robin Michel. Building on the Culture Shoes Project, students designed shoes embodying their FoA avatars, using gameplay to surface ideological tensions — safety vs. freedom, now vs. future, utility vs. culture. Through research, discussion, and critical reflection, each student imprinted a personal message onto their shoe sole. These Adobe Illustrator designs were realized as laser-cut rubber stamps at the UTS innovation hub. Echoing Allora and Calzadilla's politically engaged interventions, this critical-making work asks: What marks do we leave behind as learners, and how do these traces shape the paths available to those who follow? papers.title: Insights from International Partnerships on Infrastructuring for Maker Education
papers.authors: Yuval Segev, Yotam Hod, Shiri Kashi, Akshay Nagarajan, Alekh Velayudhan, Ann Berger Valente, Anna Santo
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Maker education is a disruptive innovation spreading globally, fundamentally challenging schooling by shifting focus from abstract ideas to creating and sharing tangible artifacts. Often driven by grassroots enthusiasm rather than top- down mandates, this diffusion lacks corresponding supportive infrastructure from established systems, posing a timely question: What can be learned about the infrastructures and infrastructuring processes required to support the integration of maker learning? Maker education offers an opportunity to employ infrastructuring as a conceptual lens and strategy to analyze the inherent tensions between this movement and formal schooling. This structured poster symposia embodies the Annual Meeting's theme, Partnering with Purpose . It convenes international research groups who actively collaborate with local stakeholders to share diverse insights from their efforts to integrate maker learning into school systems. By illuminating these infrastructuring processes, we aim to inform a more robust theory of sustainable, systemic change within the Learning Sciences.

papers.authors: Morgan Vickery, Elena Bai, Kyle Beyersdorf, Jie Sheng, Aman Desai, Srijita Chakraburty

papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of Learning Sciences scholarship makes it challenging for newcomers to navigate diverse theories, methods, and contexts. We present the Interactive Literature Review Database Template, an open-source tool that turns any corpus into a dynamic, filterable database. As demonstrated by Journal of the Learning Sciences articles and student- built instances, the tool enables sustainable, transparent, and easily updated literature exploration while lowering technical barriers for researchers.

papers.abstract: Resisting dignity-denying practices in education is urgent. This paper is guided by Poza’s (2021) call to center racialized multilingual students as rights- bearing individuals through a dignity frame grounded in meaningful participation, social agency, and social equality. Using secondary qualitative analysis of our own prior studies in science classrooms, we reexamine classroom moments to identify how dignity is conferred. Two cases illustrate this frame: bilingual students’ poetic talk during formative assessment, and a teacher’s curriculum design that leveraged multimodality as poetic “talk” and inclusive sensemaking. Findings highlight how discourse moves, translanguaging, and multimodality can confer dignity by affirming students’ humanity and agency. The dignity frame provides educators and researchers with an analytic and pedagogical tool to identify, enact, and design dignity-conferring classroom interactions.

papers.title: Learning through Chatbot Design: Examining Children’s AI Understanding and Hallucination Awareness
papers.authors: Deniz Ozturk, Xiaoyi Tian, Joey Huang, Tiffany Barnes
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Middle School Students; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Young learners increasingly interact with AI chatbots in classrooms and daily life, as educators explore their potential to support learning. While chatbots can personalize instruction and enhance engagement, they also produce hallucinations, which are plausible but incorrect responses. Because such errors arise from the probabilistic nature of generative AI, it is essential to help students develop literacy in recognizing and addressing them. Grounded in constructionist approaches to AI literacy, this study engaged 47 middle school students in designing and testing their own chatbots using a LUMI environment equipped with hallucination detection tools. Through hands -on creation and peer evaluation, students developed a deeper understanding of how AI systems function and where their limitations emerge. Findings show significant gains in AI understanding, hallucination awareness, and students’ ability to propose concrete detection and mitigation strategies. The study demonstrates how we can cultivate critical and reflective engagement with youth through emerging AI technologies.

Drawing on a multi -year partnership with te achers, we analyze the co -design and classroom enactment of a collaborative AI partner, CoBi , and associated “revisiting community agreement” routines. Using video data and thematic analysis, we show how these routines functioned as boundary objects linking design intent with classroom practice. Teachers enacted the routines with high integrity and creatively adapted them to local contexts, leveraging AI errors to foster AI literacy and critical reflection. Students engaged in meta -collaborative discussions that positioned AI as a phenomenon for critique rather than a source of authority. Findings illustrate how curriculum routines can align human and technological agency, sustaining equity -centered and reflective collaboration in AI - embedded classrooms.

papers.title: “I was so confused about the gases unit until now”: Mapping the Dynamics of Epistemic Affects and Cognitive Processing in Learning Gas Laws on YouTube
papers.authors: Nuodi Zhang, Ran Bi, Hui Shi, Shiyao Wei
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: YouTube has emerged as a key space for informal science learning, where learners actively engage with complex ideas outside formal instruction. This exploratory study examines how epistemic affects and cognitive processing interact during science learning on YouTube, focusing on the topic of Gas Laws. Using search terms from Ambitious Science Teaching and the Next Generation Science Standards, 131 videos and 18,290 viewer comments were analyzed through a human- in-the-loop, AI -assisted coding process based on epistemic affect s and Bloom’s taxonomy. Preliminary findings indicate that curiosity, vexation, and joy often co - occurred with higher -order cognitive processes such as analyzing and evaluating, suggesting that both positive and negative emotions can stimulate deeper reasoning and conceptual understanding. The study underscores the importance of recognizing learners’ affective expressions as integral to their cognitive engagement and offers new insights for designing emotionally and intellectually supportive environments in informal digital science learning.

papers.title: How CS Educators Can Mobilize Knowledge from PD Experiences: Building Bridges Between Research and Practice
papers.authors: Cassandra Kelley, Deniz Sonmez Unal, Sarina Saran, Janet Bih Fofang, Erin Walker, Judi Fusco
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines how PreK–12 teacher leaders facilitate knowledge mobilization (KMb) in computer science (CS), acting as brokers between research and classroom practice. Based on interviews with 20 U.S. teachers, it highlights how professional developme nt (PD) supports teachers in applying research, integrating emerging technologies, and navigating systemic barriers. Findings emphasize the importance of positioning teachers as active agents who use, share, and co-construct knowledge, and recommend participatory, iterative PD models that foster collaboration and shape the broader direction of CS education.

papers.authors: Akin Adediji, Jinhee Lee
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study examines sociotechnical efficacy in 3D environment modeling through the Roblox Developers Forum. Ito & Reich’s (2017) equity- centered principles explore how youth learning participation is fostered in creative spaces. Available curriculum, plugins, and developer feedback built around “hanging out”, “messing around”, “geeking out” (HOMAGO) emphasize the “hanging out” dimension (Ito, 2009). Platforms enhanced by modular, adaptive assets foster equitable access and social connectedness, shifting learning between participatory HOMAGO to supporting agency and connectivist models.

papers.title: Entangled Learning: Farmers, Phones, and the Politics of Informal Agricultural Learning in Rural Jamaica
papers.authors: Alexis Carr, Engida Gebre
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study examines how smallholder farmers in rural Jamaica engage with mobile phones and digital platforms as part of ‘ informal’ learning apparatuses. Drawing on Barad’s (2007) theory of agential realism, it conceptualizes learning as a dynamic, relational process shaped by entangled human and non- human agencies. Based on interviews and observations with 18 farmer s, the analysis explores how mobile devices, algorithms, social networks, ecological feedback, and experiential knowledge co -produce authority and shape learning. Central to this process are agential cuts —material discursive boundary -making practices through which farmers distinguish between valid/ invalid and traditional/non-traditional knowledge. Farmers actively sift, interpret, and reconfigure knowledge through iterative intra - actions with platforms, people, and place. The findings challenge binary framings of digital learning as either human -centered or technologically deterministic, revealing instead the recursive and negotiated nature of learning. This research offers critical insights for developing inclusive and context-responsive agricultural mLearning interventions.

papers.title: Towards a Real-time Reciprocal Metacognition Feedback Paradigm in Introductory Computer Science Classrooms
papers.authors: Nicholas Diana, Carly Grizzaffi, Noah Apthorpe
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students
papers.abstract: Learning is a continuous process, with a student's level of mastery constantly evolving alongside instruction. While traditional assessment methods excel at assessing mastery at a particular moment in time, they are ill- suited for capturing the incremental nature of learning. We propose a novel system that allows students to provide continuous feedback about their perceived mastery throughout a lecture. With this data, instructors could more effectively respond to individual and class -wide misunderstandings in real -time. This new interaction paradigm would also promote metacognitive reasoning skills and allow the students to "dog- ear" moments of confusion during the lecture that could be returned to while studying. Through a series of user studies with both students and faculty, we explored the unique interaction challenges of this design space. This paper describes the key components of the proposed paradigm, drawing on these empirical insights to address design challenges .

papers.title: Speculative Futuring for Understanding River Socio-Ecology
papers.authors: Aakriti Bisht, Symone Gyles, Yuxi Huang, Rossella Santagata, Hosun Kang, Jennifer Long
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study investigates how Speculative Futuring (SF) can create space for high school students to critically engage with environmental challenges and envision alternative futures for their communities. Our findings show that students drew on multiple form s of knowledge such as lived experiences, and scientific information to shape their understanding around addressing socio- environmental challenges such as water quality, and accessibility of the natural resources. Artifacts developed during SF reflected their understanding of current socio-ecological systems while envisioning possibilities for the future.

papers.title: Quantum Computational Thinking: A Conceptual Exploration
papers.authors: Raquel Coelho, Raja Krishnaswamy, Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa, Junyu Liu
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Computational Thinking (CT) frameworks have expanded over the past two decades to address technological advances and sociotechnical concerns, yet they remain grounded in classical, deterministic computational logic. Quantum information science introduces fundamentally different principles for representing and processing information, requiring learners to engage with non-intuitive, probabilistic, and relational forms of reasoning that depart from classical computational models. Drawing on frameworks by Brennan and Resnick and Kafai et al., we explore what Quantum Computational Thinking (QCT) might entail and open a dialogue about how the learning sciences community might prepare learners for a quantum - mediated world, with attention to access, democratic participation, and the challenge s of developing new intuitions.

papers.title: Learning With and Against Place Towards Spatial Justice
papers.authors: Max Sherard, Suraj Uttamchandani, Ari Hock, Kemper Lipscomb, Charlie Mahoney, Matthew X. Curinga
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: In this symposium, we consider the diversity of ways that learners conceptualize and engage with places. Building on growing work in the Learning Sciences on learning in/with places, we bring together contributions that highlight the gap between learning with a place and learning about a place by examining cases in which learners complicate ideas of places as good or bad. The contributions show a wide variety of ways this can happen, from students’ changing concepts of a “developed” place, to how prior knowledge of a city can shape one’s perception of neighborhoods as safe or unsafe, to how children might reclaim or resist visions of their school as policed, to how community members resist simplified representation of their places. Together this work suggests increasingly nuanced ways of treating place that can in turn support designs of just learning in places.

papers.title: Designing for Radical Imagination
papers.authors: Brit Claiborne
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This dissertation examines how learning environments for K–12 teachers can be designed to foster radical imagination through speculative activities. Data were collected across four mathematics teacher education courses at a large U.S. university, and a core group of participants joined a collective inquiry group to explore how to create elements of their imagined futures in their present classrooms. Anticipated findings include design principles that promote radical imagination among teachers, the forms of collectivity that emerged within the inquiry group, and the focal points of teachers’ radical reimaginings of mathematics teaching and schooling. Goals and background The aim of the present study is to design and analyze various learning environments where K-12 mathematics teachers engage with radical imagination and collective futuring. Radical imagination is the act of crafting new possibilities for the future that are not constrained by systemic structures or the status-quo of the “possible.” Neoliberal logics typically locate the source and the solution of (educational) problems in the individual, and thus leave unexamined the structures and collective action needed to challenge systemic forces (Barker & Scheele, 2016). Radical imagination by collectives of teachers, and fostering that imagination through teacher education, intentionally endeavors to rewrite the dominant power structures that maintain the status quo of capitalist, white supremacist, and settler-colonial systems in education. This is of particular importance in mathematics teacher education, as the discipline of mathematics is viewed as politically neutral (Harouni, 2015), which ultimately serves to maintain hierarchies of power and underscores patriarchal ways of knowing (Hesse-Biber et al., 2004). Specifically, this research explores: (1) How can learning environments in mathematics education be designed to contribute to the development of teacher radical imagination, and (2) How can collectives of teachers act on their imagined future in the present? Study design and methods This qualitative dissertation comprises of three studies with data collected in the mathematics teacher education department of a large U.S. university. Across the studies, 40 participants consented to include their data for analysis, and I collected over 170 speculative writing artifacts. In study 1, I incorporated identical speculative writing prompts into four education courses to explore the content of teachers’ imagined futures. papers.title: Peer Feedback’s Role in Undergraduates’ Interdisciplinary Collaborative Learning Outcomes and Regulated Learning Patterns
papers.authors: Guo Su, Wenli Chen, Gaoxia Zhu, Yubei Shi, Li Wei, Chencheng Le
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Interdisciplinary collaborative learning (ICL) is critical in 21st- century education, yet supporting disciplinary boundary crossing remains challenging. Peer feedback has the potential to help students cross boundaries by identifying the gaps between single-disciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches. However, the impact of peer feedback on ICL outcomes and regulated learning patterns is underexplored, despite the critical role of regulatory processes in students’ engagement in collaborative learning. This study employed a counterbalanced design with 52 undergraduates randomly assigned to two clusters experiencing conditions with and without peer feedback in reverse sequence. Group concept maps and verbal discussions from the 50-minute learning task were collected and analyzed. Results showed that groups performed significantly better with peer feedback in involving diverse perspectives, integrating knowledge, and reflecting on solution impacts and limitations. Additionally, students learning with peer feedback demonstrated an evaluation-engaged regulatory pattern, whereas they showed a planning- engaged regulatory pattern when peer feedback was not given. These findings suggest peer feedback’s potential for supporting ICL.

papers.title: Democratizing Algebra: Advancing Conceptual Understanding Through Purpose -Driven Research-Practice-Industry Partnership
papers.authors: Tarik Buli, Amanda Wortman, Stefani Pautz Stephenson, Rebecca Banks
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This RPIP study refined From Here to There (FH2T), a game -based algebra application, by positioning educators as pedagogical architects. Through iterative feedback loops, practitioners directly influenced critical features like the Teacher Console, ensuring classroom-readiness and scalability. Results demonstrate that FH2T democratizes math by decoupling conceptual logic from computational barriers. By grounding learning in perceptual engagement, the game transforms students from passive rule -followers into agentic "Doers," dismantling traditional gatekeepers to algebraic success.

papers.title: Partnering Through Ceremony: A Multimodal Design for Collaborative Healing and Learning
papers.authors: Karla Trujillo
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This poster presents an early -stage ceremonial design for collaborative learning rooted in Indigenous methodologies and relational accountability. Through multimodal documentation and AI assisted poetic co creation, the work explores how ceremony can support healing centered learning across generations and technologies. The poster highlights design commitments, a simplified conjecture map and emerging expressions that invite discussion about how socio-technical systems can participate in relational meaning making.

papers.title: Designing at the Speed of Trust: Unearthing Implicit Values and Vibes
papers.authors: Ananda Marin
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Design Based Research (DBR) is a slow, tedious, and overwhelming process. Over the years of their existence, DBR research teams develop into tiny publics where new ways of being and doing develop. While tools such as conjecture maps were developed to support documenting the relationship between theoretical and design-based conjectures, we have found that the conceptual level of these conjectures do not quite capture our idiosyncratic axiologies, or the values, flavor, and vibes that became implicit or taken for granted. In this paper we share reflections from the Choreographing Science project, describing how the choice to end the project by designing something new helped us (1) reveal taken for granted design values and principles that we developed during our 4 years of collaboration, (2) work at a faster, more confident pace, and (3) create something shareable with stakeholders we care about. Shifting design practices to capture cultivated values and vibes As a hallmark of the Learning Sciences, Design Based Research (DBR) (Brown, 1992; Collins, 1992) allows us to advance theories of learning and design together through an iterative, collaborative process of conjecturing, enacting, and analyzing. DBR is a slow, tedious, and often overwhelming process requiring years of engagement. During this time research teams develop into tiny publics (Fine, 2012), where new ways of being and doing can emerge. Bang and colleagues expanded DBR to include attention to relational processes and products as consequential to design (Bang et al., 2016; Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). While tools such as conjecture maps (Sandoval, 2014) were developed to support documenting links between theoretical and design conjectures across iterative cycles, tools for unearthing axiological commitments have remained less clear. In this paper we share a DBR case in which shifting from researcher -led design practices to artistic -led (endogenous) design practices helped us unearth sticky, implicit axiologies we had developed yet taken for granted over our four- year collaboration. As an interdisciplinary team of Learning scientists, Artists, & Scientists, we worked on the Choreographing Science project with a clear sense of our shared values. We set out to disrupt knowledge hierarchies by uplifting embodied, choreographic ways of knowing in order to desettle established ways of doing science that historically dismissed youth perspectives (Vogelstein et al., 2022). We leveraged improvisational choreographic tools for science modeling in the design of summer camps that brought middle schoolers, scientists, & choreographers together. Our traditional social sciences analytic work produced academic papers that highlighted how participants leveraged choreographic tools to make sense of scientific phenomena by doing things like comparing how humans and computational agents interpret and enact movement rules (Wagh, Vogelstein, & Champion, 2024), developing movement rules for scientific entities (Vogelstein, Wagh, & Champion, 2025), and reflecting on the experience of responding to others’ move ment ideas (Vogelstein et al., 2024). While these analytic insights were generative, papers felt limited as our only products. Papers don’t spur movement or make collective choreography. We realized we needed a product that would promote inquiry through movement, and to do so, we switched our mode of design. We let choreographic design methods lead us as we designed a deck of movement cards to support facilitators in getting groups of people thinking by moving together. This process enlivened & aligned our tiny public once more, putting our axiological commitments to practice in the learning spaces we valued most. In this paper we describe how the choice to end our project by switching design methods to design something new helped us (1) reveal consequential, taken for granted design values and principles that we developed during our four-year collaboration, (2) work at a faster, more confident pace, and (3) create something shareable with stakeholders we care about. Our values are reflected in a product that centers uncertainty and begets new questions. Our MOVE about it cards engage our stakeholders as collaborators, replicating our design-based, pedagogical value of engaging our Choreographing Science participants as collaborators and thinking partners. What we made: MOVE about it The Choreographing Science project was a four -year (2021- 2025) DBR project run by Learning Scientists, Dancer-Choreographers, & Scientists who believed that bringing choreographic modeling and agent -based modeling together could help create inroads for middle schoolers to contribute to scientists’ inquiry and support 1957 scientists in learning from both embodied and youth perspectives. Over four years, we iteratively designed and implemented three 1-2 week-long, free summer camps in which middle schoolers, scientists, and choreographers engaged in scientific inquiry together using choreographic and agent -based modeling tools. The structure of the camps foregrounded the use of choreographic practices and tools to raise and explore questions about the scientists’ research topics. Our formal analytic work thus far has resulted in six ISLS papers (not including this), and multiple in-process journal articles. In the Winter of 2025, as we began to plan for the ending of the project, we found ourselves in the midst of a federal funding crisis in the US. This crisis left us uncertain whether or not we would be able to finish our project as planned, and left our team with an urgency to create something useful. Our scientist partners had expressed impassioned interest in bringing the activities and tools from our camps into their labs and classrooms, and our friends and colleagues in a multitude of educational spaces were just as excited to get their communities moving alongside these ideas. It was in this action -oriented, communal context that we refocused our efforts toward creating a tangible product with these communities at the forefront. In the end, we printed 200 copies of a deck of movement prompt cards which we named MOVE about it: prompts to get groups thinking together through movement. The MOVE about it deck included 90 cards in total and was composed of 6 instruction cards, 19 ways in cards, 22 ways through cards, 22 ways together cards, & 21 ways out cards. Through a process of choreographic design which included brainstorming, enacting, and grouping, we developed four main categories of cards (like parent codes) and five kinds of each category (like child codes, see Column 1 Table 1). Ways in cards were simple and meant to get people up and moving in approachable ways, ways through were more complicated, ways together explicitly focused on moving in relation to others, and ways out focused on grounded endings (Table 1). The instruction cards gave descriptions for the four categories of movement prompts in the deck (Column 2 Table 1) as well as three activity proposals (multi -card sequencing, body segmenting, & leaders and mirrors). Additionally, we added a new, vital member to our team: dancer, visual artist, and assistant professor of dance, MK Ford. MK created custom illustrations for all 20 sub- categories of cards. In the rest of this paper, we describe the implicit values displayed in our cards, reflections on the process of designing them, and the new audiences and communities these cards allow us to be in conversation with. We conclude by making the argument that this process enabled us to surface implicit axiologies in our design work and create a functional tool for a multitude of formal and informal learning spaces that will live on far beyond the end date of our work together. Table 1 Descriptions & Examples of the Four Kinds of Cards in our MOVE about it Deck Type of Card Description Example from Deck ways in ways to walk make circles orientation breathe speed Ways in cards build on familiar actions like walking, breathing, and changing direction to offer approachable ways to get a group in motion. Getting people to move together can be challenging: we often sit still to think and forget we have creative, expressive bodies. We hope ways in cards feel doable and spark curiosity. ways through shake coordinate vivid imagery quality balance Ways through cards build on the foundation of ways in, expanding on movement variety, quality, and complexity. Ways through cards invite new coordination patterns and vivid imagery. While ways in help movers trust their instincts, ways through stretch those instincts into uncharted territories and open space to feel surprised. ways together imagination contact if, then spatial relations music & rhythm Ways together cards explicitly focus on moving in relation to others. Ways together cards foster movement “conversations,” where choices are shaped by the group. Through movement conversations, individuals can become a connected whole, shifting from feeling like a group of “I’s” to one “We.” In this space, ideas emerge that can only be understood together. ways out grounding self agency together stillness space Ways out cards provide intentional transitions that honor how movement changes us. Ways out cards ground participants, restore simplicity, and guide toward an ending. Rather than an abrupt stop, ways out cards provide a thoughtful conclusion, respecting the shared experience and preparing integrated, curious bodies for whatever comes next. 1958 Revealing taken for granted values: Reaching for novelty, variety, and surprise Anyone can dance. Any movement (or stillness) can be dance. Dance is not just for trained, lean, not-yet-disabled bodies to perform challenging feats. Interesting and compelling choreography can be danced by any-body and can be sourced from a wide range of movement choices. We take these principles from a lineage of postmodern dance artists that began in the downtown New York City dance scene in the 1960’s (Banes, 1987). Two of their radical commitments remain in our work: choreography can e merge from dancers’ myriad interpretations of movement prompts, and starting with pedestrian movements can be generative. Through our traditional analytic work, we documented our use of movement prompts (or rules) for generating choreography because of their similarity to code that agents follow in ABM. However, we had taken for granted some of the underlying principles and values embedded in our use of movement prompts, which became explicit as we created our cards. Movement prompts for structuring creativity and switching things up Our dance values come from traditions that assert that “good” improvisational dance (Henley, 2025) relies on structure and boundness in order to support expansive embodied explorations. To this end, restrictions are helpful and generative. Asking people to just “dance” will not generate “good” choreography. And by good we mean that the movements are novel in some way or unexpected and surprise us as movers and observers. We value variety and surprise. Prompts should be structured to inspire, switch up, and allow participants the choice of leaving their comfortable movement homeostases (if only for a few seconds at a time). Some of our ways in cards highlight this value. For example, “walk sideways” restricts movements to walking, an everyday way of moving for many people, and instead of enacting it forward, which is very common, the direction is switched to sideways. How one enacts “walk sideways” is still open-ended. You could walk sideways with a mobility aid, at a slow or fast pace, leading with your head or hip, to your right or left, crossing your feet over each other or shuffling. Prompts such as, “circle your elbow,” bring your attention to a body part not often foregrounded in everyday movement, activating creative, unique movement possibilities. The prompts “change your speed,” or, “find a new place in the room,” ask dancers to alter their first impulses, making small changes that open up new possibilities without naming or assuming the presence of body parts. In addition, we also value reminding mover s that silliness and play can generate expansive thinking. Sometimes you just need to “shake to the sky” & see what happens next! Movement prompts for leveraging imagery to try the “impossible” Novelty and surprise were baked into our movement pedagogy. Dance improvisation tools such as imagery and “impossible” tasks were utilized to enact these values. We found that responding to imaginative prompts such as “move like a blade of grass” were more physically challenging than concrete and direct tasks like “walk sideways.” This differentiation led us to create distinct ways in and ways through cards. Some of the more abstract or imaginative movement prompts leveraged movement qualities derived from imagery such as “allow your body to float through the space,” or “travel through the space like a bolt of lightning.” Floating or lightning images were meant to inspire expansive movement qualities and interpretations. Words, however, were not always the best or only way of sparking one’s movement imagination, which brought us to collaborate with MK on adding a visual element. MK’s art, like the grounding image (Table 1, Row 5, Column 3), shows what might be invisible to the eye, but felt in the body. Additionally, their art displays a diverse array of bodies engaging with the movement ideas. The surrealist nature of these provocations (both prompts and images) undergirds the idea of offering “impossible” tasks. You cannot move as fast as a bolt of lightning, nor can you “reach far away through the walls of the room,” or “keep a forcefield between you and someone else.” But we can enact the physical effort and imaginative, communal space of doing so. Not only can we enact these ideas, but it is generative to do so. Stretching our imagination can stretch our movement explorations and choreographic possibilities. Movement prompts for attending to felt sensations as intentional ways to start and end While it became clear that an implicit goal in our work was to get people exploring new ways to move, it also became apparent that beginning and ending these explorations required careful attention. It’s really hard to get a group of people up and moving! We often do not make explicit the vulnerability and bravery it takes to move and dance with others. Even amongst ourselves, a collective of researchers committed to the power of movement for learning, it took a great deal of effort for us to get up from seated, sedentary positions and move. Once we got groups moving, sometimes it was hard to stop. Endings functioned as transitions from a shared movement experience to (most often) a sedentary, verbal discussion. Bringing movers’ attention inward to how their bodies felt while moving acted as a way to ground both the start and end of movement explorations. Some of the ways in cards focused on moving in synchrony with your breath, amplifying movements already happening in your 1959 body: “get bigger as you inhale and smaller as you exhale.” Some of the ways out cards focused on attending to comfort in your body such as, “find a movement that feels like home.” Movements that arise from attending to how your body feels and what it wants to do are good ways to activate movement -based explorations and bring them to a thoughtful close to prepare for whatever comes next. Sometimes choosing what feels “good” or “right” is more important than reaching for novelty and variability in a mover’s interpretations and choice making. Working at the speed of confidence and trust: “This was of me” It took us about six months to design and print our MOVE about it decks. Six months is much shorter than the time it takes to write and revise a journal manuscript (which in the top Learning Sciences journals often takes a few years), but a little longer than the amount of time it takes to write a conference paper like t his one (about a month or two). Our timeline felt fast because of how we moved through the process. We gave ourselves freedom to create without exhaustively describing or defending our rationale or pointing to an empirical moment in our large data corpus to justify each decision we made. Our fast pace was not always easy. It actually made Lauren uncomfortable. She even tried to slow down the group by going back to the data to pinpoint similarities between movement prompts used during our camps and in our developing deck. While the group humored her, they also pushed back against traditional methodological moves that stifled our creative design process. Our collaborator, Curtis Thomas, reminded us that we knew what we were doing and encouraged us to work from a place of confidence and trust: “Who are we trying to convince right now? Because I just believe it. You know, like I have the experience. And to me, I’m like, I don’t necessarily need to go back [to the data] and look because I’m like, oh yeah this was of me.” (Curtis Thomas 5/27/25). For Curtis, returning to the data was a move used to convince others, not ourselves, of the validity of our choices. This shift in design practices felt radical to Lauren who loves and has been trained in the painstakingly slow and labored work of grounding design decisions in empirical evidence. Eventually, we all moved forward with more confidence that our decisions were grounded in what we knew from our designs and implementations, as well as our bodies and experiences as movers. Moving confidently and quickly freed us to consider new questions related to marketing and scope, including purpose & audience, that we previously did not have space for when focused on justifying our decisions to research audiences. Broadening audience Shifting the pace of our design work from the minutia of traditional academic analyses to the more confident, quicker decision-making pace of choreographic design opened us to new kinds of work. We engage d with ideas related to marketing, such as purpose, scope, and audience, that we had not wrestled with before. We worked hard to develop clear and succinct pitches for the usefulness of our deck, articulating our problem space (“When we’re thinking, we often have to stay still and only move to take a break or get the wiggles out of our system. But we are made to move! What if movement could be part of our thinking?”) and affordances (“When we MOVE about it together, we can: (1) see ourselves build on each other’ s ideas, (2) pose questions, explore relationships, and express ideas as a group, and (2) try out many ideas at the same time”). As we focused our pitch, we also worked to specify our audience. This was challenging because we saw the benefits of moving together relevant everywhere, since most human activity entails working in groups and generating a variety of ideas. We focused on our partner scientists who expressed interest in a deck like this, burnt-out educators who are often too exhausted to disrupt business as usual in their classrooms, dance makers and educators, and after-school space educators, all of whom support learning across “classrooms, workshops, laboratories, and community spaces.” Exposing taken for granted axiological commitments Our MOVE about it cards represent the values we cultivated over four -years together: uplifting communities of movers, expansive creativity, rigorous empathy, and openness for change. We made this deck because we wanted to be useful to communities we care about. Our decision to leverage endogenous choreographic design methods to design something new but related to our DBR project initially felt like a move away from DBR. However, we now see this move as serving key DBR goals by acting as a magnifying glass to expose taken for granted axiologies so fundamental and shared that we did not think to make them explicit. Changing the mode of design changed the kinds of axiologies we were able to see embedded in our work. We see this building on calls in DBR to consider designing for spread and not scale (Taylor et al., 2019), in response to learner ingenuity (Brady & Vogelstein, 2022), and towards axiological innovations (Bang et al., 2016). Shifting our leading epistemological logics felt satisfying in the end. We are excited about gifting educators decks, sharing them with our friends and family, creating art with them (Vogelstein et al., 2026), and researching new adaptations. We designed these cards with the hope that they will live a generative like far beyond the end date of our project. Not knowing what that will entail feels like a fitting end to our design story. 1960 References Banes, S. (1987). Terpsichore in sneakers: post-modern dance. Wesleyan University Press. papers.title: Reimagining Early AI Literacies: A Care-Centered Co-Design Study with Parents and Young Children
papers.authors: Grace Yaxin Xing
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: While AI literacy has gained increasing attention in education, existing frameworks often privilege technical competencies and workforce preparation, overlooking the developmental, relational, and ethical concerns central to early childhood education. Grounded in socio-constructionist theories and an ethics-of-care lens, my dissertation reimagines AI literacy as a care-centered, co-constructed practice within family ecologies. This three-paper dissertation includes: (1) a care-centered critical review of AI literacy frameworks that advances a new conceptualization of early AI literacies in ECE; (2) a techno-ethnographic study investigating parents’ beliefs, practices, and contexts shaping children’s AI learning at home; and (3) participatory co-design with parent–child dyads to iteratively develop a Family AI Literacy Starter Kit. These studies bridge conceptual, perceptual, and design perspectives by identifying gaps in current frameworks, mapping parental engagement, and co-creating developmentally appropriate resources toward justice-oriented early AI literacies in families.

papers.title: Designing Equitable Partnerships for the Future of Play
papers.authors: Cristina Paul, Anna Terrazas, Christine Lee
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Educators and a university researcher co -designed play-based learning to support children to gain a deep and enduring understanding of scientific concepts, critical consciousness, and practicing joy. We present how reciprocity emerged through our equitabl e partnerships and how these partnerships make research, theory, praxis, and student learning more robust. Play Play is messy; while we wanted to include play in our classrooms as social justice advocates and practitioners, the structures, schedules, and everyday boundaries of typical classrooms make it a challenge. Play allows us to grasp important ideas from multiple angles with empathy and care, both as educators and students. This is a freedom we are slowly losing with the rise of standardized curricula, testing, and the prevalence of unfeeling screen-based learning. Standardized and for-profit curricula can also strip educators of autonomy. Play is learning. Play advocacy and research aren’t just about joy—they’re about justice too. We present four design components from our equitable partnership that made our participatory design- based research successful. Our poster shares how we practiced reciprocity in our researcher -educator partnership. Understanding how future educator - researcher collaborations can design their partnerships in equitable ways is critical for the future of design -based research. Co-designing play The goal of our partnership was to design an interdisciplinary environmental curriculum that empowered young students to learn through play. Throughout the school year, we designed play lessons to support students in learning about interdependent relationships between people, pollinators, and plants. Cristina and Anna are elementary teachers of mixed -age 1st and 2nd grade students at an elementary school in Los Angeles. Cristina teaches in a dual language bilingual education (DLBE) program with 90% instruction in Spanish and 10% instruction in English. Christine, a university researcher, has been interested in designing a curriculum for environmental education through play and has been collaborating with Cristina and Anna since the Spring of 2022. Throughout the academic school year, our team met weekly to co -plan play-based lessons. Our year -long play-based curriculum had three parts that wove together play and movement: first, we investigated plants and flowers; then, we investigated bees as pollinators; an d finally, we investigated how people impact and rely on plants and pollinators. Designing partnerships: Reciprocity While our participatory design-based research study (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) aimed to integrate play into our curriculum, the goal of our poster is to reflect on the design of our equitable partnership that made it possible. The data in this poster are fro m our collective experiences and reflections on educator -researcher relationships in design-based work. Through reflection, we identify and present four components that made our work reciprocal. Our partnership was built on curiosity, trust, humility, and multiple competencies. Instead of focusing on the distinct tasks of rigid roles, we practiced reciprocity through equitable partnerships –sharing responsibilities and making decisions together about how to implement play. Component one: Play Play is a human need and everyone has the right to play (United Nations, 1989). Throughout our work, play was a goal and a means for children, teachers, and researchers. We intentionally designed our curriculum with embedded play, and to accomplish this, we also played with one another and alongside our students. Of course, we played with our lesson designs, with how to collect data on students’ learning, and even played with the design of our classroom spaces by moving furniture to make room for play. More importantly, we made and played with costumes, created art, and pretended to be creatures and plants alongside our students. Play helped us to reflect on and refine our thinking–not only with our own experiences to anticipate challenges, but to revise our lessons, and to make decisions about lesson sequences. This freed us from restrictive, static, and hierarchical ways of learning, designing, and researching. 2907 Component two: Autonomy for all While traditional research methodologies tend to uphold a sense of control in research settings, our participatory work is grounded in the context of our classrooms. We rejected the notion that we could have complete control over research and what happens in the classroom. Instead of controlling how teaching and learning should occur, we embraced unscripted, yet meaningful interactions, discoveries, questions, and misconceptions. For example, children unexpectedly sang during play lessons. When teachers asked children about word choice and how they mixed Spanish and English, the volume, and/or speed of their singing, the children’s responses demonstrated the intentionality of their decisions and their nuanced understanding of big ideas like pollination. If t eachers had simply asked children not to sing during a dance lesson or to follow the instructions with more fidelity and play quietly like a pollinator, these understandings may have never emerged and developed. Play offers opportunities for children to participate in expansive and joyful ways. It gives students space and agency to explore ideas, negotiate meaning, and co -create rules of engagement as they interact with peers. It is impossible to predict all the ways children may engage in a topic, and that should delight educators and researchers. Component three: Support for all Our classrooms have a diverse student population, which includes neurodiverse students, students with disabilities, and emergent multilingual learners. We wanted to design play for all, not just for the majority of our students. Throughout the school year, we noticed some neurodiverse students struggled with noise, lack of explicit directions, and more freedom in moving in classroom spaces. This led us to modify our lesson designs. Some of the design changes included frontloading ideas for where to play, roles to take on with which students might feel most comfortable, creating boundaries in our indoor and outdoor spaces, using noise -reducing headphones for certain children, and including children in decision- making about classroom set up for play. When desi gning classroom spaces or thinking about how to use available outdoor spaces, we ask ourselves if the physical, emotional, and academic environment we’ve created is autonomy -supportive (Amado et al., 2020). Are the materials, furniture, and structures for participation accessible to all children? Are relationships being tended to with care and curiosity? Are researchers and teachers modeling care and curiosity for students? Sometimes it’s not simply the chairs that must be moved; it’s our hearts and minds. Component four: Data sharing Our partnership was designed to share knowledge and resources, which often led us to teach one another new skills. Taking photos or videos for formal research analysis was new for Cristina and Anna. Video recordings allowed us to see and hear movement, con versation, negotiation, discussion, and problem- solving that led to the creation of each movement during play. We could see and hear students' reasoning and decision- making, which demonstrated a clear understanding of the function of each part of a flower. In a busy classroom of students, it is difficult to observe and gain a deep understanding of how each student is making sense of the information. As teachers, video recordings made it possible to follow children’s understanding; we could see how knowledge cross-pollinated between students so they could make deeper connections to the content and each other. More importantly, analyzing and re -watching the video alongside Christine changed how Anna viewed participation structures when students were playing. It changed how Anna listens, observes, and builds on students’ ideas in new ways. Concluding remarks The future we dream of is one of delight. Yet, education and academia are fraught with constraints and seeming barriers to joy -filled work. Educators are taught behavior management strategies. Administrators and other evaluators that walk through classrooms expect to see a level of control that demonstrates that children's behavior is being effectively "managed." Play is the antidote to control. The future is relational. To be in healthy relationships with each other as researchers, teachers, and students is to relate to each other in mutually respectful ways—ways of being that anticipate the beauty and logic of knowledge created in collaboration rather than in isolation. We cannot do reciprocal work without being in equitable partnerships. The future we hope for is one of reciprocity between students and teachers, teachers and researchers, and researchers and children. The democratization of knowledge and expertise in our classrooms and research wasn't accidental. It was dignity -affirming (Espinoza et al., 2020) and humanizing for children, educators, and researchers. 2908 References Amado, D., Molero, P., Del Villar, F., Tapia -Serrano, M.
