papers.title: Reimagining Learning through Arts and Making: Creative Identity Work in Partnership
papers.authors: Kristina Stamatis, Joseph L. Polman, Jrène Rahm, Sanne Akkerman, Jeroen Vermeulen, Antero G. Garcia, Royston
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This hybrid symposium brings together learning sciences research exploring intergenerational identity development in relation to the arts and making as a means of deepening partnership. We look across continents through projects that center art and making as identity work, particularly for people navigating historic oppression, to better understand the ways these creative acts can provide pathways of resistance and reimagination. We follow the conference theme to reimagine the ways that learning scientists interpret “impactful learning experiences” (Fishman et al., 2013) in partnerships that emphasize notions of joy and creation as meaningful forms of reimagining learning in our present global context. Each paper reimagines how intergenerational participants inscribe themselves into the world, positioning acts of identity building as a deeply rooted engagement in possibility. Through this session, we strive to build conversations across these nine projects and in collaboration with attendees toward more nuanced, critical, and culturally grounded notions of partnership. Overview This proposed hybrid symposium brings into conversation learning sciences research exploring how people develop identities across lifespans in relation to the arts —broadly conceived as making and tinkering, creating, writing, composing, and creatively engaging with others toward more transformative futures. Drawing from traditions of design- based research (e.g., Brown, 1992), participatory design research (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016), testimonio and pláticas (e.g., Delgado -Bernal, 2012), and decolonizing and indigenous methodologies (e.g., Bang, 2020; Patel, 2016), we examine the ways that partnerships resonate and grow alongside the identities of participants when grounded in notions of joy, play, creativity, and belonging (Mirra & Garcia, 2024). In this symposium, we collectively define learning as ontological, a process of becoming someone new (e.g., Lee, 2016), 2340 and view learning and associated identities as expansive, developing along pathways in relation to our histories, communities, partnerships, and collective ecologies (e.g., Bang, 2020; Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Nasir et al., 2020). We see identity as an ever -changing part of human experience, both related to and disruptive of structures of power that have continuously led to oppression and genocide based on race, ethnicity, culture, religion, language, gender, socioeconomic status, ability, and the growing number of traits deemed “illegal” by those in power in the U.S. and other nations. We follow theorists whose work has pushed boundaries of what it means to embody artistry, particularly for historically marginalized peoples whose collective efforts have alwa ys been the catalyst for movements toward more equitable futures (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). Our aim with this collective conversation is to look across our projects, all of which center art and making as part of learning trajectories through which people build identities (Nasir et al., 2020), particularly for people navigating historic oppression, to better understand the ways creative acts can provide pathways of resistance, reimagination, and transformation in relationship with and to one another, our environments, and the more -than-human beings whose ecologies we share. This session will center on the questions: 1) How can projects focused on identity-building within creative contexts help to reimagine the ways partnerships operate toward more joyful, just, and transformative ends? 2) How can conversations across projects move the learning sciences to more deeply attend to the creativity essential for reinvention of systems and structures? In this symposium, we discuss papers in three 18- minute rounds, ending with collaborative discussion with Dr. McKinney de Royston, audience, and participants, to push back against restrictive notions of identification, instead taking up dialogical approaches to identity (e.g., Akkerman & Meijer, 2011). Across these papers, scholars examine the ways that making and the arts can extend toward more transformative notions of what it means to be and become a certain kind of person (Enyedy et al., 2014). We bring into conversation projects drawing from narrative (e.g., Delgado- Bernal, 2012), proleptic (Lee, 2016), and liberatory notions of identity development across generations (Nasir et al., 2020), and engage in conversations to push these silos toward more holistic and transformative ends. Framing identity building as an artistic process, rather than a solely scientific one, we reimagine how young people and their elders inscribe themselves into the world. We position every act of identification as a potential artistic act of defiance, imagination, and creation toward more transformative futures. In considering the call for this year’s conference, we use these pieces to speak together about the ways that partnership and design can act as levers to engage in joyful resistance and creative reimagining of structures of power (Hayes & Kaba, 2023). The scholars in this symposium draw from sociocultural, sociocritical, and constructionist theories of learning, as well as notions of criticality, embodiment, temporality, and design to reconsider the ways that our work can build knowledge and community collectively. Although the papers feature a variety of methods, all share perspectives that data can and should be representative of the multiple and complex ways learners navigate the world (Bridges, 2020). This complexity is part of our session structure, where we offer both traditional and creative opportunities for participants across modalities to engage and build knowledge collaboratively and in partnership. Despite differences in epistemology and analysis, each project suggests new ways of understanding identity development as a deeply cultural and artistic process of reimagining both oneself and the world. Paper abstracts are listed below alphabetically by first author and referred to here by number. While all papers engage in examining arts and identity development through design, partnership, and collaboration, the projects differ in stages of development and are situated across varying contexts, nations, and continents with an array of participants. Papers 1, 3, 5, and 6 examine the ways university students engage across settings to build identities artistically alongside diverse communities of learners. P apers 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 8 take up notions of intergenerational identification and learning to examine the ways that making and the arts can support attunement to new conceptions of self as activist and part of a “political-ethical becoming” (Vossoughi et al., 2021). Paper 9 acts as an overarching commentary across the papers, examining making and tinkering and proposing new ways of framing acts of artistry as supportive of learners’ critical consciousness (Freire, 1970). Each of the papers focuses on a diverse community of learners, where participants with historically marginalized identifications as well as other actors draw upon powerful identity resources (Nasir and Cooks, 2009) to support the reimagining of self and the world as a joyful and creative act, deeply rooted in cultural pathways of learning (Nasir et al., 2020). Together, these papers offer rich groundwork for conversations in the learning sciences, pushing on notions of partnership and learning as identity-making, while interrogating disparate yet deeply interconnected sociopolitical contexts. Paper 1: Identity work in a community and art based engaged university program Sanne Akkerman, Jeroen Vermeulen 2341 This paper reports on identity work taking place in a transdisciplinary community -engaged master’s track at Utrecht University. In this year-long program, students are invited into the everyday life of an urban public park, where they meet, talk with, and collaborate alongside local citizens representing a wide range of interest -based communities, including skaters, graffiti artists, rappers, youth care workers, and caretakers of trees, grass, and water. Through the track, students are asked to move beyond predefined disciplinary orientations and questions. They are challenged to explore the stories and practices of these communities, while inviting and bringing diverse community members and groups together to exchange perspectives and potentially build new relations around central communal themes. In this paper, we examine what it means for students to engage in what in this track is intended as a form of ontological synchronization with what happens and matters to local communities at a specific site and what it means for community members to become involved in prescenery science (Akkerman, Bakker, & Penuel, 2021). Our focus is on identity work that emerges in the process of synchronization and community engagement. Following Akkerman and Meijer (2011), we understand identity work from a dialogical perspective, where people come to explore and dynamically understand themselves through relations and collaborations with others. In the context of this track, we analyze how students and community members from various subcultures develop new understandings by relating to others with less familiar backgrounds and perspectives. We consider motivation letters, reports of interest, week ly meetings during the year and the communal creation of a light -art story and public event over time. Findings show the ways in which students and community members of the park take outside and inside perspectives of others but also develop new shared perspectives in the art works being produced functioning as an effective boundary object (Star, 1989) to materialize and structure the open, and at times discomfortable, educational process of mutual engagement. Paper 2: Joyful immigrant family storytelling during politically perilous times Antero G. Garcia, Alix Dick, Christián Thaniari This paper shares findings from a yearlong community- engaged storytelling project with immigrant parents and their children. In the final weeks before the 2025 U.S. presidential inauguration, immigrant families prepared for the worst, based on President -elect Trump’s ongoing vows to implement “the largest domestic deportation operation in American history” (Colvin, 2023). As the future for immigrant families remained uncertain even in “sanctuary” states like California, the narratives around immigrant life focused on hopeless narratives of struggle (Dick & Garcia, 2024). And yet, despite these dire contexts, immigrant families thrive. Amidst a climate of fear, immigrant families sustain joy not in spite of dire policy consequences but as ongoing, embodied pr actice. This paper shares how immigrant families manifested joyful identities through storytelling in perilous times. This paper builds on sociocultural literacies scholarship that centers immigrant and transnational identities (Bernal, 2001; Delgado- Gaitan, 2005; Villenas, 2005). Further, the emphasis on immigrant family artmaking practices also guides this work (e.g. Flores 2018; 2022). Finally, recognizing family storytelling as occurring with a community of practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991), this project extends understanding of identity and expertise within transnational informal learning environments. This qualitative case study (Dyson & Genishi, 2005; Yin, 2013) was conducted entirely online. Monthly, the community of families would convene online to share and reflect on the multimodal artifacts they created. These meetings concluded with a design prompt to take up for the following month. Methodologically, this project is situated within Chicana feminist plática methodology (e.g. Fierros & Delgado Bernal, 2016; Hannegan- Martinez, 2023). This approach centers participants’ lived experiences as forms of expertise. The ongoing conversation—plática —of each meeting guides how joy is named, measured, and shared in this group. In addition to recordings of community meetings, data for this project included the multimodal artifacts parents and children made together as well as individual interviews conducted with each family twice throughout the yearlong project. All data was inductively coded alongside a cadre of youth and parent community members. These community- created testimonies of hope ( testimonios de esperanza) acted as opportunities to explore political and structural contexts of joy. Participants’ artifacts centered communal expertise and joy tied to familial pride, cultural identity, and expressed hope for future generations. Notably, families centered “struggle” as a kind of superpower. This work, as demonstrated in poems, photo- based family trees, and family -created collages revealed ongoing narratives of solidarity that emerged through c ommunity-based artmaking. Participants’ proleptic vision of cultural identity interweaves multimodal storytelling of joy across varied timescales. In contrast to dominant, deficit narratives of immigrant experiences, findings from this study illuminate an alternative, speculative narrative of immigrant ingenuity. These findings illustrate sustained community joy through collected, family-made artifacts. The field of education does not yet utilize specific forms 2342 of joyful creation by marginalized families; the possibilities for leveraging these as assets for pedagogical application in various settings pose clear guidance for future research and design. Paper 3: Identity work in a community and art based engaged university program Teyona James-Harris, Shirin Vossoughi, Lulu Madise This paper examines educator learning and mutual becoming in a longstanding STEAM and storytelling program serving Black, Latinx/e and Asian/South Asian middle schoolers. We ask: What conditions support learning across an intergenerational collective of ed ucators of color? How do educators describe the identity shifts and forms of mutual becoming they experience over time? Here mutual becoming refers to moments when student and educator learning are dynamically interrelated and mutually generative. Research has identified key conditions that support teachers’ professional learning and efficacy (e.g., communities of practice, guidance around equitable pedagogies, instructional materials designed for teacher learning [Patton & Parker, 2017; Wei, et. al ., 2010]). Yet there is a need to better understand the paradigmatic identity shifts and forms of political- ethical becoming that can emerge for educators in settings that reimagine disciplinary domains and social relations, and practice expansive forms of arts and political education. Here we draw on Vossoughi et al.’s (2021) definition of political-ethical becoming as “not only reorganizing our thoughts but reshaping our relations,” and Rogoff’s (2023) fractals as attuning to mutually constituting processes at smaller and larger scales over time. Utilizing interpretive ethnography (Erickson, 1985) and participatory design research (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) we report on a data set documenting student and educator learning within a 6- week summer STEAM/Storytelling program over eight years through audio -video recordings, field notes, student and educator interviews, and documentation of co- design processes. We share findings developed through qualitative coding and memoing of pre - and post-program educator interviews, analysis of one focal educators’ t rajectory across years, and field notes that capture mutual becoming through educators’ reflections on key interactions with students. Our analytic approach involves working closely with an intergenerational group of educators of color (ages 13-62) who blend the role of teachers, artists, and researchers. Our findings show how participants describe both structural and relational conditions of educator learning as consequential to the identity shifts they experience. Structural conditions include intergenerational apprenticeship, daily debriefs and educator reflections, opportunities to witness and try out others’ pedagogical moves, and fieldnote writing. Relational conditions include intentional community building and care among educators, encouragement to show up as their full selves, and a culture of playful communion that aligned with the forms of artistic creation supported among students. Patterns across field notes and educators’ pre- and post-interviews reveal the ways educator learning and political-ethical becoming involved embodying the artistic ways of being supported with students (e.g., taking our imaginations seriously, embracing the process of creation and learning, engaging in various forms of language work and conceptual revision) in ways that connected with educators’ own complex histories with schooling, learning, and life. One educator, for example, discussed the ways she was taught to avoid mistakes within a rigid schooling context, and how she needed to learn to soften this tendency within herself as she supported our middle school students to embrace process. Another example of language revision shows how the kinds of thinki ng we were supporting our students to engage around rethinking inherited terms was taken up by novice educators. One undergraduate educator referred to Red Winged Black Birds during an outdoor walk as “territorial” and then later revised his language to “protective,” sharing with students the “why” of his revision. Our paper also includes a deeper look at one teacher’s trajectory over time and the ways she took up storywork. Pedagogical storytelling was a routine practice within this setting and involved careful decision making on the part of educators around language and nourishing forms of political education and storytelling for middle school students. This teacher's journey reveals how guided feedback and revision of her story through intergenerational apprenticeship played a key role in expanding not only what she offered youth story listeners, but how she thought about and walked with her own story over time. We also found educators practiced these ways of being in relationships and contexts outside the learning environment, with family and friends. This included discussing the ways they noticed their language changing in conversations with others, and how they are enacting new forms of careful noticing and attunement to others and the world outside the educational settings. We found that all educator interviews narrated this type of “rippling out” of learning as a key indicator of the identity shifts supported by transformative projects. Such findings can support intentional design of the conditions that cultivate transformative educator learning, and ways of conceptualizing educator learning as a deep process of identity work and political -ethical 2343 becoming. Further, mutual becoming both troubles student -teacher binaries common within oppressive educational structures (Freire, 1970) and helps theorize identity shifts in ways that carefully attune to the centrality of relationality and creativity in human learning. Paper 4: “We are all becoming”: Exploring the design of improvisational activity within researcher-artist collaborations and zine making Lindsay Lindberg, Ananda Marin, Shivani Davé, Brenda Lopez, Trinity Collins Artistic identities develop across time, through conversation, and within creative practices. Throughout a co- design project with five improvisational jazz artists, including co -design conversations and performances, artists drew on identity-relevant experiences to reflect on their distinct and developing roles as individuals and ensemble members. We focus on how storywork (Archibald, 2008) shapes artists’ and researchers’ participation in improvised modes of creative activity including art making, music making, and analytic processes. We understand identity as one’s sense of self and the roles they embody in relation to others. From this perspective identities are always in a process of becoming, as individuals participate in and explore the roles that are available to them within communities of practice ( Nasir & Cooks, 2009) . Learning alongside collaborators, we also understand identity as connected to the creation of an expressive multi -modal language that is rooted in experiences and places. papers.title: Epistemic Practices, Emotion, and Belonging in a Right-Wing Education Podcast
papers.authors: Tanner Vea, Audrey L. Harris, June Jackson
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Political contestation about epistemic worlds is consequential for curriculum and the dignity of youth and educators. We analyze one venue where a right-wing epistemic world about US education is constructed, “The Joyful Warriors Podcast” YouTube podcast by Moms for Liberty. We use discourse and interaction analysis of one episode to understand how epistemic practices, emotion, and ideology combine to produce a view of the world in which medical and education experts are corrupt enemies, children are at -risk from “gender ideology,” and “commonsense” mothers are defenders of their children and the nation. The study has implications for learning sciences research on epistemic engagement and LGBTQ+ learners.

papers.title: Belonging Infrastructure: A Designable Construct for Cultivating Teacher Agency in RPPs
papers.authors: Gregory Benedis-Grab, Alexandra Gendreau Chakarov
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) often rely on boundary infrastructure to explain how collaboration is organized, but this lens overlooks how teacher agency is cultivated. We introduce belonging infrastructure, the designable features of collaboration that legitimize participant contributions and make belonging visible. Evidence from a teacher co -design workshop demonstrates how this construct provides a new lens for intentionally designing partnerships that foster teacher leadership, build district capacity, and expand who feels authorized to teach computer science.

papers.title: Bridging Gaps: Participatory Design as a Tool for Social Justice in Education
papers.authors: Tugce Aldemir, Rogers Kaliisa, Rotem Israel-Fishelson, Nitzan Koren, Emily Oswald, Paulo Blikstein, Danielle P. Espino, Seung B. Lee, Eric R. Hamilton
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This symposium explores how participatory design (PD) can disrupt the "one -size- fits-all" approach by fostering equitable, responsive, and contextually relevant practices in the learning sciences. Leveraging PD to address systemic inequities, the symposium showcases studies that empower immigrant teens as co -designers and learners in crafting experiences for informed civic participation, employ micro-genetic analyses to examine equitable partnerships among diverse stakeholders, explore curriculum co -design in resource-constrained settings to enhance teacher agency, utilise cooperative inquiry for designing inclusive schools for LGBTQIA+ students, and use of participatory design to advance inclusiveness in an international network of informal STEM clubs. This symposium illustrates how PD can change educational spaces and advance the Learning Sciences' commitment to social justice, ethical collaboration, and inclusive practices through case studies, methodological insights, and interactive discussions. Overview and significance Participatory design (PD) is increasingly recognised for its potential to advance equity and inclusion in education. Rooted in collaboration, PD engages learners, educators, researchers, and community members in co -designing learning environments, tools, a nd systems that address diverse experiences and needs. The Learning Sciences community has long emphasised the creation of ethical, inclusive practices that disrupt systemic inequities and foster equitable learning opportunities (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Gomez et al., 2021). However, despite the continued focus on inclusion within the learning sciences, empirical evidence and case studies that highlight how marginalised and underrepresented voices are included remain limited. This symposium aligns with the learning sciences’ commitment to social justice by showcasing how PD can challenge the "one -size-fits-all" approach to education. PD provides a pathway to address systemic challenges such as language barriers, identity affirmation, and power dynamics, creating equitable and contextually relevant educational practices (DiSalvo & DiSalvo, 2014; Hoadley, 2017; Vossoughi, 2020). PD fosters inclusive practices that support all stakeholders, particularly in diverse, resource-constrained settings, by including marginalised voices. The symposium presents five contributions that cover a wide range of educational contexts, including empowering immigrant teens as co-designers and learners in crafting civic engagement experiences, using micro- genetic analysis to explore teacher- stakeholder collaborations in curriculum co- design, designing inclusive schools for LGBTQIA+ youth through Cooperative Inquiry, and how participatory design can advance inclusiveness in an international network of informal STEM clubs. These cases illustrate how PD can adapt to real-world constraints, enhance agency, and create educational spaces aligning with the learning sciences' commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion. Through interactive presentations, participants will engage with empirical, methodological, and theoretical insights, fostering discussions that bridge research and practice. This symposium not only advances the understanding of PD as a tool for social justice but also invites the learning 2365 sciences community to reimagine educational research and design for a more equitable future, echoing calls for ethical and inclusive practices (Gomez et al., 2021; Uttamchandani et al., 2020). Paper 1: Participatory design to promote teen civic engagement Nitzan Koren Abstract: This paper discusses the benefits of Participatory Design for empowering and engaging teens from immigrant backgrounds in informed politics. papers.title: Making Science Ours: Inclusive Discourse, Legitimation, and the Formation of Learning Communities
papers.authors: Esma N. Kahveci, Shakhnoza Kayumova
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study investigates how teachers’ inclusive discourse, particularly the use of the pronoun we, shapes students’ participation, belonging, and identity development in science learning. Grounded in a sociocultural perspective, the analysis examines how language mediates legitimate access to the practices and norms of scientific inquiry. Drawing on c lassroom interactions from a two -week STEAM program with multilingual youth, we show that the teacher’s strategic use of we during moments of uncertainty, procedural error, and conceptual ambiguity reorganized epistemic authority, reframed mistakes as data, and positioned students as co-participants in scientific sense -making. Rather than treating we as inherently inclusive, the findings reveal its pow er as a responsive and situational discursive resource that opens participation when it is most at risk. This work highlights how teachers’ linguistic attunement can transform classroom talk into a form of apprenticeship that cultivates belonging, agency, and authentic engagement in science.

papers.title: Making Sense of Systemic Racism in a High School Biology Classroom: The “Just Genetics” Unit
papers.authors: Dalia Hassan, Ravit Golan Duncan, Rishi Krishnamoorthy, Na'ama Av-Shalom, Mariam Hassan
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Drawing on frameworks for Justice -Centered Pedagogy and Rightful Presence, we designed a genetics unit that engages students with reasoning about racial health disparities in the context of diabetes. The unit focuses on the relationship between past and ongoing structural racial inequities, the resulting non -neutrality o f physical and social environments, and their outcomes for the health of marginalized communities. We provide a design story tracing our design conjecture, how we embodied it in learning activities and artifacts, and the ways in which these were taken up b y high school students in terms of their understanding of the structural aspect of racism. Our findings suggest that while students recognized that racialized groups endure harmful environments, they did not fully grasp how historical and ongoing racism created and reproduces these environments.

papers.title: Broadening the Boundaries of the Learning Sciences: Reclaiming the Territory of Latin American Contributions to Educational Research

papers.abstract: From Mapuche palikantun rhythms in Chile to Uruguayan rural futures, from WhatsApp organizing at the Mexico-US border to Brazilian constructionist reinterpretations— this symposium weaves together studies reimagining the Learning Sciences through Latin American epistemologies. We gather not to import theories from distant academies, but to honor knowledge systems flowering in our territories: mathematical wisdom in Mapuche weaving, learning that unfolds at the Tijuana -San Diego border, resistance enacted through digital practices. Our work traces how communities transform constraints into creativity, how intergenerational memory becomes a pedagogical method, how the periphery generates its own centers of gravity. Through empirical studies spanning Colombia, Ecuador, and beyond, we demonstrate the generative potential of putting Learning Sciences theories in dialogue with Latin American frameworks —where constructionism converses with conscientização, ethnomathematics meets epistemic footprints, and speculation becomes decolonial praxis. Together, we offer distinctive interpretative lenses that expand the field by centering community knowledge and lived experiences situated in Latin America.

papers.title: Telling the Spiders’ Stories: Relationship Building as Essential Infrastructuring for Climate Justice Learning
papers.authors: Helen L. Fitzmaurice, Emily V. Reigh, Chris Jadallah, Michelle Hernandez Romero, Lauren Daus
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: There is growing attention to the need to design climate and environmental learning opportunities that support collective action towards more just futures. In this symposium, we explore the many kinds of connections required for collective work: connecting diverse knowledge traditions and cultural paradigms, connecting histories to futures, and connecting youth and teachers with community-based actors who are advancing environmental justice. We use the metaphor of spiderwebs to describe the networks of knowledges, worldviews, and stakeholders that foster visions of more just futures. Moreover, we draw attention to the work of spiders, referring to the human actors who build and sustain these webs. Our studies explore the complexity of maintaining spiderwebs across disciplinary and institutional boundaries and underscore the relational work needed to address the associated power differentials. We argue that this web-weaving constitutes critical infrastructuring for climate justice teaching, learning, and action, and advocate for recognition and support of this indispensable form of labor. Symposium theme and overview Although climate change has typically been treated as a technical problem in science (e.g., Clark, 2024), there is growing recognition that it is a sociopolitical issue that has been driven by capitalism (Oreskes & Conway, 2010), colonialism ( Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2022), and other forms of environmental racism (Bullard, 1993). As a result, climate change exacerbates inequities that already exist for marginalized communities around the world, who face substantial barriers to protection and recovery. Young people today understand the severity of this issue; more than 85% of young people in the US experience climate anxiety (e.g. , Lewandowski et al., 2024). While there is a need to address climate change and the attendant inequities, teaching that is focused solely on histories of oppression can be disheartening and deepen students’ sense of despair about the future. Recent studies have pointed to the power of collective action to help youth develop a sense of critical hope for the future (Schwartz et al., 2023), an approach to “partnering with purpose” that warrants increased attention in science learning spaces. Through engaging in collective action, students develop their own identities as knowers, visionaries, organizers, and builders who can affect social and environmental change. Rather than framing climate action narrowly in terms of mitigation and adaptation, we echo the stance of Isha Clarke, a youth activist from Oakland who explained, “Climate justice is about completely reimagining the way that we live on the planet ... It is about collective liberation and dismantling systems of oppression in every way that they exist” (Milagro Henriquez, 2021). For models of this kind of work, we look to the “lifeworlds 2387 of Black, Indigenous, and Third World peoples” who have repeatedly survived world -ending events and bring long histories of collective struggle against injustice to “[build] the world anew” (Jadallah et al., 2025, pp. 9–11). By learning from and acting in solidarity with these communities who are again on the frontlines of injustice, we can work together to imagine new social systems. We aim to create opportunities for climate learning that are consequential (Hall & Jurow, 2015; Jurow et al., 2016), meaning that they move beyond the acquisition of knowledge and skills by considering the implications for students' lives. Climate and environmental learning are made consequential through spiderwebs, or constellations of people, institutions , and geographies. These spiderwebs bridge sites of formal learning and spaces of community -based action, fostering collaboration across different worldviews, knowledge -building practices, and timescales in ways that promote social transformation. We also shine a light on the importance of spiders, or the individuals who build and sustain relationships across learning ecologies to foster collective action. Sometimes the spiders are the youth themselves. Other times, the spiders are community organizers, parents, teachers, or school district administrators. Spiders do the complex work of navigating institutional norms, constraints, and power dynamics within and across learning environments, working both within and outside of existing institutional structures. The webs that they construct are dynamic and precarious; they are constantly torn, reattached, mended, and reformed , requiring substantial time, skill, and emotional labor to maintain. We position the spiderwebs describe d across our work as critical infrastructure for climate justice teaching, learning, and research. “Infrastructuring” reflects the activity required to “redesign components, relations, and routines of schools” in order to sustain learning innovations (Penuel, 2019, p. 1). Much of the current work on infrastructuring focuses on aspects of the schooling system, such as national standards, district policies, and instructional practices, as well as the people who enact them, such as teachers and administrators. In contrast, we build on the work of scholars who have suggested that infrastructuring for justice -focused innovation in schools requires the inclusion of a wider range of stakeholders, including those whose voices are not typically heard in formal schooling spaces (e.g., Calabrese Barton & Tan, 2022). Similarly, our papers argue that infrastructuring for climate justice requires designing for the inclusion of the experiences and worldviews of communities on the frontlines of climate change. In this symposium, we explore how climate justice learning can be made consequential by creating spiderwebs that bring diverse stakeholders together to work towards social change. Each paper offers a perspective on building these relational webs. Across papers, we present theoretical tools (paper 2), design principles (paper 3), instructional activities and practices (papers 1 and 4), and relational practices (paper 5). We demonstrate how these approaches support learners in building connections across timescales (papers 1 and 2), knowledge systems (papers 1, 2, 3), and school- and community-based learning sites (papers 3, 4, and 5). In this symposium, we position infrastructuring for climate and environmental justice as an essential aspect of “partnering with purpose.” Collectively, we will consider the extent to which the learning sciences community—as individuals, within institutions, and as a field —contributes to the work of web- building and how we can and should deepen that work. The presentation portion of the symposium will be arranged in three sections: (1) The chairs (Drs. Fitzmaurice and Reigh) will introduce the theme of the symposium, provide an overview of the sessions, and ask audience members to briefly reflect on their own involvement in web building [~7 min]. (2) Each presenter will present their work [~10 min each, 50 min total]. (3) Our discussant Heather Clark, a former high school scie nce teacher and expert in justice- focused climate change education who collaborates deeply with teachers, will synthesize and reflect on findings [10 min]. The remainder of the symposium will be devoted to discussion. Audience members will first discuss a series of questions in small groups and share their responses [~18 min]. Questions include: How should teacher educators and researchers engage in building or supporting networks of relationships across institutions, geographies, and positionalities through their work in the context of climate change or environmental justice? What barriers or supports exist within our own institutions for this work? What p ractices have we developed in our individual work contexts that build just and equitable partnerships? How do we negotiate the tensions related to time scales (the urgency of climate change and the long timescales of justice-focused learning surfaced in our studies) or length scales (the global nature of climate change and the importance of engaging learners in critical pedagogies of place and forming local connections)? Finally, the session chairs will facilitate audience questions for the presenters [~10 min]. 2388 Paper 1: Weaving relational webs across generations and geographies Chris Jadallah, Michelle Hernandez Romero, Lauren Daus Theoretical framework Building climate justice necessitates “looking back to look forward” (Winn & Tottenham, 2025, p. 70), where we weave relational webs that connect past, present, and future and that bring together human beings and the rest of the natural world in ways that recognize our mutually connected destinies (Simpson, 2017). Looking back provides an opportunity to re-member the ancestral knowledge and practices from which we have been dis - membered via colonial histories (wa Thiong’o, 2009), which provide a compass for living in better relation with lands and waters (Takeuchi et al., 2024). We theorize learning as a process of re -membering and weaving relational webs (Jurow et al., 2025; Meixi, 2022). In doing so, we draw on conceptualizations of learning as movement across home, school, and other community settings through which learners weave across these spaces, and across time, to “become conscious historical actors who begin to understand their present and future selves in relation to broader historical forces and spatial architectures” (Gutiérrez, 2020, p. 2). These perspectives support our work to design and study new forms of participation, learning, and relational becoming (Meixi, 2022) that are culturally sustaining and revitalizing (McCarty & Lee, 2014).

papers.title: Exploring Epistemic Affect in Middle School Students’ Peer Critique
papers.authors: Qiuyu Lin, Ravit Golan Duncan, Clark A. Chinn, Ava Lubin, Jinzhi Zhou, Joshua Danish
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Peer critique is a social epistemic practice. Productive engagement in critique requires attention to its affective dynamics. We conducted discourse analysis of two focus groups across two rounds of peer critique. The groups showed different understandings and enactments of epistemic ideals for critique. The negative epistemic affect that emerged signaled differences in students’ epistemic ideals . Yet students strategically managed affect and negotiated epistemic ideals, thereby transforming affective tensions into opportunities for shared understanding.

papers.title: Unveiling Role Dynamics in AR-Based Collaborative Inquiry
papers.authors: Xinyue Jiao, Zifeng Liu
papers.design_stakeholders: Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Augmented Reality (AR) has emerged as a transformative tool in education, offering authentic and interactive environments for collaborative inquiry. However, collaborative interaction among group members in AR-based inquiry, particularly how roles are enacted and exchanged, remains underexplored. This study investigates role interaction patterns in AR - supported collaborative inquiry and analyzes how role dynamics between group members influence learning outcomes. Eighty students working in pairs engaged in AR-based scientific inquiry tasks. Video recordings were coded and analyzed. Cluster analysis shows that three distinct patterns emerged: Balanced, Dominant, and Passive. The Balanced pattern featured reciprocal Question–Respond–Experiment–Share behavioral sequences; Dominant dyads exhibited leader–follower dynamics, while Passive dyads demonstrated minimal engagement and weak regulation. Quantitative results showed that active participation, regardless of balance or dominance , was associated with higher learning outcomes. These findings advance understanding of how role dynamics unfold in immersive learning environments, offering insights for promoting effective collaboration.

papers.authors: Hakeoung Hannah Lee, Gi Woong Choi
papers.design_stakeholders: Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines how informal learning unfolds on a video-sharing social media platform, focusing on interpretive discourse surrounding explanation videos of a music video. Introducing a mixed methods approach, we integrate computational techniques, including topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and regex- based categorization , with qualitative thematic analysis. This approach enables the examination of a large corpus of comments that would be impractical to analyze manually, carried out across three distinct analytic phases. Our findings reveal that users collaboratively construct meaning through questioning, interpreting, speculating, and debating, engaging in discourse that reflects critical, situated learning practices. These comment sections emerge as dynamic, participatory spaces where cultural interpretation and symbolic analysis are actively negotiated. In addition to these insights, the study presents a scalable, transferable method for analyzing large- scale user-generated discourse in inf ormal, digitally mediated learning environments.

Findings show this agency as a hesitant yet protective stance, growing critical consciousness, and action. It emerged through engagement with community epistemologies, relational and cultural anchors, and home-school alliances. We argue that cultivating such agency is essential for advancing climate justice education and community collective thriving.

papers.abstract: Recent scholarship has called for the examination of young people’s identifications in relation to histories of marginalization and oppression, and as part of learning trajectories that are simultaneously social, cultural, and historical. The Rehacer el mundo project is a participatory design project with youth, museum educators, artists, and researchers to engage Latine and other historically marginalized youth and families in developing a youth- professional collaborative art exhibit. The project, located in an urban Latine arts museum, was designed to create opportunities for communities of historically marginalized youth to engage in reimagining public discourse. In this paper, we draw upon notions of artmaking to describe the ways youth from historically marginalized communities engage in identity building as historical actors. Our findings illustrate these metaphors have potential to expand understandings of learning and identity development as an inherently cultural process.

papers.title: This Is How We Write: University Student Voices on Their Collaborative Writing Approaches
papers.authors: Karen Putzeys, Fien De Smedt, Bram De Wever
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students
papers.abstract: This study examines the collaborative writing strategies and work modes employed by university students during collaborative writing tasks. 32 first-year master’s students in educational sciences completed a nine-week collaborative research paper in dyads without specific writing or collaboration guidance. Data were collected through shared Google Docs, logbooks, and semi-structured interviews. The findings indicate that students predominantly utilized horizontal-division writing involving the division of text sections to individual members, often initiated by group single-author writing (i.e., joint text planning). The asynchronous work mode was most frequently used, but students alternated these with face-to-face interactions, particularly near deadlines. These findings suggest that students balance independent and collaborative work, raising implications for designing interventions and exploring how collaboration impacts learning outcomes and text quality.

Participatory agency measured using degree centrality each of PDM. Furthermore, thematic analysis of student activity reflections used to assess transformative agency. Results indicated that student participatory agency increased during PDM activities. Additionally, students demonstrated transformative agency by identifying the strengths, weaknesses, and areas for improvement the PDM. A correlation between participatory and transformative agency also found. The implications of the findings for the further development of PDM are discussed.

papers.authors: Mrinalini Mattoo, Renato Carvalho, James D. Slotta, Preeti Raman

papers.abstract: This paper discuss the recent developments of a Critical Action Learning Exchange with a K-12 school in India. Briefly examining a Participatory Action Research (PAR) project curricula where a pair of local teachers designed a community-engaged learning project about fibre and fabrics. This PAR curriculum was cross-analyzed in relation to the CALE framework, teacher and student reflections, and cultural aspects. Future directions and implications of the project are also discussed.

papers.title: Freeze Framing: A Socio-Spatial Approach for Capturing Out-of-School Time Engagement
papers.authors: Peri Green, Nichole Pinkard
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Out-of-school time (OST) landscapes offer critical opportunities for youth to explore interests, build agency, and develop socio-spatial connections that traditional schooling often overlooks. However, inequities in mobility, resource distribution, and access to OST opportunities persist, limiting youth engagement in these spaces. This study introduces Freeze Framing, an iterative activity system that employs Freeze Frame, its eponymous geocapture app enabling youth to document and reflect on their OST experiences. Grounded in Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) and Expansive Learning, Freeze Framing is designed to reveal socio-spatial patterns of youth engagement and foster agency in navigating OST landscapes. Through spatial mapping, thematic coding, and activity system analysis, findings highlight the tensions and contradictions shaping youth participation, such as mobility constraints and social influence. By addressing these dynamics, Freeze Framing offers a promising model for how designing youth-driven activity systems can reveal socio-spatial inequities and inform the design of more equitable and accessible OST opportunities.

papers.title: Developing Active Learning Pedagogy in Teacher Candidates: Bridging Theory to Future Practice
papers.authors: Garrick Burron, Alexandre Cavalcante, James D. Slotta
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: This study explores active learning pedagogies in a Secondary-Level Math Pedagogy course at a large teacher’s training faculty in Canada. Using the ICAP Framework, the research presents various active learning activities to develop teacher candidates' (TCs) active learning pedagogy. Observations and interviews reveal that smaller activities, such as problem-solving on whiteboards and mind-mapping, effectively engage TCs. Larger activities, like a Collatz Conjecture Representation activity, create authentic mathematical problems that provide deep, interactive, and domain-specific active learning experiences. The study suggests that simple, adaptable activities can significantly prepare TCs for implementing active learning in their future classrooms.

papers.title: From Accommodation to Inclusive Play: A Culturally Sustaining Design Approach to Play and Learning
papers.authors: Isabella T. Seccia, Kelsyann Cervera, Diana Romano, Victoria V. Hays, Jessica Blake-West, Marina Bers, Leiny Garcia, Jennifer Cross, Chris Rogers, Andres Bustamante, June Ahn

papers.abstract: This project moves beyond accommodation for individuals with disabilities toward true inclusion in learning spaces. In collaboration with a community organization and public school district, we employed participatory design to transform playgrounds into inclusive computational thinking environments for kindergarteners. We shifted from accommodation-focused design to centering the experiences of learners with disabilities. These vignettes highlight how culturally sustaining design can empower marginalized communities, extend design paradigms, and create equitable educational environments that serve all children through inclusive play.

papers.title: Leveraging Simulations in Higher Education to Transform Learning and Professional Practice
papers.authors: Anu Kajamaa, Hanni Muukkonen, Camilla Wiig, Riikka Hofmann, Ruby Woodward, Gerry Gormley, Sarah O’Hare, Richard Conn, Roger Säljö
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Undergraduate / Graduate Students
papers.abstract: Despite the growing popularity and educational potential of simulation-based learning, a notable research gap exists in understanding the role of theoretical frameworks and research-based analytical models in facilitating learning through simulation in the context of work. This gap is critical as the complexity of organizational systems increases, necessitating a comprehensive understanding of how in situ simulation can drive individual, collective and interdisciplinary learning. To address this gap, this symposium presents studies on in situ simulation in higher education settings, focusing on sociocultural studies that support practice change, collective learning and the development of the simulation participants' transformative agency. Understanding the simulation participants as active transformative agents or world-makers of the future is essential for developing effective in situ simulation interventions that can enhance high-quality education and promote students’ learning.

papers.title: Data Reels: An Analytic Approach to Creating Data Stories in Video Analysis
papers.authors: Amy Stornaiuolo, Rabani Garg
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the data reel as an analytic approach to working with video data. Like social media reels in which users curate and layer together multimodal content, data reels are short, annotated texts that stitch together video and other multimodal clips to ‘story’ the data. This paper describes how data reels emerged as an analytic approach in a design-research study about youth writing with generative AI. In illustrating how youth writers developed strategies to ensure their writerly voices were not overpowered by AI, we sought to use the methods of the medium to create data stories with screen capture video and other multimodal data collected at different points in time. We found that data reels served as a form of multimodal analysis that made researchers' interpretive work visible and opened space for sense-making with significant (often overwhelming) amounts of video data.

papers.title: Constructions of Feasibility within Expansive Designs for Justice with Communities
papers.authors: Michael Alan Chang, Antti Rajala, Thomas M. Philip, Arturo Cortez, Mia Shaw, Jarmo Lehtinen, Ilona Taimela, Jorge Eduardo Garcia, Aditya Vishwanath, Roy Pea, Nicole Mirra
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Design-based research (DBR) has served as an important methodological building block for researchers interested in working with communities to envision equitable possibilities for learning, particularly ones that differ from the status quo. Especially within these expansive design contexts, feasibility is a thorny issue precisely because it has historically been leveraged as a rigid, objective means to delimit what is possible in the world as it is, as opposed to what it could be. At the same time, we cannot ignore issues of feasibility if our goal is to realize expansive designs in real learning environments. This symposium brings together five papers across different phases of DBR and collectively illustrate a conception of feasibility that is dynamic, contextual, and contested. We design this symposium specifically to engage the learning sciences community about how such conceptions of feasibility can open up expansive possibilities for design.

papers.title: Exploring eSports as a Learning Space for Identity, Community, and Ethical Engagement
papers.authors: Somi Lee
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students
papers.abstract: This study is about how eSports, a global phenomenon in organized, competitive video gaming, serves as a dynamic learning platform for university students. Through identity exploration, community building, and ethical engagement, students developed critical skills such as teamwork, resilience, and digital citizenship. Over six weeks, 109 students participated in gameplay, written reflections, class discussions, and follow-up interviews that offered deeper insight into their experiences. The analysis is grounded in sociocultural learning theory, affinity spaces, and digital self-representation. Findings position eSports as a valuable educational tool that bridges formal education and digital culture, supporting personal growth and meaningful social connections.

papers.title: From the Dominance of Authorities to Residents’ Inclusion to Decision-Making Processes
papers.authors: Virpi Lund
papers.design_stakeholders: Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study aims to investigate the collaboration of civil society and municipal administration in the systematic change process of a neighborhood. Five community workshops were conducted in the City of Espoo, Finland. The method of community workshop provided a structure for examining a complex urban situation and facilitated collective problem-solving. The methodology of cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) enabled to identify the expansive learning actions and follow the transformation of the object of activity during the workshop process. The study shows that the expansive learning actions helped the residents and civil servants collectively resolve contradictions. This in turn enabled them to see the developmental potential of their activities and take actions to transform them. This study reveals a learning process in the context of urban development by addressing contradictions as valuable resources for learning and development.

papers.title: How Do Researchers and Teachers Co-Design Computational Thinking Education? A Synergistic Approach for Professional Learning
papers.authors: Zhichun Liu, Xuechun Shi, Kun Wang, Ruohan Liu
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper examines the dynamics of a researcher-teacher partnership in co-designing computational thinking (CT) learning experiences for young children. While CT integration in early childhood education has gained increasing attention, the gap between theoretical frameworks and practical implementation remains a significant challenge. Through the lens of co-design in professional learning, we analyze the synergistic effort between researchers and a teacher during a five-day summer program involving 14 children (ages 4-12) in eastern China. Our findings reveal distinct patterns of engagement among different stakeholders, highlighting the complementary nature of theoretical and practical expertise in the co-design practices. The insights contribute to our understanding of effective professional learning experiences for CT education and offer practical implications for scaling similar initiatives in diverse cultural contexts.

papers.authors: Matthew Li, Aimee Chen, Qingna Jin

Findings indicate that through collaborative activities, students developed their knowledge about climate change-related topics and strategies for critically evaluating digital information, demonstrating increased empowerment and engagement.

papers.title: Play Across Disciplines, Across Ages: What is Lost Without Play?
papers.authors: Alice Anderson, Cassie J. Brownell, Joshua Danish, Melissa Gresalfi, Madison Knowe, Adam V. Maltese, Amy Parks, Kelli Paul, Lauren Penney, Zach Ryan, Amber Simpson, Jon M. Wargo
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This symposium asks one central question: what is missing when we don’t make room for play? The papers in this symposium foreground play and examine its role across diverse disciplinary contexts (math, literacy, and science), and across the lifespan (from five-year-olds to practicing teachers). Together, we consider the potential for play in supporting disciplinary learning as well as student autonomy and agency and make a case for why the disappearance of play is about more than a loss of simple fun.

papers.title: Exploring the Design of Pedagogical Agent Roles in Collaborative STEM+C Learning
papers.authors: Clayton Cohn, Joyce Horn Fonteles, Caitlin Snyder, Namrata Srivastava, Ashwin T. S., Desmond Campbell, Justin Montenegro, Gautam Biswas
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper explores the design of two types of pedagogical agents—teaching and peer—in a collaborative STEM+C learning environment, C2STEM, where high school students learn physics (kinematics) and computing by building computational models that simulate the motion of objects. Through in-depth case study interviews with teachers and students, we identify role-based features for these agents to support collaborative learning in open-ended STEM+C learning environments. We propose twelve design principles—four for teaching agents, four for peer agents, and four shared by both—contributing to foundational guidelines for developing agents that enhance collaborative learning through computational modeling.

papers.title: Learning on the Move: Ljavek’s Indigenous Mobilities and Relationalities in Taiwan’s Urban Spaces
papers.authors: Yang-Hsun Susan Hou
papers.design_stakeholders: Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This project centers the intergenerational teaching and learning practices necessary within Indigenous sovereignties during forced and coerced relocation and displacement, collaborating with Ljavek, a Paiwan Indigenous community in Taiwan. Globally, Indigenous mobilities are shaped by ongoing settler colonialism that perpetuates Indigenous erasure and elimination, but Indigenous mobilities are also informed by Indigenous agency, self-determination, and survivance that re-makes relational structures to ensure the flourishing of communities, lands, and waters. Displaced by urban expansion, Ljavek resisted relocation through legal trials, built a Paiwan community on lands and waters that they were not familiar with, and created kinships that subverted capitalistic pressures and perpetuated Paiwan languages and cultural practices. By working alongside Ljavek and informed by Indigenous Research Methodologies and Participatory Action Research, this qualitative research project expands definitions of where learning takes place and what constitutes learning by focusing on learning in resistance, community building, partnerships, and placemaking.

papers.title: Design Future(s) Collective: New Directions for Educational Design Research
papers.authors: Anna Keune, Eve Manz, Christina Siry, Jasmine Y., Jennifer Rowsell, Kathrin Dörfler, Kristiina Kumpulainen, Kylie Peppler, Meike Schalk, Naomi Thompson, Pierluigi D’Acunto, Sara Wilmes, Susan Jurow
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Advancing new directions in design research is crucial, especially as our understanding of learning is confronted by novel semi-autonomous and AI technologies, social phenomena, and global environmental crises. This symposium seeks to advance a vision for the future(s) of educational design research and consider questions that rupture core assumptions about design in the learning sciences. These include who and what design agents are, how sustainability can become core to educational design, and how design processes and responsibilities can shift considering new design purposes and partners. The papers present four contributions to design research, allowing us to explore: (1) Commitments and groundings for design, (2) lifecycle approaches made visible when materials are treated as contributors, (3) the importance of new co-analysis approaches, and (4) the unfinished and unexpected nature of educational design.

papers.title: Research-Practice Partnership Fostering Educational Change – Case: Digital Citizenship Competencies Roadmap
papers.authors: Milja Mäntynen, Tiina Korhonen, Netta Tiippana, Hanna Reinius
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This practice-oriented paper seeks to examine the role of Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) in promoting educational improvement in the digital era. The RPP co-development project described here aimed to bridge the gap between research and practice by providing school practitioners with research-informed knowledge while simultaneously offering researchers insights into practical development processes. The study focuses on a case school participating in the RPP co-development project to enhance its development initiatives through additional support in the form of knowledge and resources. The university partner played a pivotal role by supplying research-based knowledge, resources for data collection and analysis, and ongoing mentoring throughout the iterative co-development cycle. This two-year collaboration resulted in significant structural and pedagogical advancements within the school, as well as substantial professional growth for participating teachers. Key areas of development included enhancing home-school collaboration, effectively utilizing digital tools for internal communication, and fostering students’ well-being and sense of belonging.

papers.title: Centering Community-Rooted Actions of Hope: Beyond Knowledge Monoculture
papers.authors: Miwa A. Takeuchi, Deborah Dutta, Fernanda Coelho Liberali, Tyrell Anderson, Racquel Banazsak, Michael Bakal, Michael Cole, Moises Esteban-Guitart, Lisa Ghost, Kris D. Gutiérrez, Shakhnoza Kayumova, Meixi, Erma Mujic, Samira Mukherjee, Preeti Patil, Antti Rajala, George Spears, Darci Ann Sigana
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Our symposium is a confluence of researchers/pedagogues/designers/practitioners who embrace porousness of these identity categories, toward collectively questioning and challenging knowledge and environmental monoculture (Shiva, 1993). We recognize the resurgence of endangered ways of knowing and ways of living as a necessary intervention to environmental destruction and coloniality. While facing the overwhelming devastation of environmental degradation and repercussions from globalization and colonialism, we refuse to cede with ontological negation (Bang, 2020). Instead, we together seek to ground ourselves in community-rooted praxis and pedagogy of hope (Freire, 1992; Gutiérrez, 2016). We collectively present locally and globally relevant socio-environmental issues that arose from communities beyond academic siloes. Together, we highlight community-based actions of hope representing diverse geographical localities and histories. Collectively, we gesture toward knowledge polyculture that is life affirming and orients us toward plural alternative visions of multi-species flourishing.

papers.title: Empowering Youth as Researchers: A Case Study of Community-based Participatory Action Research at the Downtown Boxing Gym
papers.authors: Shahnaz Safitri, Viviana Piceno, Tugce Karatas, Yiheng Zhou, Amanda Case, Nielsen Pereira
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This paper explores an approach to mentoring youth researchers for a community-based participatory research project and the impact of that approach on the youth researchers. The paper highlights the importance of providing both training and continued support after training to ensure youth researchers feel empowered as members of the research team and have opportunities to develop transferable skills like communication, critical thinking, and ownership. In examining the impact of the training, findings revealed the youth gained practical research experience, as well as developed a deeper understanding of interview techniques and ethical considerations. The project emphasized the value of youth-led research in amplifying underrepresented voices and offering young people a platform to actively engage in decision-making processes. Ultimately, the study concludes that equipping young people with research skills, alongside ongoing support, profoundly impacts their personal growth and enables meaningful contributions to their communities.

papers.title: Meaningful Automated Feedback? Balancing Tensions in Participatory Learning Analytics Design
papers.authors: Susan Harrington, Sonja Klein, Alice Catherine Fratoni, Charlott Sellberg, Oskar Lindwall
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Simulators have become central in professional training, in this case maritime education, where they support the development and assessment of skills and competencies required of competent seafarers. This study aims to inform the design of a learning analytics dashboard utilizing multimodal learning analytics to deliver automated, adaptive feedback to maritime students. Feedback is critical in simulator-based training, yet the characteristics of meaningful automated feedback in professional training remain underexplored. Drawing on a participatory design workshop with maritime students, the study examines tensions arising from the conceptualization of automated feedback. Using cultural historical activity theory, we frame tensions as opportunities for innovation, highlighting the dynamic interplay between students, instructors, and technology. In doing so, we offer insights into designing meaningful automated feedback for simulation training, and the need to balance students’ dual roles as learners and future professionals, reconciling collaborative learning with personalized feedback, and prioritizing educational goals over technological innovation.

papers.title: Desiring Learning in a Hospital School Arts Education Program
papers.authors: Christian Ehret, Ji Yoon Chung
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study analyzes desire as a dynamic force driving learning in a children’s hospital school arts education program. Data come from an ongoing, three-year co-design project addressing a challenge for hospital schools in designing learning opportunities that move students to participate through ongoing social and emotional disruption, and that maintain continuity in students’ sense of themselves as learners. Analysis shows how students’ affective revelations while working collaboratively on a map-based art project are inseparable from the ongoing production of desiring learning that is essential to their elective participation. This conceptualization of affective revelations contributes to learning sciences research theorizing how affect relates to learning and learning ecology design. Drawing on critical design-based research in the learning sciences, the project challenges infirming narratives of children undergoing hospitalization, and it illustrates how coming to feel differently is an essential dimension of coming to know differently while learning in the arts.

papers.title: Being “Someone Actually Doing This” Work: Consequential Learning by Youth Through the Travel of People, Knowledge, and Practices
papers.authors: Vivian Leung, Bodong Chen
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study examines mechanisms of consequential learning by tracing the “travels” of people, knowledge, and practices across contexts. Drawing on sociocultural perspectives, we analyze the experiences of three high school students who engaged in tackling interdisciplinary, data-intensive environmental justice issues. Through qualitative case studies, we explore how travel—both literal and metaphorical—enabled students to connect disciplinary knowledge with real-world problems, navigate tensions between knowledge systems, and develop agency and aspirations. Findings highlight travel as a mechanism that fosters authentic engagement and consequential learning that are transformative for learners. This study advances the consequential learning literature and contributes to equity-oriented educational research by surfacing practical pathways for bridging disciplines, communities, and identities, as well as obstacles to making these learning opportunities even more authentic and meaningful.

papers.title: “I Am an Engineering Person, I Just Don’t Call It That”: Rural Library Professionals’ Engineering Identities-in-Practice
papers.authors: Soo Hyeon Kim, Gi Woong Choi, Ju Hui Kang, Mansi Kasar
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Educators’ self-perception as individuals who could engineer influences their motivation and support they provide during engineering learning. This study examines ways to support engineering identity development of library professionals and position them as educators for children’s engineering learning. Drawing from the theory of identities-in-practice and the concept of boundary crossing, this study conducts a case study to investigate how rural library professionals developed traces of emerging engineering identity. By examining nine library professionals’ engagement over two years in a three-year project to co-design and facilitate an online engineering program for children and their parents, this study contributes to the understanding of how public library professionals perform boundary crossing practices to position themselves as engineering learners and educators. The study further illuminates the potential of public libraries to serve as transformative spaces for engineering engagement and encourages public libraries to redefine library professionals’ roles.

papers.title: Doors, Decisions, and Discovery: An Interactive Smart Door Lock System to Promote Children’s Understanding of AI Classification
papers.authors: Aayushi Dangol, Robert Wolfe, Rotem Landesman, Jason C. Yip, Julie A. Kientz
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children
papers.abstract: Understanding AI’s decision-making process is essential for children as they navigate a world increasingly influenced by AI-driven technologies. Despite frequently interacting with AI-powered systems, children often have limited knowledge about how these systems make classification decisions. We present AI-Smartlock, an educational platform designed to teach young learners about the various parameters that influence AI classification, including classification rules, confidence scores, and decision thresholds. Through image classification tasks that simulate a smart door lock, children can interactively explore these parameters. This paper describes how we designed the system and our results from a participatory design session with a group of seven children (ages 7-12).

papers.title: Equity-Logics for Designing New Activity Systems Toward Rightful Familial Presence in Middle School STEM
papers.authors: Angela Calabrese Barton, Edna Tan, Wisam Sedawi
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Minoritized parents have historically been sidelined in parent-school engagement opportunities. Research-practice-partnerships (RPP) have been one way to bring together stakeholders across communities in collective sense-making. We explore the design and enactment of a new activity system where minoritized parents, their middle school children and science teacher and researchers, engaged in the FamJam RPP, to co-design and enact engineering curriculum that centers community and seeds rightful familial presence in middle school STEM. Guided by frameworks of rightful presence, RPPs for learning at the boundaries, and cultural historical activity theory, the findings highlight new possibilities for family engagement through considering the underlying logics of equity. These include spatial and temporal equity, solidarity for equitable collaboration, collective responsibility for justice-oriented STEM, and fostering STEM for thriving and democratic citizenry. The study explores how these equity-focused logics can disrupt and transform systemic injustices in educational practices through new modes of relationalities and role/boundary mediation.
