papers.title: Leveraging Architectural Visualization and AI Design Tools to Enhance the design of Active Learning Curriculum
papers.authors: Chenxuan Meng, James D. Slotta
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: Higher education is experiencing an increase in the use of Active Learning Classrooms (ALCs), which present educators with the challenge of utilizing the spatial and technological resources of these spaces effectively to foster dynamic, student-centered learning. Traditional tools often fail to provide practical and flexible strategies to optimize the use of ALC spaces. To fill this gap, this paper presents the Intelligent Design Environment for Active Learning (IDEAL) project, an AI-assisted design environment leveraging two architectural visualization approaches. IDEAL enables educators to rethink and redesign curriculum tailored for ALCs by managing hands-on spatial understanding through physical models or interactive scenario planning using a 3D virtual environment. The project not only inspires innovative curriculum design but also deepens educators’ engagement with ALC resources, fostering collaborative communities for future curriculum development.

papers.title: Community-Wide Infrastructuring: Extending Infrastructure Theories Toward Learning Ecosystems
papers.authors: Wade Berger, Ronni Hayden
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This paper examines community-wide infrastructuring as a framework for fostering equitable learning ecosystems. Motivated by the need to address inequities in access to educational opportunities across learning experiences in a community, we extend prior theories of infrastructuring to community-level contexts. We apply infrastructuring theoretical models to recent work on learning ecosystem mapping and design. This highlights the potential of community-wide infrastructuring to surface invisible infrastructures, identify key social actors, and address systemic barriers. By bridging theoretical concepts with practical considerations, the paper offers a lens for designing learning ecosystems that are locally resonant and collaboratively developed. This work provides an opening for future research on addressing inequities through participatory and sustainable infrastructuring practices.

papers.title: “I Guess It Makes Me Feel Better About Myself”: High-Achievement of Adolescent Girls in Middle School
papers.authors: Bernice d’Anjou, Sophie Derman, Carol Gilligan
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This research explores how high-achieving middle school girls see themselves as learners and how academic performance shapes their sense of self. Aiming to provide a nuanced understanding of the stresses, pressures, and coping strategies these girls experience, the study uses the Listening Guide method, a feminist, qualitative, voice-centered approach to discovery through listening. Data include multiple interviews with 19 high-achieving middle school girls from a large city in the northeastern United States, highlighting four key narratives. The findings contribute to the larger academic discourse on the extreme levels of daily stresses these girls experience and adds novel insights to how it affects their sense of self as learners, the coping mechanisms they adopt, and the impact of rigidly adhering to a high-achieving identity.

papers.abstract: This study examines the integration of digitally enhanced indoor spaces and outdoor natural environments in efforts to support transdisciplinary learning through curatorial public pedagogy. By incorporating biodegradable artworks and digital media, student curators engaged in participatory practices aimed at connecting audiences with art across distinct settings. The findings suggest that blending natural and digital spaces may enhance collaborative learning, audience engagement, and ecological awareness. These efforts aim to contribute to ongoing discussions on inclusive and interdisciplinary educational approaches within curatorial practices.

papers.title: Instructional Principles for Inclusive AI in K-12 Education
papers.authors: Hyejeong Lee, Hyojung Kim, Wei Yan
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: As AI becomes prevalent in education, it offers transformative opportunities but also risks widening inequalities, particularly for underserved students. This study explores instructional strategies and design considerations for fostering inclusive participation in AI and technology through a scoping review. After applying screening criteria, 17 articles were analyzed, revealing five main themes and 14 pedagogical principles. These findings provide valuable insights for educators and researchers in developing inclusive and equitable AI curricula.

papers.title: Non-Disruptive Teacher Evaluation: From Case Analysis to Key Implementation Processes
papers.authors: Yi Chen, Hanbing Yan
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Reforming teacher evaluation is essential for promoting educational innovation and advancing sustainable development goals. Non-disruptive assessment offers a promising direction by embedding evaluation into everyday teaching practices with minimal interference. Yet, its implementation remains conceptually and practically underdeveloped. This study investigates the theoretical foundations and design principles of non-disruptive teacher evaluation through six representative cases. It identifies three key challenges: (1) technological tools support seamless data capture, but struggle with diagnostic precision; (2) online representations of teaching are expanding, yet fail to reflect critical offline practices; and (3) indicator frameworks are advancing, but linking evidence to competencies remains difficult. In response, we propose a four-step process—unify concepts, clarify standards, establish mappings, and formulate guidelines—to guide system design and support teacher growth through embedded, adaptive evaluation. The framework aims to support professional growth while contributing to more equitable and sustainable education systems.

While teachers felt knowledgeable about HCD, they preferred incorporating individual tools into existing lesson plans rather than creating multi-day lessons.

papers.title: Rapid Testing, Duck Lips, and Tilted Cameras: Youth Everyday Algorithm Auditing Practices with Generative AI Filters
papers.authors: Lauren Vogelstein, Vedya Konda, Deborah Fields, Yasmin Kafai, Luis Morales-Navarro, Danaé Metaxa
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Today’s youth have extensive experience interacting with artificial intelligence and machine learning applications on popular social media platforms, putting youth in a unique position to examine, evaluate, and even challenge these applications. Algorithm auditing is a promising candidate for connecting youth’s everyday practices in using AI applications with more formal scientific literacies (i.e., syncretic designs). In this paper, we analyze high school youth participants’ everyday algorithm auditing practices when interacting with generative AI filters on TikTok, revealing thorough and extensive examinations, with youth rapidly testing filters with sophisticated camera variations and facial manipulations to identify filter limitations. In the discussion, we address how these findings can provide a foundation for developing designs that bring together everyday and more formal algorithm auditing.

papers.title: Co-Designing and Teaching Science in Students’ Heritage Language
papers.authors: Ana Bañuelos, April Valdez Garcia, Perla Ramos Carranza, Alejandra Yep, Jasmine Nation
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Through university-community partnerships (UCPs), educators and practitioners identify practices that leverage students’ assets to enhance science learning. We study Nuestra Ciencia, a UCP where undergraduates teach microbiology in Spanish to elementary students in bilingual schools in the United States. We describe how the program’s design transformations impacted elementary and undergraduate students’ perceptions of science, scientists, and their heritage language. Design-based framing enabled ongoing programmatic adjustments while identifying best practices for asset-based science learning. From analyzing 200 pre-post questionnaires, we found elementary students learned microbiology content and felt more like scientists after activities. We also analyzed focus groups with 34 Spanish-speaking undergraduates, revealing three themes related to science identity: using Spanish as a tool, reframing science as relevant, and healing their younger self. We describe how participants’ perceptions of science and science education helped us understand the impact of the program and ways to improve it.

papers.title: Fostering Familial Presence in STEM Education through an Identities-in-Practice Perspective
papers.authors: Wisam Sedawi, Angela Calabrese Barton, Edna Tan
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Supporting parental/familial presence in STEM education requires forging new parent-teacher relationships and epistemologies to bridge home and school. Through the FamJam project, using participatory critical design ethnographic methods, we collaborated with an urban public-school teacher, immigrant students, and their mothers to foster familial rightful presence in a STEM unit focused on engineering for sustainable communities. Our study employs the “Identities-in-Practice” framework to investigate how relationships among mothers, teachers, and students cultivate emerging epistemologies and new social learning practices. Findings reveal how teachers and mothers acted as allies, developing new relations that yielded three powerful practices: 1) fostering porous boundaries in STEM; 2) incubating new epistemologies into STEM; and 3) authoring new identities/positions among teachers, mothers, and students, while disrupting normative perspectives in STEM learning. We argue for recognizing, supporting, and leveraging new relationships among identities-in-practice to expand opportunities for parent engagement and advance justice in STEM learning.

papers.title: Culturally Revitalizing STEAM Learning as a Space for Ecologically Situated Identity Work
papers.authors: Kay E. Ramey, Alicia Velasquez, Kirk Cheyney, Margaret Beck, Marianna Cota, Bianca Schamberger, Zahra Baradaran Shoraka
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study examined the experiences of Indigenous American youth and adults participating in a culturally revitalizing science, technology, engineering, arts, and math (STEAM) learning workshop. Specifically, we examined how this workshop provided space for participants to explore, develop, and express their individual and collective identities through their creation of ribbon skirts and ribbon shirts, incorporating electronics and digital embroidery, and pottery beads painted with locally sourced, earth-based pigments. We analyzed video recordings, interviews, field notes, surveys, and participant-created artifacts, collected as part of a participatory design study. Drawing on situated, sociocultural, and ecological theories of learning, we identified five types of identities expressed and developed through design work during the workshop: individual identities, family identities, tribal identities, Indigenous community identities, and dual or hybrid identities. We also identified aspects of the workshop design, such as intergenerational, community based, and participant-driven learning that supported the exploration and expression of these identities.

papers.title: Routine Care to Build Trust in Co-Research with Young Children
papers.authors: D. Teo Keifert, Andria Gentry, Little Poof, Big Book
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Counter to pejorative representations of children’s competencies, we show young children can lead co-research when they trust adults will follow. Our research team—child, caregiver, university-based members—present interactional, multimodal analysis of video data in a relational learning ecology. We examine the role of talk, gaze, touch, body orientation, and facial expressions in communicating care. We then link patterns of care to the establishment of trust; namely children’s trust that adults will follow. We begin with an opening moment of our seventh visit (roughly 6 months into our partnership) to illustrate trust in action, and then detail a focal child’s showing of a valued artifact as a coordinated display of care and affirmation of the child’s dignity as learner and leader.

papers.title: How Do Libraries, Archives, and Museums Portray Learning? A Discourse Analysis of Mission and Vision Statements
papers.authors: Eileen J. Manchester, Kimberly M. Sheridan
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents
papers.abstract: Approaches to learning in library, archive, and museum (LAM) spaces vary and institutional barriers make it challenging to design connected learning experiences involving more than one type of LAM. To support the design of high-quality educational experiences, this discourse analysis investigates learning in LAMs as portrayed by their mission and vision statements. The analysis reveals that libraries, archives, and museums use similar linguistic strategies to construct rhetorical communities along geographic, disciplinary, and interest-driven lines. Libraries and archives differed from museums in that they positioned themselves as conduits to learning resources rather than as direct providers of learning experiences. Shared elements of organizational discourses around learning present promising starting points for conversation and collaboration.

papers.abstract: The COALESCE framework extends DBIR principles to AI-powered educational technology development, positioning educators as active co-creators. This study evaluates COALESCE through its application in designing an AI-assisted lesson-planning tool. Our findings show how deep educator involvement supports trust, ownership, and domain-specific improvements in AI-generated content. We discuss implications for participatory AI design and offer a replicable model for context-aware, educator-aligned innovation.

Together the papers serve as an invitation and a provocation to unsettle normative colonial knowledge practices within the Learning Sciences. We ask, ‘how might the Learning Sciences rearticulate theories of learning that serve life rather than capital accumulation, and racialized and gendered hierarchy?’

Findings contribute to the growing literature on teachers as boundary spanners and their roles in making educational change sustainable.

papers.authors: Emily Southerton, Daniel Pimentel, Shannon Gallagher

papers.abstract: This study examines youth designers’ insights on the Publication Facts Label (PFL), a tool designed to enhance the evaluation of research articles. Using a Youth Participatory Design Research approach, high school students redesigned the PFL to better meet local needs. Students emphasized features like summative evaluations of trustworthiness (e.g., approval stamps, percentage scores) and simplified access to critical information. We discuss implications for empowering communities to evaluate information while fostering critical literacy skills.

papers.title: The Components to “Make it Your Own”: A Framework to Study Youth Agency via Modification in Science Center Demonstrations
papers.authors: Phebe Chew, Susan LeTourneau
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Science center demonstrations allow science to come alive on the floor through youth facilitators. However, they replicate presentations of epistemic hegemony in science that perpetuate inequitable access and identification with STEM. This paper centers youth agency, as studied through modification of science demonstrations, as a learning process with possible contribution to transforming epistemic practices in out-of-school science. In a science center where youth work as facilitators of science demonstrations, we present a framework for places of agency in science demonstrations: introduction of ideas, session scaffolding and framing, physical environment and materials, and incorporation of audience. We discuss how differences in these categories across cases led to unique affordances and constraints to modification and present implications for the design of facilitative science sessions and professional development for facilitators.

papers.title: Climate Education for Justice: Navigating Geographies, Data, and Agency
papers.authors: Asli Sezen-Barrie, Hosun Kang, Mary K. Stapleton, Kathryn Lanouette, Katie Headrick Taylor, Giulia Tasquier, Wonyong Park, Noemi Waight, Christopher St. Vil, Jennifer Tripp, Fatemeh Mozaffari, Helen L. Fitzmaurice, Jacob C. Barton, Michelle H. Wilkerson, Emily V. Reigh, Gita Dunhill

papers.abstract: This symposium brings together diverse research exploring the intersections of climate change education, social justice, and community empowerment. As climate change increasingly impacts vulnerable populations, the importance of integrating justice-oriented approaches in K-12 education becomes urgent. Studies featured in this symposium investigate how climate education can leverage community strengths, foster empathy through quantitative reasoning, and critique the racialized nature of data to promote environmental justice. Presentations will examine innovative uses of data in teaching, highlighting its role in addressing inequities and engaging students in climate justice advocacy. Key themes include fostering climate agency through cross-disciplinary approaches, rethinking the "natural disaster" narrative to highlight systemic inequalities, and designing professional learning programs to equip educators with tools to navigate climate-related injustices. Together, these studies underscore the need for inclusive, justice-focused climate education that empowers students to engage meaningfully with the climate crisis and advocate for systemic change.

papers.title: Thematic Issues: Three Design Models to Address The Challenge of a New Interdisciplinary Course
papers.authors: Selma Hamdani, Elizabeth S. Charles, Annie-Hélène Samson, Michael Dugdale, Kevin Lenton

papers.abstract: The increasing complexity of societal challenges requires interdisciplinary approaches in education to cultivate critical thinking, adaptability, and a holistic understanding of global issues. In response, the Quebec college system’s Social Science program introduced the Thematic Issues course (TI), a single-instructor course designed to engage students in interdisciplinary inquiry through instructor-selected themes and three prescribed social science disciplines. To navigate the challenges of teaching across disciplines in an unstructured framework, instructors formed a Faculty Learning Community (FLC) to collaboratively refine course design and instructional strategies. This paper examines three TI course models: the serial model, offering compartmentalized insights; the spiral model, promoting cumulative, integrated learning; and the jigsaw model emphasizes collaborative synthesis by combining specialized disciplinary perspectives into a cohesive understanding. By analyzing these models, this practice-centered study highlights the pedagogical affordances and constraints of single-teacher interdisciplinary instruction.

papers.title: Designing a Culturally Grounded Ecology for Mediating Multimodal Literacy Experiences through Parent-Child Technology Interactions
papers.authors: Pierre-Valery Njenji Tchetgen
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: The Urban Griots Playground (UGP) study investigates how culturally grounded, embodied learning environments impact early literacy and socio-emotional development in young children through a family workshop series. Using the researcher-developed Drumball-Alphariddims system—a digital tool integrating rhythmic call-and-response—UGP helped scaffold literacy and social skills in five child-parent dyads over four weeks. Findings suggest that this embodied, rhythmic and multimodal approach stimulated early literacy behaviors and social participation, though younger children struggled with the complexity of the Alphariddim code. The workshops also improved emotional understanding through storytelling and culturally relevant proverbs. While the study highlights the potential of culturally grounded, family-centered music-based interventions (MBI) for at-risk children, limitations such as small sample size and technological constraints call for further refinement and longitudinal research.

papers.title: Research Practice Partnership Model for Non-Western Education Settings: A Case Study from Rural India
papers.authors: Akshay Kedari, Sameer Honwad, Devayani Tirthali, Mukta Kapre, Madhura Kashikar, Abhijit Kapre
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Theories and methods in the Learning Sciences have pointed out that building research-practice partnerships is an impactful pathway to designing equitable learning environments. However, most of the research on building research-practice partnerships is being conducted in Western contexts. In this paper, we describe a research practice partnership model that is being built in rural India. Researchers from Learning Sciences and educators/practitioners who work with a rural school that serves Tribal and Rural students in western India started to work together three years ago to think about how to teach critical thinking and collaboration skills to students from Tribal and rural parts of India. This paper focuses on the process of how the partnership was built and contributes to the theories of design-based implementation research and participatory design research.

papers.title: A World-Making Lens Towards Relational Understandings of Data
papers.authors: Heather Killen, Samuel T. Arnold, Vien Nguyen, Ashley Quiterio, Trang C. Tran, Ashieda McKoy, RaeSheena Kennedy, Iris Tabak
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: World-making has not been commonly considered in data science education. We were inspired to explore how a lens of world-making might deepen and expand our relational understandings of data. We are scholars working in diverse contexts united by a broad interpretation of what data is and can be. By entering a collaborative, sustained dialog, grounded within and across our research projects, we recognized that adopting a world-making lens supported us to envision the now and future more pluralistically and agentically by recognizing the multidimensional, multifaceted world(s) present in our research. Exploring world-making prompted explication and clarification of obscured relations, pointed to bridges across worlds, and surfaced assumptions about worlds. We convene this symposium to share how world-making operated in our work and to invite symposium attendees to take up these approaches in positioning data and data science education in service of greater societal and global goals.

papers.title: Amplifying Teacher Voice in Collaborative Research
papers.authors: April Luehmann, Elizabeth A. van Es, Adma Gama-Krummel, Alison Munzer, Elizabeth Wilson
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Research practice partnerships (RPPs) are a promising approach to transforming educational practice by amplifying the voices of teachers. This approach is especially powerful for disrupting educational inequities by positioning local actors as experts to generate solutions and take action. This cross-case study examines how engaging mathematics and science teachers in collaborative inquiry gave voice to teachers’ experiences as they sought to transform their instruction for equity and justice. Informed by process and practice theory perspectives, we describe how the social arrangement of cowriting supported teacher researchers in generating new concepts and practices for equitable and just instruction. We identify four specific practices - gaining clarity and consensus on equity for STEM instruction, generating representations, thinking through example cases, and cycles of feedback and accountability. Together, these practices enabled teachers to contribute to knowledge generation by advancing theory on instructional practice for justice-oriented practice through experimentation and analysis of teaching practice.

papers.title: “Is There Anyone in This Room Who Wouldn’t Be Counted?” Pedagogy at the Intersection of History, Data Literacy, and Justice
papers.authors: Regina Lisinker, David DeLiema, Cassandra Scharber, Bodong Chen, Mary Voigt
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Data literacy explorations are becoming commonplace across a wide range of school subjects. While disciplinary inquiry with data is relatively new to the history classroom, social justice topics are familiar to the setting. Pedagogical practices at the intersection of history, data literacy, and justice have not been studied in depth. This paper identifies pedagogical practices and reflections that shape justice-oriented, high school U.S. history units that center data literacy. Videos of curriculum design meetings, whole-classroom pedagogy, and post hoc reflections on the curricular units were collected and analyzed. Themes from the units, which center the U.S. Census Act of 1790 and W.E.B. Du Bois’ transformative work in data visualization, highlight historical inquiry with data and the ways in which data can be used for social change toward justice visions.

papers.title: Breaking Silos: Promoting Systems Thinking through Multi-Sector Environmental Education Partnerships
papers.authors: Shaghig Chaparian
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This conceptual paper explores the integration of Systems Thinking (ST) into Environmental Education (EE) to address interconnected socio-environmental challenges, drawing on theories of critical pedagogy, Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), and Situated Learning Theory (SLT). It argues that promoting environmental stewardship necessitates a transdisciplinary and systemic approach beyond fragmented and siloed practices. Using Engeström’s (2009) Activity Theory, the research frames EE programs across public, private, and civil society sectors as activity systems and investigates how their interactions can create new collective activity systems through multi-sector partnerships (MSPs). These partnerships are analyzed through the lens of boundary objects emphasizing collaboration, shared goals, and expansive learning. The paper proposes viewing different sectors that implement EE programs as collective activity systems to facilitate the co-construction of local EE programs that are more systems-thinking oriented approaches.

papers.title: Educating for World-Making in Makerspaces
papers.authors: Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, Camilla Groth, Kaiju Kangas, Sini Davies, Niina Niinimäki, Kati Sormunen, Ingrid Holmboe Høibo, Lovise Søyland, Brynjar Olafsson, Larysa Kolesnyk, Anna Keune
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This symposium gathers the results from several different research projects conducted in maker education in Finland and Norway. Educational makerspaces, in connection to school premises, offer multiple possibilities for students to take part in world-making - quite concretely. The enthusiastic and participatory approach inherited from the maker-movement meets the more static frames of our formal education systems, shaking them up in a good way. When given open-ended design tasks related to real-world problems in the form of projects-based learning, students are encouraged to acknowledge their role in the preferred “futuring” of their own worlds, their personal beliefs and wishes, their home environment, their school or their local neighborhoods. Research results will be presented and discussed by educational researchers, who have studied how maker-centered practices can educate for personal growth, creativity, innovation, citizenship, equity and participatory democracy – all skills and abilities in the important work of world-making for a better future.

papers.title: Toward a Collective Understanding of Designing STEM Learning for Equity and Justice
papers.authors: Symone Gyles, Veronica Cassone McGowan, Elizabeth Starks, Bryan White, Megan Bang, Carrie Tzou
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Due to assumptions of “cultural neutrality,” STEM education has neglected designing for equity and justice, especially in higher education. This study investigates how a group of learning scientists, STEM faculty, and a computer scientist engaged in collective knowledge building to develop a common understanding of designing for equity and justice in STEM. Findings demonstrate how critical readings and discussions supported building a common foundation of what designing for equity and justice means across STEM disciplines.

papers.title: “Yes, And” or “Yes, Let’s Reflect”: Children and Adult Perceptions of Journaling in Cooperative Inquiry Co-design
papers.authors: Elana Blinder, Tamara Clegg, Elizabeth Bonsignore
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Within the learning sciences, reflection is portrayed as an important component of learning. Written reflection, in the form of journaling, has been shown to improve learners’ self-awareness, development, intentionality, and agency; however, it can be difficult to foster in out-of-classroom informal learning contexts. In this paper, we explore how adults and children in one such context—Cooperative Inquiry adult-child co-design teams—conceptualized the goals, opportunities, and challenges associated with reflective journaling. We interviewed six children and eleven adults with Cooperative Inquiry expertise about their perspectives and experiences with journaling in co-design. Our findings indicate tensions between children’s and adults’ perceptions of journaling objectives and practical and ideological challenges that complicated the implementation of journaling routines. Based on these findings, we highlight four opportunities to enhance reflective journaling in co-design and other informal learning contexts.

papers.title: Youth as Designers of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Technologies: What Do We Know About the Opportunities and Challenges of K-12 Students Creating Their Own Applications?
papers.authors: Yasmin Kafai, R. Benjamin Shapiro, Franz Jetzinger, Tilman Michaeli, Matti Tedre, Henriikka Vartiainen, Netta Iivari, Line Have Musaeus, Ole Sejer Iversen, Safinah Ali, Herminio Bodon, Meg Butler, Khushbu Kshirsagar, Michael Smith, Ashley Quiterio, Marcelo Worsley, Vishesh Kumar, Luis Morales-Navarro, Daniel Noh, Roy Pea, Thomas M. Philip
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Over the past decade there has been exponential growth in artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) applications moving out of the lab and into the world, impacting everyday lives. To date, most AI/ML and learning research efforts have centered learners as recipients of instruction from, or collaborators with, AI agents. This symposium brings together a group of scholars who will discuss how learners and teachers can engage with AI/ML technologies as creative resources, or CreateAI. CreateAI refers to the use of AI tools and methods for creative expression, that is, involving students not just in using AI for pre-determined productive ends, but also as creators who can design and build projects with AI/ML.

papers.title: Learning to Serve: Building a Research-Practice Partnership Informed by Ethnic Studies to Improve Higher Education for Asian American and Pacific Islander Students
papers.authors: Ung-Sang Lee, Odorico San Nicolas, Xinghua Wu, Mike Hoa Nguyen, Federick Ngo, Caroline Hong, Amy Wan, Annabelle Park, Soniya Munshi
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Federal Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander Serving Institutions (AANAPISI) funding is intended to serve the racialized needs of Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) students in higher education (HE) in the United States. This requires institutions, and practitioners within them, to learn to move beyond colorblind norms in HE and offer race-conscious programming. We report on how a research-practice partnership (RPP) between an AANAPISI program and a research team organized learning to ensure the AANAPISI program responds to the racialized contexts and needs of AAPI students. We share three core practices in the partnership that organizes learning: building on Asian American and Ethnic Studies, leveraging interdisciplinary expertise, and engaging in multi-level sensemaking.

papers.title: MORF ENA – A Tool for Making MOOC Discussion Forum Data More Accessible for Epistemic Network Analysis
papers.authors: Zhanlan Wei, Xiner Liu, Amanda Barany, Kirk Vanacore, Ryan S. Baker, Stefan Slater, Jade Pratt, Mamta Shah, Michael Mogessie
papers.design_stakeholders: Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: MOOC discussion forum data can help researchers answer questions about learners' engagement, thought processes, and knowledge development. However, this data is often inaccessible due to technical and privacy constraints. We introduce MORF-ENA, an automated tool that enables researchers to conduct Quantitative Ethnographic research using Epistemic Network Analysis on MOOC data without direct access to learner data. Developed through a participatory design approach, MORF-ENA enables researchers to visualize and explore learners' behaviors within discussions. We present the tool's capabilities with an example, examining how learners' engagement with MOOCs changed before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. The results of this design process point toward future directions for the tool's development and use in learning sciences as well as for improving access to learning data.

papers.title: Educational Makerspaces: Embodied Learning for World-Making
papers.authors: Camilla Groth, Lovise Søyland, Larysa Kolesnyk, Ingrid Holmboe Høibo, Brynjar Olafsson
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: How can we educate for worldmaking in makerspaces? In our study on Makerspaces in the Norwegian context we conducted research-practice partnerships in several school-based makers spaces over a period of three years. Through engaging in the teachers and students everyday school life and context, we were able to follow, learn and co-create the events unfolding in them. In this paper we present two learning settings and the understandings that were developed in them. The two settings both pointed at opportunities for worldmaking in relation to personal sense making through material interactions and the role of the environment for equitable engagement and inclusivity. We also saw the importance of having enough time for planning truly meaningful learning experiences that involve open ended embodied exploration of materials and technologies.

papers.title: Queer and Trans Learning: Placemaking, Non/Dominant Imaginaries, and Educational Dignity Towards Resistance
papers.authors: Suraj Uttamchandani, Dylan Paré, Ali R. Blake, Grace A. Chen, Jasmine Y., Joe Curnow, Anny Chen, Erica McNabb, Harper B. Keenan, Rishi Krishnamoorthy, Palak Desai, Ananya Banerjee, Breneil Malcolm, Miwa A. Takeuchi, Son Edworthy, Afoke Oyibocha, Eric Knee, Tanner Vea
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This symposium, presented as a hybrid structured poster session, brings together work that helps us grow queer-trans perspectives within the learning sciences. Contributors examine a variety of spaces that work either with or against LGBTQ+ youth and adults. We think with prior work in the learning sciences and deploy queer theories, designs, methodologies, and axiologies to better understand learning. These papers are united by their engagement with queer people, places, and perspectives to advance understandings of learning in the current political climate. The papers help us understand how communities position LGBTQ+ people, for good or for ill. The studies here highlight how learning can unfold as oppressive or can unfold as joy, resistance, or resilience in the face of oppression. Together, these papers put queerness and learning into conversation to highlight the affordances of queer-trans perspectives for building actionable, equitable, and rigorous theories of learning.

papers.title: From Questions to Impact: Unveiling Teachers' Power to Support Actionable Learning Analytics Design
papers.authors: Nan Wang, Nancy Law
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: With the widespread adoption of e-learning and advances in educational data mining and AI, research publications in learning analytics (LA) have surged in recent years. However, LA has not significantly impacted learning and teaching in authentic educational contexts. As teachers’ uptake of LA depends on whether their pedagogical concerns are addressed, it is important to understand teachers’ LA needs in relation to their learning design contexts. We report on an investigation of the nature of teachers’ LA questions at different levels of design granularity—a learning task, a task sequence, or a course—identified through a systematic review of published empirical LA studies that engage teachers at some stage of the LA research process. The findings show that teachers seek actionable feedback on learning processes and progress. However, available LA often focus on course-level performance or task-level engagement, yet actionable insights need to consider relationships among a sequence of tasks.

papers.title: Co-Creation of Visual Stories: Representing Agency for Mathematics Learning with Forcibly Displaced Students
papers.authors: Shima Dadkhahfard, Miwa A. Takeuchi
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study examines the impact of visual stories co-created with forcibly displaced children to express their agentic possibilities within the school context, particularly in mathematics classrooms. Using participatory co-design processes, six arts-based workshops were designed and facilitated for families to collaboratively illustrate stories of agency, identity, and belonging. Findings, in the form of co-designed visual stories, demonstrate students' use of visual representations to reclaim agency after experiencing forced displacement. The visual stories also highlight educators' roles in facilitating in-school mathematics learning experiences. This research underscores the potential of arts-based co-creation as a tool for children experiencing intersectional oppression to voice their lived experiences.

papers.title: Teachers as Transformational Agents of Change Inside and Outside Classrooms
papers.authors: Thomas M. Philip, Michael Alan Chang, Jayne Everson, Amy J. Ko, McKenna Lane, Catherine Dornfeld Tissenbaum, Joanna Goode, Gayithri Jayathirtha, Gail Chapman, Elizabeth B. Dyer, Bethany Parker, Nafisa Ibrahim, John F. Smith, Enrique Suárez
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This symposium brings together research aimed at better understanding how teachers and educators take on roles such as curriculum co-designers, reflective practitioners, and collaborators, bridging relationships across classroom walls while being transformational agents of change within and outside their classrooms. Each of the contributions considers teachers’ work in relation to culturally responsive and/or critical pedagogies. We frame this work in the context of rising resistance to equity, diversity, and inclusion work, and continued deprofessionalization of teachers through “teacher-proof” approaches to curriculum and technological tool design. In this symposium, we bring together teams that have explored different roles teachers take on, their voices, and experiences, as world-making agents and as learners themselves.

papers.title: Using AI-driven Conversational Agents to Support Student-Led Collaborative Scientific Inquiry
papers.authors: Megan Humburg, Daeun Hong, Mengxi Zhou, Chen Feng, Joshua Danish, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Tianshu Wang, Krista Glazewski, Yeo Jin Kim, Vikram Kumaran, James C. Lester
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students
papers.abstract: This study explores leveraging AI conversational agents for student learning that are responsive to the data privacy concerns and pedagogical needs of public schools. We articulate how our agents are developed and trained, student experiences with and feedback on the agent capabilities, and some of the ethical considerations our team has wrestled with regarding how and why to integrate AI agents into game-based, narrative-centered learning.

papers.title: Design AI for My Community: A Case Study of Collaborative Learning in a Freedom-to-Read Summer Camp
papers.authors: Xiaofei Zhou, Yunfan Gong, Yichen Yu, Yi Zhang, Jeremy Smith, Zhen Bai
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Fostering AI literacy among youth from diverse communities with unique values and challenges is crucial. This requires critical pedagogy and education inclusion that empower students—especially those from marginalized backgrounds—to engage with technology meaningfully and address societal inequities. We developed a summer camp with the theme “Protect the Freedom to READ”. By inviting students to collaboratively design AI for their community, the camp deepened their AI understanding and empowered them to create applications that honor their community’s values. Collaborative AI design developed higher-order thinking skills. Additionally, critical pedagogy played a key role in enabling children to apply AI skills toward innovative, community-focused applications, positioning them as advocates for ethical and inclusive technology.

papers.title: Expansive Learning for Enacting Utopias: Methodological Challenges
papers.authors: Yrjö Engeström, Annalisa Sannino, Ge Wei, José W. Meléndez, Mattia Favaretto, Kris D. Gutiérrez, Marco Pereira Querol
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This symposium brings together leading scholars from four continents to discuss the methodological challenges of fostering and analyzing expansive learning for enacting utopian visions. By drawing on the theoretical framework of cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT), the symposium highlights the new possibilities for interventionist studies of learning opened up when expansive learning examined in activities facing critical societal contradictions and transformations. The contributions presented in this symposium showcase a diverse range of case studies, including community-based initiatives, formative interventions, and social movements. These studies demonstrate how expansive learning can be used to challenge the status quo, enact alternative futures, and create more just and equitable societies.

papers.title: Co-Constructing Research Questions with Informal Practitioners within a Networked Improvement Community
papers.authors: Lauren Penney, Alice Anderson, Amber Simpson, Jonathan Bijur, Desiree Garcia, Adam V. Maltese
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Through a collaboration among six informal learning organizations and a research team across the United States, our goal was to consider how to engage parents, caregivers, and classroom teachers as facilitators of learning with their children when experiencing failure within making activities. In this paper, we describe how we worked together to develop research questions that recognize the complexity of collaborating with organizations that have different ideas, theories of change, and organizational capacity. We further highlight this through sharing the journey of one organization, Creative Reuse Center. We intend for this paper to serve as an example for building partnerships focused on solving problems of practice according to practitioners’ needs rather than researchers’ interests.

papers.authors: Somi Lee, Beaumie Kim
papers.design_stakeholders: Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This project explored how placemaking principles and participatory art can transform dental offices into engaging and collaborative environments. Over four months (May - September, 2014), 15 patients and four dental specialists co-created digital storyboards, building connections and reducing anxiety within the space. By integrating art and storytelling, the initiative enhanced patient engagement and learning. The findings demonstrate how creativity and collaboration can redefine a healthcare space as an inclusive place that fosters a sense of community.

papers.title: Personal Authentic, Expansively Framed, and Culturally Sustaining Cybersecurity and STEM Education
papers.authors: Daniel T. Hickey, Ronald J. Kantor
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; K-12 Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: A 2021 expert consensus study report from the US National Academies of Sciences highlighted personal authenticity to improve computing education. Forming personal connections with new content is consistent with culturally sustaining pedagogy and other asset-based approaches for teaching marginalized learners. This is also consistent with the situative design principles for expansive framing from Randi Engle (1965-2012). The report contrasted personally authentic learning with the more common professionally authentic learning associated with socio-constructivist approaches such as problem-based learning. Our theoretical integration and example curricula use cybersecurity education to illustrate the synergy between personally authentic learning, expansive framing, and culturally relevant pedagogy. We extend Engle’s five explanations of expansive framing to incorporate personal authenticity and culturally relevant pedagogy, all supporting generative learning that transfers readily and widely.

papers.title: Unpacking Paradox in Co-Design
papers.authors: Adam Papendieck, Gavin Tierney, Kevin Nguyen, Nikki James
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Here we examine “paradox,” a particular kind of contradiction inherent in participatory design and co-design. As with any perceived contradiction in human experience, paradoxes may urgently demand resolution, thereby motivating and orienting learning and changemaking through design. However, resolving a paradox involves grappling with an apparent antinomy between equally sound, justified or valued perspectives, processes or solutions. This may drive very rational, inclusive and well-structured co-design processes towards activities and outcomes that may seem irrational, ironically counterproductive and even absurd. We examine examples of paradox in participatory/co-design, showing how participants grapple with paradox in different ways, and how unpacking “paradox in practice” helps us understand (and potentially avoid) undesirable ends. We make the case that attention to paradox is critical for equitable design.

papers.title: Empowering Voices: Promoting Equitable Participation in Student-Inclusive Co-Design Research-Practice Partnerships
papers.authors: Tugce Aldemir, Jooeun Shim, Susan A. Yoon
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study explored equitable participation and collaborative dynamics in a co-design workshop where students were introduced to an established research-practice partnership that focused on designing and refining a STEM-integrated bioinformatics high-school curriculum. We define equitable participation as partners’ equal say in the decisions and balanced contributions to the co-design processes and outcomes. Accordingly, interviews with two teachers and three students who collaborated with researchers to revise the curriculum were analyzed to explore their perceived participation behaviors. The analysis revealed two primary themes: inclusive contributions through mediation and student-influenced teacher autonomy. Results showed that separate groups for students and teachers and mediation strategies facilitated inclusive contributions and influences on the design outcomes. In addition, strategies promoting psychological safety and balancing knowledge asymmetries were identified. The study contributes insights into achieving democratic and inclusive co-design practices, emphasizing the complexity of establishing equity in co-design partnerships.

papers.title: Training an Avatar-Based Conversational AI Chatbot and Investigating the Implementation of Communicative Action Principles
papers.authors: Erum Afzal, Julia Fecke, Lenuta Alboaie, Edith Braun
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: Conversational AI shows promising outcomes in developing essential communicative skills for prospective teachers. However, existing models often lack training in educational and social science theories, like Habermas' communicative action design theory. To bridge this gap, the aim of our research is to train an AI avatar-based system using Knowledge Graph (KG) technology for developing authentic communicative action skillset among early-stage professionals. The first insight into the effectiveness of Conversational AI in developing these skills has been demonstrated in pilot projects through role-play simulations on Avatar-based learning platforms. This synergistic approach aims to generate more authentic and human-like conversations.

papers.title: Impact of Spatial Positioning on Collaborative Small Group Equity
papers.authors: Benjamin Orman, Paul Hutchison
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Using video of collaborative small group work, we focus on three low-participating students in relatively inequitable small groups to develop a better understanding of what contextual features afford and constrain their participation. Several potential features emerged. In this paper, we focus on how students’ spatial positioning impacts in/equitable group dynamics. We propose the concept of a group’s “center of attention” to better understand why certain positioning affords or constrains students’ opportunities to learn. We find these low-participating students’ participation is afforded when their spatial positioning is improved and constrained otherwise. This finding may support more equitable small groups by suggesting strategies to increase the participation of the students who suffer the most from inequity.

papers.title: Teaching Socio-Scientific Argumentation in two Chinese Science Classrooms: A Case Study
papers.authors: Nannan Fan, Minghui Zhu, Sihan Xiao
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Engaging students in socio-scientific argumentation is proven effective for resolving everyday issues, yet its integration and implementation in Chinese science classrooms face challenges due to limited curriculum resources and traditional didactic Confucian pedagogy. To investigate these integration efforts, we collaborated with a Chinese science teacher, analyzing four episodes of her SSI argumentation teaching. We found that the teacher consistently framed SSI argumentation activities as addressing everyday problems and tended to engage students in a more authentic version of science practice along with restricted shared epistemic agency. Our fine-grained analysis on teacher’s discourse moves that facilitated whole-class argumentation revealed four frequently employed categories: setting norms, revoicing, pressing, and summarizing, all contributing to either sustaining or advancing the whole-class argumentation process. Despite challenges, this study provides insights into effective SSI argumentation integration in Chinese science classrooms.

papers.title: Exploring Interest-Driven Data Science Through Participatory Design
papers.authors: Rotem Israel-Fishelson, Peter F. Moon, Daniel Pauw, David Weintrop
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Interest is a powerful catalyst for learning. Cultivating student interest is critical in data science education, where complex concepts and practical skills intersect. This paper explores the use of participatory design as a methodology for applying interest development theory to inform the design of an innovative data science curriculum for high school students. This study presents an analysis of participatory design activities using the Integrated Interest Development for Computing Education Framework (Michalis & Weintrop, 2022), highlighting various operationalizations of interest in data science contexts. By examining the multifaceted dimensions of interest, this work demonstrates how diverse activities provide a context for students to voice their interests. The paper’s findings contribute to the discourse on innovative educational approaches that engage students in data science by aligning with their interests.

papers.title: AI-Human Partnership to Help Students Write Science Explanations
papers.authors: Sadhana Puntambekar, Dana Gnesdilow, Rebecca Passonneau, Chanmin Kim
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a case study of designing AI-human partnerships in a real-world context of science classrooms. We designed a classroom environment where AI technologies, teachers and peers worked synergistically to support students’ writing in science. In addition to an NLP algorithm to automatically assess students’ essays, we also designed (i) feedback that was easier for students to understand; (ii) participatory structures in the classroom focusing on reflection, peer review and discussion, and (iii) scaffolding by teachers to help students understand the feedback. Our results showed that students improved their written explanations, after receiving feedback and engaging in reflection activities. Our case study illustrates that Augmented Intelligence (USDoE, 2023), in which the strengths of AI complement the strengths of teachers and peers, while also overcoming the limitations of each, can provide multiple forms of support to foster learning and teaching.

papers.title: Re-Mapping Possibilities for Educational Justice through Arts-Based Research Methods: A Cross-Field Poster Session
papers.authors: Mia S. Shaw, Ankhi Thakurta, Kalonji Nzinga, Marlene Palomar, Shawn O'Neal, Alexander Williams, Ali R. Blake, Melita Morales, Teyona James-Harris, Melissa Perez, Day Greenberg, Angela Calabrese Barton, Aliyah Brown, Stephanie T. Jones
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This session aims to curate a collection of posters by cross-field scholars who integrate arts-based methods for equity-oriented education research in and beyond the learning sciences. Historically, education research has perpetuated colonial approaches to knowledge production that have harmed non-dominant communities under the guises of “rigor” and “objectivity”. This session will provide attendees with concrete examples of how scholar-artists are using arts-based research methods to 1) unsettle what it is to “know” in education research from diverse locations in the field and 2) pursue humanizing directions alongside historically-marginalized communities. Given educational research’s complicity in perpetrating harm against nondominant communities, this session aims to provide a space at ISLS for attendees to imagine alongside presenters how arts-based methods can be mobilized for justice.

papers.title: Understanding and Promoting Epistemic Growth: Applying the AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks
papers.authors: Clark A. Chinn, Sarit Barzilai, Sharona T. Levy, Ravit Golan Duncan, Na'ama Av-Shalom, Huma Hussain-Abidi, Kyle Hunkar, Qiuyu Lin, Rishi Krishnamoorthy, Edna Tan, Susan A. Yoon, Noora F. Noushad, Zhitong Yang, Christiana Varda, Eleni Kyza, Yuyao Tong, Carol K. K. Chan, Jeffrey A. Greene, Victor M. Deekens, Brain M. Cartiff, Ala Samarapungavan
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This symposium features eight projects that present findings and insights unfolding from the application of the AIR and/or Apt-AIR frameworks—two frameworks addressing the design and analysis of epistemic growth. Through dialogue within and across papers, we highlight the theoretical, methodological, and design advances these frameworks afford, from epistemic scaffolds to epistemic moves, and from social media contexts to classroom communities. We also discuss interfaces with other theoretical frameworks, including knowledge building, rightful presence, and self-regulated learning. This interactive session will promote insights into epistemic growth and how to promote it and into the development and application of frameworks for epistemic growth.

papers.title: Theorizing Mathematics Teacher Noticing for Equity Through Collaborative Design
papers.authors: Ethan Rubin, Elizabeth A. van Es
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Research on equity in teacher noticing indicates the multi-dimensionality of teacher noticing and the sociopolitical awareness teachers employ to disrupt longstanding practices that persistently marginalize students from culturally, racially, and linguistically diverse communities. We draw on participatory design research to emphasize the value of theorizing with teachers, as methodologies that center practitioner expertise provide insight into the unique character of noticing and how it unfolds in local contexts. Informed by this perspective, we collaborated with mathematics teachers to jointly develop a model of noticing for equity rooted in their perspectives and experience. In doing so, we shed light on how noticing for equity is enacted in practice, bridging between theories of noticing and firsthand experiences of noticing and decision making that teachers engage in during instruction.

We report on a formative intervention (Engeström et al., 2014) for a community of teachers in Egypt, and the collective expansive learning they experienced through the process of designing culturally relevant pedagogies centered on 21st-century competencies. This study was conducted as part of the Critical Action Learning Exchange (CALE), an international community of critical educators (Carvalho et al., 2021).

papers.title: Stepping Outside the Ivory Tower: How Can We Implement Multimodal Learning Analytics in Ecological Settings, and Turn Complex Temporal Data Sources into Actionable Insights?
papers.authors: Bertrand Schneider, Richard Davis, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Gautam Biswas, Marcelo Worsley, Nikol Rummel
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: The field of Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) is expanding, allowing researchers to capture rich, fine-grained data on learning processes in a variety of learning environments. High-quality process data can open the door for new insights on how people learn, creative interventions to support them, and build the foundation for personalized learning platforms. There is, however, a growing recognition that there is a lack of ecological implementations in MMLA (Cukurova, Giannakos & Martinez-Maldonado, 2020): the vast majority of projects are lab-based, which limit the generalizability and impact of multimodal sensing in education. This symposium brings together researchers who have used MMLA methods in the wild. The panel will discuss obstacles to the use of multimodal data in real-world settings, share lessons learned from current projects, and propose productive next steps for the field to become more ecologically relevant.

This paper discusses the learning outcomes immigrant youth achieved through community out-of-school learning centered on their contexts. Youth were invited to lead the learning process as design protagonists, which urged educators to serve in multiple roles to support them.

papers.title: A Womanist Analysis of an Asset-Based Anti-Gun Violence Curriculum
papers.authors: Kayla DesPortes, Mia S. Shaw, Bella Afra Boateng, Dejarelle Gaines, Clarisa James
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Researchers collaborated with a social justice organization to co-design a curriculum for elementary and middle school youth to create an interactive map highlighting community assets as an exploration towards how they might combat gun violence. The curriculum was designed around Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD) to engage students in asset mapping for social action. However, the researchers noted a lack of guidance for addressing the systemic underpinnings of gun-violence. In response, the researchers applied a womanist lens—which reflects Black women and women of color’s everyday strategies for ending all forms of oppression—to examine how it might shape reflection and iteration on the curriculum. Analyzing curricular resources and codesign notes, the findings highlight the importance of fostering relationships to redistribute power, center dialogue for engaging in tensions, defining a collective communitarian approach with learners, supporting learners in storying their communities, and engaging in care and wellness as resistance.

papers.title: Applying Syncretic Frameworks in the Learning Sciences
papers.authors: Karis Jones, Scott Storm, Sarah Beck, Cherise McBride, Emily Reigh, Michelle H. Wilkerson, Tatiana Becerra, Enith Lambraño, Lauren Vogelstein, Jasmine Y., Wendy Barrales, Joyce Wu, Felix Wu, Sara Vogel, Sarah Radke, Christopher Hoadley, Laura Ascenzi-Moreno, Kris Gutiérrez
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Syncretism has been proposed as a framework that is valuable for understanding learning. Four papers across a range of formal and informal instructor-led contexts take up concepts from Gutiérrez (2014) like syncretic literacies and syncretic designs for learning in service of shared questions: How can teachers design for syncretic learning in practice? What does it look like to put syncretism in conversation with academic contexts/formal schooling in generative youth-centric ways? Where should the learning sciences go next with respect to syncretic designs for learning?

papers.title: Learning for Every Body: Intersectional Dimensions of Embodied Learning
papers.authors: Sofia Tancredi, Morgan Vickery, Christina Krause, Jessica Benally, Dionne Champion, Foloshadé Solomon, Farha Najah Hussain, Maisie L. Gholson, Jasmine Y., Ananda Marin, Lindsay Lindberg, Brenda Yvonne Lopez, Shivani Davé, Nitasha Mathayas, Selena Steinberg, Megan Humburg, Shirin Vossoughi
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: As embodiment research gains popularity within the learning sciences, this symposium both leverages and critiques embodiment perspectives as they reveal the learning of marginalized students. We highlight the manifold ways in which bodies that do not conform, subscribe, or satisfy the imagined, normative ‘ideal’ standard in educational settings—be they racialized, gendered, disabled, indigenous, multilingual, queer, and/or politicized—construct and are constructed within explicitly embodied learning settings.

papers.title: “We were doing science, not just talking about science”: Embodied Learning and Science Identity Development
papers.authors: Selena Steinberg, Joshua Danish
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: In this paper, we explore the affordances of embodied activities for supporting elementary school students to participate in and develop positive relationships with science. We draw on sociocultural perspectives on identity: viewing identity as dynamic and emerging in interaction between students and their environment. We analyze post interviews in which students reflected on their experiences with and feelings about a ten-day series of embodied science activities, and then focus on three focal students in classroom video to understand how these views may have developed. We found that students both enjoyed and felt competent at the embodied science activities; positive views of science seemed to emerge through: a climate where all students could contribute ideas, expert positionings of students, positive socio-emotional experiences during embodiment, and validating challenges. We argue that foregrounding embodiment can be a valuable way to foster positive science identities.

papers.title: Making Space for Critical Action: Re-visioning Computational Thinking
papers.authors: Preeti Raman, Rubaina Khan, Meera Sharma, Renato Carvalho, Chandan Dasgupta, Aakriti Mahajan, James D. Slotta

papers.abstract: While school makerspaces promise to inspire and excite, the challenge of meaningfully integrating them into schools remains. Guided by a philosophy of praxis that stresses the need for education to interweave theory, action, and reflection to advance positive social change in our communities (Freire, 1970), this paper reports on the co-design of a school space called the Critical Action Learning Lab (CALL) for inclusive making to support computational thinking and critical action through curriculum-informed learning.

papers.title: How does Gender Influence Math Classes?: A case of a Storytelling Activity about Learning Vector
papers.authors: Fuyi Feng, Yilang Zhao
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: In this study, the teacher specifically uses storytelling as a tool for drama-based learning, which offers a space for students to co-construct meaning together. The teacher embeds the storytelling teaching method into a math class for a new educational lens. By collecting classroom data and trying to focus on the students’ understanding and engagement, we explore students’ different perspectives on learning the concept of vectors. Through classroom dialogues and students’ storytelling performances, we aim to figure out the relationships between students’ genders and storytelling activities. This study incorporates learning observation and interviews with three 8th graders.

papers.title: Identification of Different Patterns in Solving Collaborative Jigsaw Puzzle Tasks Using Hidden Markov Models
papers.authors: Qizhi Xu, Zongting Ge, Mengxiao Zhu, Ziwei Dou, Jing Wang
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: To assess learner’s collaborative problem-solving (CPS) skills, it is necessary to identify their behavior patterns in completing collaborative tasks. These patterns are concealed within the collaboration and problem-solving processes, and can only be analyzed through modeling of the detailed process data. This study utilized Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) to analyze 15,767 instances of process data generated by 63 students in an online collaborative jigsaw puzzle task. With the goal of comparing low and high performing teams, we identified three hidden states in the low-scoring group, including Warm-up, Action, and Strategy Execution and Validation states, and four hidden states for the high-scoring group, including the three states for the low-scoring group plus a new Strategy Optimization state. Furthermore, the results showed that even though both groups initiated the task with the Warm-up state, the high-scoring group exhibited more complex transitions between states than the low-scoring group.

papers.title: A Case Study of Activity Structures and Resources that Support Teacher Agency and Leadership in an RPP
papers.authors: Kelly Billings, Marcia C. Linn
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This case study reveals how one teacher’s agency and leadership in a Research Practice Partnership (RPP) impacted the design of a justice-centered science unit. We analyze RPP documents and data, from design meetings, workshop transcripts, observations, and informal co-design conversations, to reveal the ways RPP activity structures helped to support the teachers’ leadership. We report our findings in three illustrative episodes. Episode 1 reveals how the teachers’ longstanding involvement with the RPP empowered him to bring a new unit topic to the collaboration. Episode 2 documents the teachers’ leadership during workshops. Episode 3 reveals how conversations between the teacher and the learning scientist during unit implementation supported the refinement of the unit and reflection on teaching practice.

papers.title: Epistemic Trajectories: Classroom Communities’ Development of Socio-epistemic Disciplinary Norms
papers.authors: Na’ama Y. Av-Shalom
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Science is a social practice involving epistemic engagement with scientific norms, which are established by the scientific through epistemic discourse. Similarly, classroom communities can engage in discourse towards developing socio-epistemic disciplinary (SED) norms: shared norms around what constitute appropriate contributions to science classroom discussions. Using the AIR model of Epistemic Cognition and the Apt-AIR framework, this research presents an analysis of the discourse in a middle school science inquiry intervention to explore how SED norms were negotiated by class communities—i.e., the epistemic trajectories of the norms. The findings highlight two different epistemic trajectories: in one, an SED norm was used and renegotiated throughout the intervention. In the other, the class community was faced with its limited utility and phased it out. This paper furthers our understanding of how science class communities develop norms that inform and are informed by their engagement with authentic scientific practices.

papers.title: Supporting Preservice Teachers’ Responsive Teaching in Artificial Intelligence-integrated Simulations
papers.authors: Nuodi Zhang, Fengfeng Ke, Chih-Pu Dai, Alex Barrett

papers.abstract: This mixed-methods study explored how preservice teachers (PSTs) practiced responsive teaching in an AI-integrated teaching simulation. Twenty PSTs practiced teaching with AI students in virtual world-supported participatory simulations. Data triangulated from dialogue transcripts, observations, and interviews indicated that AI-integrated participatory simulations enabled authentic, analytical, and reflective learning experiences that empowered PSTs to attend to students’ ideas. Moreover, virtual students bring nascent resources as productive beginnings of reasoning that PSTs can build on.

Though care is expansively conceived (care between researchers, between researchers and participants, for collective video viewing), our participation in IA labs will organize our work.

papers.title: The Beauty in Science: Understanding the Role of Art in Youth STEAM Identity Development
papers.authors: Kristy Hill, Carrie D. Allen, D. Teo Keifert
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: In this paper we expand on discussions of STEM identity to make space for including discourse on creativity, art, and making within science spaces and further normalize the use of STEAM (STEM plus Art) in academic discourse, and within science practice. ArtScience provides a space for youth and adults in a STEM project setting to honor the appreciation of aesthetics within science practice and further our understanding of STEAM identity development. We present findings from a participatory design research project involving high school youth and educators working alongside scientists to further their interests in STEM areas.

papers.title: “Driving the Ship” or Laying Buoys: Teachers’ Use of Metaphor for Meaning-Making with Storylines

papers.abstract: Science curricula require new conceptualizations of how teachers relate to their materials. In this study of teacher learning, we analyze an experienced group of practicing Storylines teachers’ use of metaphor to describe the roles and responsibilities of students and teachers in curriculum enactment. We found that every metaphor that teachers used to describe the uses of Storylines curriculum entailed a sort of wayfinding: a destination, a timeframe, a place, a journey, or the students’ or teachers’ respective position in that pursuit. These findings continue to indicate the usefulness of metaphor in foregrounding the central role that students play in NGSS-aligned instruction/materials, as well as the institutional forces that shape how curriculum materials get enacted inside the classroom. This study builds and contributes to current scholarship that aims to support teachers in reconceptualizing their role, relationship to students, and the institution of schooling, in the context of constructivist curricula.
